value.text: Martin County commissioners are asking staff to bring back a proposal for a possible one-year pause on large-scale data center development as they examine the potential effects on the community. The discussion was not originally scheduled for Tuesday’s County Commission meeting, but it followed public comments from residents and others who urged commissioners to act. It’s not the technology that I’m so concerned about at this point, but it’s about the protection of the resources we have here in Florida, said Ann Vander Steal, a resident during public comment. Hyperscale data centers consume an extraordinary amount of energy. They require large cooling systems, occupy hundreds of acres transmission infrastructure, generators, roads, pavements, all this other industrial development into communities that were never designed for this scale of use, said Vander Steal. Majority of Commissioners voted to have a moratorium proposal brought back for formal consideration. I think before Martin County decides whether hyperscale data centers belong here, we need to answer a much more fundamental question: What are we trying to preserve? Because once we answer that, the decision becomes remarkably simple, said Maureen Steels, a resident during public comment. Former gubernatorial candidate and businessman James Fishback was among those who spoke during public comment, raising concerns about possible effects on electricity costs, water supply and nearby property values. We have to ask ourselves, despite all of the drawbacks of data centers, are there really any upsides? Are there upsides to building a data center that we are now being told the internet won’t work because there’s a two-million-square-foot facility built just outside of our neighborhood? Netflix, email, ChatGPT will suddenly shut down unless Martin County residents accept higher electric bills, lower water pressure and lower property values. Commissioners said they want more information before deciding whether to restrict new applications for hyperscale data centers in unincorporated Martin County. What are we going to sacrifice to power this AI intelligence economy? Our water, our farms, our ranches, our electric grid, our quiet communities, our aquifers, our privacy, our children’s quality of life, said Vander Steal. Commissioner Ed Ciampi said the county should study what data centers could mean for the environment, economy and community while allowing residents and experts to weigh in. Commissioner Sarah Heard Vargas said she supports a hard pause while officials continue researching the issue. County staff and the county attorney are expected to return with information about the county’s authority to impose a moratorium, including potential legal questions involving state laws SB 180 and SB 484. During Tuesday night's meeting, the county attorney said the laws create a legal gray area. While SB 180 limits certain local moratoriums, SB 484 i ncludes language encouraging local governments to address data center issues through comprehensive planning and land development regulations. Any proposed ordinance establishing a moratorium would likely require two public hearings. A moratorium is not currently in effect in Martin County, and commissioners have not yet set a date for the proposal to return for a formal vote. People came here and stayed here because this county still has something much of Florida has already lost: a sense of place, and once you destroy that, you can’t get it back, said Steels. This is a developing story.

A Martin County Sheriff’s Office helicopter crew is being credited with spotting a large fire late Sunday night and helping get firefighters to the scene before the flames spread to a nearby home. The MCSO Air One pilot and tactical flight observer were on patrol around 10:30 p.m. when they noticed flames coming from a detached garage along Southwest Martin Highway, according to the sheriff’s office. The crew immediately alerted deputies and Martin County Fire Rescue. Firefighters arrived to find the roughly 1,600-square-foot structure engulfed in flames, with its roof already gone. The sheriff’s office said the fire was threatening the main home on the property. See also: Funnel cloud spotted above Port St. Lucie neighborhood amid tornado warning Crews were able to contain the blaze before it reached the house. The homeowners were not home at the time, according to MCSO. Firefighters found a Class C motorhome and a Jeep inside the structure. The sheriff’s office said the garage and both vehicles were completely destroyed. MCSO praised the Air One crew and responding deputies and firefighters, saying the helicopter crew’s discovery allowed emergency crews to reach the property in time to keep the flames from spreading to the home. Martin County Fire Rescue said the State Fire Marshal was notified. The cause of the fire remains under investigation.

A large law enforcement perimeter is in place in a Palm City neighborhood as deputies search for a hit-and-run suspect who fled on foot Wednesday afternoon. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office is urging residents in the area of SW Rivers End Way and the Windstone community to use extreme caution and do not approach the suspect. See also: One red-light camera ticket led to suspended license, criminal citation for PBC man The suspect is described as a Black man wearing a black shirt with blue writing on the back and black pants. He was last seen running westbound into the Windstone community. Multiple K-9 units and air support have been deployed as deputies continue the search. Anyone who sees the suspect is urged to call 911 immediately. Residents should continue to monitor the Martin County Sheriff’s Office Facebook page for updates.

Lucie City Council is set to hold a public hearing Monday night before voting on a proposed increase to the annual solid waste assessment charged to residential properties. The assessment would rise $14.83 per dwelling unit, from $467.33 to $482.16 for the fiscal year beginning Oct. That works out to about $1.24 more per month. The non-ad valorem assessment pays for solid waste and recycling collection, disposal services, facilities, and related programs. It is collected through property tax bills. City officials said the increase is required under Port St. Lucie’s solid waste franchise agreement with FCC Environmental Service . Public Information Officer Scott Samples said the adjustment reflects inflationary costs for labor, equipment, vehicle maintenance and fuel. This is standard for most solid waste contracts throughout the country, Samples said. The proposed increase arrives after years of frustration over trash service in Port St. The city won a $24 million settlement with Waste Pro over poor service, but residents received a tax credit rather than refund checks. Lucie mayor's race is tied to lingering trash problems Trash collection also became a central issue in this year’s mayoral campaign , with residents and candidates debating the reliability of service and whether the city should restore twice-weekly garbage pickup. Voters are expected to weigh in on that question on the November ballot . The city adopted a preliminary rate resolution in July and mailed notices to affected residential property owners, according to the proposed final rate resolution. Council members will hear public comments and objections before considering the final rate. The proposed $482.16 annual assessment remains below the city’s previously established maximum rate of $513.70. If approved, the new assessment would take effect Oct.

The Miami Dolphins are working against the clock to finalize their 53-man roster ahead of Sunday's 6 p.m. NFL deadline, with the preseason finale against the Atlanta Falcons at Hard Rock Stadium serving as the last opportunity for players to make their case.Head Coach Jeff Hafley addressed his team Tuesday morning as roster decisions loom for more than 30 players currently on one-year contracts.WATCH BELOW: Dolphins race to finalize roster ahead of Sunday's NFL deadline"In a perfect world, yeah, I would, and where we're at with a couple of injuries right now, we've gone back and forth with it. I would say they need to be ready to play," Hafley said.Running back Carlos Washington said the uncertainty is not a distraction."Just come in and compete, don't think about the opportunity, just embrace the opportunity in front of me and try to get better each and every day and push the guys in the room," Washington said.Quarterback Quinn Ewers is locked in a close battle for the backup quarterback spot, but an injury kept him out of last week's preseason matchup against the New York Giants. Ewers, who went through the roster cut process last year, acknowledged the emotional weight of the week."It's tough, man. I went through it last year, and the locker room seems empty the next day after that cut day," Ewers said.Despite being sidelined, Ewers said he remains focused on what he can control."Whenever you injure any body part, it definitely affects how you play. That's just part of football; people battle injuries," Ewers said.The Dolphins carry the youngest roster in the NFL, and that youth showed Tuesday when several offensive miscues led to interceptions during practice. Quarterback Malik Willis stepped in to steady the group, drawing praise from offensive tackle Patrick Paul."I think it was him just showing his leadership. We were having a lull at the start of practice. Just him being a leader and bringing us all in, getting us all on the same page, and taking a deep breath and playing the next play, don't let it have a trickle-down effect, and he did a great job with that," Paul said.The defense had a strong showing Tuesday. The offense will look to respond when the team returns to the practice field Wednesday.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A Vero Beach man is facing multiple charges after deputies say he fled a traffic stop, crashed his vehicle and hid under nearby brush. Christopher John Baptist was pulled over for a minor traffic violation, but deputies say he took off, reaching speeds more than 50 mph over the limit. The pursuit ended when Baptist crashed his vehicle and fled on foot, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office . See also: Callaway, Good Good Golf apologize following outrage over deleted driver commercial Deputies called in K9 Remy, who tracked Baptist to a nearby area and found him hiding under brush. Baptist was taken into custody and faces charges including: Fleeing and eluding at high speed Speeding more than 50 mph over the posted limit Providing false identification Resisting without violence Leaving the scene of a crash Driving with a suspended license Possession of a controlled substance Possession of drug paraphernalia Felony probation violation The sheriff's office shared the arrest as part of its latest enforcement updates. Baptist remains in custody as he faces the charges.

Suspended Palm Beach County Clerk Michael Caruso, who is currently being held without bond in an Orange County Jail, was the subject of a prior child sexual abuse investigation in 2012 that was ultimately cleared as unfounded.WATCH BELOW: Suspended clerk faced 2012 child abuse allegations but no charges filed, documents showCaruso faces charges of kidnapping, lewd or lascivious molestation, lewd or lascivious exhibition, luring or enticing a child, and child abuse causing mental injury in the current case.According to court documents, the charges stem from allegations involving multiple incidents with a child victim spanning nearly a year, including incidents during a family cruise in August 2025. The victim disclosed the abuse during a recorded interview with Orange County law enforcement and has been receiving therapeutic services since April 2026.On Dec. 30, 2012, a Delray Beach police officer responded to a home to assist a Florida Department of Children and Families investigator in reference to alleged sexual abuse of a child, according to a heavily redacted report. The officer met the investigator outside Caruso's residence and was led inside, where the investigator questioned Caruso about the alleged acts of molesting a child. An anonymous caller to DCF had stated that Caruso had been molesting the child for over a year and sleeping in the same bed with the child.According to the incident and investigation report, Caruso was in complete disbelief and was distraught over the allegations. The report said he was unable to talk at times due to being distraught.WATCH WPTV's PREVIOUS REPORT: Could Mike Caruso face death penalty?Caruso was read his Miranda warnings, which he said he understood, and told police said he had on occasion slept in the same bed with the child, but that it usually occurred when he was reading to the child and fell asleep.A person who once lived in the home told police that Caruso had been exhibiting "weird behavior" and that he once told her to get out of the home for no reason, the report said.The child's mother told investigators she had never seen or heard that anyone had ever sexually molested her child.No Child Protection Team interview was conducted, because the child did not disclose any abuse. With no witnesses to corroborate the anonymous caller's allegation, the 2012 case was cleared as unfounded and no charges were ever filed, the report said.Read more of WPTV's related content below:

An EF0 tornado touched down in Port St. Lucie Sunday evening, with maximum estimated wind gusts between 65 and 75 mph. It also moved over the St. Lucie River, where it was seen as a waterspout. According to the National Weather Service, the tornado began at 6:10 p.m. near SE Kitchen Cove Lane and SE Morningside Boulevard, with coordinates 27.253, -80.316. near SE Quay Street and SE Cody Place, with coordinates 27.244, -80.346. The track length of the tornado was 2.1 miles, with a maximum width of 200 yards. The latest: Weather coverage from WPBF 25 News Several WPBF 25 News viewers submitted photos and videos of apparent funnel clouds in the sky from Port St. Lucie, Jensen Beach to Palm City. This is a developing story and will be updated as information becomes available. Interactive radar: South Florida weather coverage from WPBF 25 News

Gail Giustino pleaded no contest Tuesday to two animal abuse charges in what officials call Martin County’s worst animal hoarding case, a case that began with the rescue of more than 100 animals from a property near Hobe Sound. Giustino, a 77-year-old mail carrier, will serve two years of probation and is prohibited from having any contact with animals. A no-contest plea means she did not admit guilt but chose not to fight the charges at trial. Attorney Josh Deckard addressed the sentence outside the Stuart courthouse. “While there was no jail time imposed, my client is required to be on probation for a period of two years … the most important caveat that she has to follow is that she has no contact with any animals,” Deckard said. The judge also ordered Giustino to undergo a mental health evaluation and follow any recommended treatment. Violating probation could mean up to two years in county jail. A total of 108 animals were rescued from the property. Tish Ott, who adopted one of those animals — a dog named Gracie Anne — described the conditions the animals were living in. “No air conditioning, bad ventilation, lots of fecal matter everywhere,” Ott said. WFLX was there when Ott first met Gracie, and Ott has since adopted her, nursing her back to health and documenting every step on Facebook . “When I saw her, she had such a look of hopelessness in her eyes, and the moment that I saw that, I just felt that I needed to step up,” Ott said. “Now she sleeps in my bed, she’s carried around in a snuggle bag 20 hours a day — and as you can see, she’s got hope, and she’s gorgeous.” Ott reflected on what the animals endured. “No animal deserves to ever, ever live in a situation like that,” Ott said. Ron DeSantis on Tuesday ordered flags across the state to be lowered to half-staff following the death of country music icon Dolly Parton.The governor's office said the order follows a directive from the president and applies to U.S. and Florida flags at all state and local government buildings, installations and grounds. The flags will remain at half-staff until sunset Sept. 1.>> RELATED: Dolly Parton's literacy legacy lives on in Palm Beach CountyThe governor’s office released the following statement:"Pursuant to the President’s order and as a mark of respect, I hereby direct the flags of the United States and the State of Florida to be flown at half-staff at all local and state buildings, installations, and grounds throughout the State of Florida until sunset on September 1, 2026."Parton died peacefully Tuesday in Nashville at age 80, according to her publicist. The Tennessee native became one of the most recognizable figures in country music during a career that spanned decades. She wrote hundreds of songs, including "Jolene," "Coat of Many Colors" and "I Will Always Love You," while also building a career in film, business and philanthropy.Parton was also known for founding the Imagination Library, which provides free books to children, and for opening Dollywood in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee.

Republican gubernatorial nominee Byron Donalds selected Miami-Dade state Sen. Bryan Avila as his running mate Tuesday, adding a Cuban-American lawmaker, educator and Florida Army National Guard captain to the GOP ticket.Donalds announced the pick at Miami’s Freedom Tower, a landmark closely tied to South Florida’s Cuban exile community. He framed the partnership around their families’ pursuit of opportunity and a shared commitment to conservative policies.“I came to Florida at 17 years old with a trunk full of clothes, chasing a dream. Bryan Avila is the son of Cuban exiles who fled communism so their children could live in freedom,” Donalds said. “We didn’t inherit political names. We didn’t inherit political birthrights, but what we inherited was the responsibility to fight for the state that gave our families everything.”Avila was born and raised in Hialeah after his parents, Adrian and Rosa Maria Avila, fled Cuba. He now lives in Miami Springs with his wife, Cindy, his high school sweetheart, and their two children.The selection gives Donalds, a Southwest Florida congressman, a running mate with deep political and personal ties to Miami-Dade and its influential Cuban-American community.Avila was first elected to the Florida House in 2014 and eventually rose to speaker pro tempore. He won election to the Senate in 2022 and currently chairs the Finance and Tax Committee.Donalds praised Avila as a “proven warrior,” pointing to his work on property taxes, toll relief, human trafficking, conservation and a new law intended to protect utility customers and water supplies as large-scale data centers expand in Florida.Avila also sponsored the Stop WOKE Act, one of Gov. Ron DeSantis’ signature culture-war measures. The law restricts certain instruction and training involving race, discrimination and privilege in schools and workplaces. Critics called it an attack on free speech, and parts of the law have been blocked by federal courts.Avila used his first speech as Donalds’ running mate to focus on his parents’ experience under communism and draw a contrast with Democrats he accused of embracing socialism.“My parents fled communist Cuba and left behind their home and their business because they knew what happens when government takes over, when freedom disappears and when socialism turns opportunity into misery,” Avila said.“So when I hear Democrats casually embracing socialism, I know where that road leads,” he added. “Our families have lived it. I can assure you this: with Byron Donalds as governor and me as your lieutenant governor, socialism will never find a home in the great state of Florida.”Democratic nominee David Jolly congratulated Avila on the selection but argued the race will remain centered on Donalds’ close political alliance with President Donald Trump.“I wish him well,” Jolly said. “But, let’s be honest: this race won’t come down to Byron Donalds’ relationship with Avila, it will come down to Byron’s relationship with Donald Trump.”Beyond politics, Avila serves as a captain in the Florida Army National Guard. His service has included hurricane response missions, command of military units and support for Florida’s COVID-19 response. He also works as an academic dean at the Doral College School of Criminal Justice.Donalds and Avila will campaign on affordability, lower taxes, public safety, parental rights and school choice. They face Jolly and his running mate, former Democratic Congresswoman Gwen Graham, in the November general election.

Martin County Police Athletic League (PAL) is inviting Jeep owners to take part in a family-friendly scavenger hunt fundraiser supporting youth mentorship, leadership and athletics programs in Martin County.The Martin County PAL Jeep Duck Scavenger Hunt is scheduled for Sept. Participants must complete the scavenger hunt in a Jeep, according to organizers.Registration costs $25 per Jeep, and participants can also purchase a $10 clue sheet that includes hints and a map to help teams navigate the scavenger hunt route.Registration information is available here.Martin County PAL Executive Director Noel DelValle said the nonprofit works closely with children and teens throughout the community through leadership and athletic programming.“Martin County Police Athletic League works with youth in Martin County,” DelValle said. “We work through leadership and athletic programs to develop kids into healthy, productive leaders of the future.”DelValle said the organization also partners with schools and the court system through intervention and diversion programs aimed at helping children stay on a positive path.“Yes, we do a lot of early intervention with kids in the school district and also with the court systems to help keep these kids on the right path to success,” DelValle said.The fundraiser centers around Jeep culture and the popular “ducking” tradition, where Jeep owners exchange decorative rubber ducks as a way to recognize customized vehicles and fellow Jeep enthusiasts.Director of Strategic Growth Meg Shirey said the event has become one of the organization’s signature fundraisers.“Our Jeep Duck Scavenger Hunt is our signature fundraiser,” Shirey said. “It is where our community gets involved, where all of the Jeeps go to local businesses. It’s a family-friendly event.”Shirey said the event helps showcase both local businesses and the nonprofit’s community programs while bringing Jeep owners together from across Martin County.Program Manager Kim Zimmerman said the Jeep community has embraced the fundraiser because of the connection many owners feel toward customizing and celebrating their vehicles.“Jeepers love to celebrate their unique Jeeps by giving other Jeepers ducks,” Zimmerman said. “That’s a way of saying, ‘I appreciate your effort and I love what you do with your Jeep.’”Zimmerman said the scavenger hunt also includes themed awards and unique Jeep duck trophies for participants.“For our Jeep scavenger hunt, we have individual Jeep duck prizes based on different categories, and each duck is given to the most unique Jeep in that category,” Zimmerman said.Organizers said proceeds from the fundraiser directly support programs that provide mentorship opportunities, athletics and leadership development for local children and teens.Martin County PAL’s Jeep Duck Scavenger Hunt is scheduled for Sept. 19 and helps raise money for youth mentorship, diversion and athletics programs. Registration is $25 per Jeep, and participants can also purchase a $10 clue sheet with hints and a map at martincountypal.org.Meet My Star Wars-Themed Jeep, “R2-Jeep-2”If you spotted a blue-and-white Jeep rolling through Palm City during Shining A Light, that was my Jeep Gladiator, “R2-Jeep-2.”I’ve spent a lot of time turning the Jeep into a rolling tribute to “Star Wars,” inspired by the legendary droid R2-D2. Inside the windshield, you’ll spot themed ducks, including Darth Vader, Chewbacca and R2-D2 ducks that my mother-in-law 3D-printed for me.Honestly, this Jeep has become one of my favorite passion projects.“I put a lot of time and a lot of energy into it, and I fail a lot,” I said during the live broadcast. “But then I get it to work eventually.”During the broadcast, Ashley Glass joked that my Jeep is impossible to miss in the WPTV parking lot.“It’s always a standout in the parking lot,” Glass said on-air. “You can’t miss it when T.A. rolls in.”For the record, though, I did have one request during the segment."It's Pretty"“My ‘Star Wars’-themed Jeep — I did not want it ever to be called pretty,” I joked on-air.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Email me at tawalker@wptv.com.

A new housing development in Palm Springs is aiming to give veterans in Palm Beach County more than just a place to live — it's designed to create stability, support and community.Stand Down PBC is building the "Village of Valor," a veteran-focused neighborhood that will include 54 affordable housing units and on-site support services for veterans and their families.Casino NightOn Nov. 7, Stand Down is hosting Casino Night at the Lake Pavilion in West Palm Beach at 6 p.m. Proceeds will fuel their mission.The project is being led by FaithHopeLove Charity Inc., also known as Stand Down, an organization founded by veteran Roy Foster."When I was released from the military in the '80s, for the next five years or so, I just drifted around and around, not realizing that I actually needed some assistance," Foster said.Foster said his experiences after leaving the military inspired him to create Stand Down after realizing how few services were available for veterans transitioning back into civilian life."I went into the VA in Miami in '89, and the realization of what was available to veterans was frightening," Foster said. "It was a situation where this can't continue to go on and on and on."Foster said the aftermath of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks further motivated him to dedicate himself full time to helping veterans."I saw the towers being hit," Foster said. "The realization was, I know what happened after Vietnam — limited services, angry veterans coming home. It couldn't continue."He said the goal now is to empower veterans rather than abandon them.Village of Valor to include affordable housing for veteransJosh Maddock, executive director of Stand Down PBC, said the Village of Valor is designed specifically to address affordable housing needs for veterans in Palm Beach County."The Village of Valor is 54 two- and three-bedroom units for our veterans," Maddock said. "It's 130 bedrooms of affordable housing in Palm Beach County."The community is being built for homeless and nearly homeless veterans and their families. Organizers say the site will also include support resources designed to help veterans build long-term stability.The project has personal meaning for many connected to the organization.Board member Sylvia Meade said seeing her husband struggle after military service showed her how important a resource like this can be."After seeing that my husband went through a moment of crisis after being in the Army, having something like this would have been such an amazing resource," Meade said.Veterans share success stories through Stand DownSeveral veterans who received support through Stand Down said transitional housing and assistance programs helped them rebuild their lives.Ariana Valentin said the organization helped her move from renting to homeownership."I'm now a homeowner from being a renter to now a homeowner," Valentin said. "Stand Down was a great resource for me."Veteran and caregiver James McFadden also credited the nonprofit for helping him achieve homeownership."I finally own my home, my first home in April," McFadden said. "I really appreciate Stand Down for helping me to do that."According to Stand Down, the organization provides more than 10,000 sheltered nights annually through Stand Down House and assists more than 1,000 veterans and family members each year through the First Stop Veterans' Resource Center.Construction on the Village of Valor began in late 2025, and organizers say the project represents a long-term effort to reduce veteran homelessness in Palm Beach County.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Oswaldo Pirela, a San Diego Padres minor league coach who was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement last week, was released from custody, his wife told ABC 10News’ Laura Acevedo.The Athletic reported the 34-year-old father of two was released on bond Monday. A family spokesperson confirmed Pirela is home with his family.The catching coordinator with the Padres’ Triple-A affiliate El Paso Chihuahuas was detained by ICE agents at El Paso International Airport on Aug. Pirela was not carrying his work permit card at the time he was detained, according to The New York Times.RELATED STORY | 5-year-old boy detained in viral Texas video deported to Mexico with fatherPirela's mother, Naivy Dominguez, told Acevedo that her son had an early-morning flight and was heading home to his wife and daughters in Peoria, Arizona, when he was detained.The Times reported Pirela and his family are from Venezuela and have pending asylum applications.In a statement following his detainment, Department of Homeland Security officials said Pirela “entered the country legally on September 10, 2014, and was granted permission by the Obama administration to remain in the country until February 10, 2018. In violation of our nation’s laws, he overstayed his welcome. When approached by law enforcement officers, he was not in possession of legal documentation granting him status in the country.”Scripps News Group's San Diego station reached out to DHS for additional details on Pirela's release, and hours after publication of this story, responded with the following statement: "On August 16, 2026, Border Patrol arrested Oswaldo Jose Pirela Dominguez, an illegal alien from Venezuela, at the El Paso International Airport. He entered the country legally but violated the terms of his admission. When approached by law enforcement officers, he was not in possession of legal documentation granting him status in the country. On August 24, he was released from ICE custody on bond pending his removal proceedings.To be clear, work authorization or a pending application do NOT confer legal status in the United States.RELATED STORY | 'Mom, what did we do?' Parents recall weeks in ICE family detentionBeing in detention is a choice. We encourage all illegal aliens to take control of their departure with the CBP Home App. The United States is offering illegal aliens $2,600 and a free flight to self-deport now. We encourage every person here illegally to take advantage of this offer and reserve the chance to come back to the U.S. the right legal way to live the American dream. If not, you will be arrested and deported without a chance to return."“We are pleased that Oswaldo Pirela has been released on bond and reunited with his family. Out of respect for his privacy and the ongoing matter, we will have no further comment at this time,” the Padres said in a statement to ABC 10News. Pirela has been with the Padres organization since 2024.This story was originally published by Jermaine Ong and Laura Acevedo with the Scripps News Group station in San Diego.

The Miami Dolphins wrapped up training camp Wednesday, just days before their final preseason matchup against the Atlanta Falcons on Friday night.It was a bounce-back day for the offense on the final day of camp, with quarterback Malik Willis connecting on touchdowns with Malik Washington and rookie Caleb Douglas.WATCH BELOW: Dolphins close training camp; roster cuts loom before Falcons game"It's great that camp is coming to an end and football is back," edge rusher Chop Robinson said.Robinson is ready to make his presence felt when the games count and compete against former Dolphins quarterback Tua Tagovailoa."It's going to be fun, especially because in practice we couldn't hit (Tagovailoa). Now it's game time, and I hope I can get close to him. He was a good guy and great teammate, and I wish him the best," Robinson said.While the mood was upbeat Wednesday, some players know Friday's game against Atlanta could be their last with the Dolphins. NFL rosters must be trimmed to the final 53 by Sunday.Wide receiver Jalen Tolbert has shown promising flashes in practice but understands the competition is fierce with the Dolphins' youth movement."My goal is to keep competing and keep going out every day and working hard to earn myself a plate on the menu to be able to be one of the receivers they trust in," Tolbert said. "It's a lot of emotions that come with the game, and I think the main thing is how we use those emotions. Go out there and play with your heart and play for your job."Receiver Tutu Atwell, a Miami native, is also fighting for a spot on the final roster but feels confident in what he's shown during camp."Overall, I feel like I did great, and I'm just going to play to my best ability no matter what, keep working hard, and prove myself," Atwell said.The Dolphins and Falcons are set to kick off at 7 p.m. Watch all the action on WPTV.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

European soccer body UEFA is set to formally withdraw its threat to boycott FIFA competitions after receiving assurances Gianni Infantino's failed World Cup sell-off plan will not be revived.UEFA's member federations are meeting Thursday in Monaco ahead of the Champions League draw, where they are expected to end the boycott threat, a person familiar with the proposal told The Associated Press on Wednesday.The person spoke on condition of anonymity ahead of the closed-doors meeting.RELATED STORY | UEFA maintains demand for FIFA president's resignation, threatens World Cup boycottRuling out a boycott will clear six European teams to continue preparing for the FIFA Under-20 Women's World Cup that kicks off Sept. 5 in Poland.France and Spain named their squads last week for the 24-nation tournament which risked becoming an unwanted battleground in European soccer's pushback against Infantino's private investor plan. England, Italy, Portugal and host Poland also will play.Infantino infuriated soccer leaders worldwide last month when his plan for a $20 billion subsidiary controlling FIFA commercial rights including the World Cup was revealed by British daily The Times. The spinoff was to be 20% owned by investors led by a New York fund created by Joshua Kushner.RELATED STORY | FIFA's Infantino sets deadline to members in Kushner-backed World Cup planThe FIFA president dropped his proposal within four days amid a furious backlash led by UEFA, including the boycott threat, with support from the Asian Football Confederation and North American soccer body CONCACAF. The furor was fueled by criticism of the plan and Infantino from senior FIFA officials.UEFA then said it wanted assurances the spinoff, to be called FIFA Forward Enterprise, would not be presented in a different form. That assurance was now received, the person told the AP.The European soccer body said Aug. 1 it had no confidence in Infantino's leadership in a clear signal it would try to stop his reelection in March next year.FIFA previously set a Nov. 18 deadline for candidates to enter the presidential contest, four months ahead of the vote by 211 member federations in Rabat, Morocco.Infantino had seemed sure to be reelected unopposed for a fourth and final term in office through 2031 until the turmoil created by his investor plan.The 55 UEFA member federations are attending the meeting in Monaco four weeks after they united in an online call to agree the threatened boycott.

Tri-Rail is expanding its registered parking program to stations in Pompano Beach, Boynton Beach and the Lake Worth Beach auxiliary lot.License-plate readers at those stations will enforce the new rules. Gabriel Arrington says he spent three hours believing he was minutes from being arrested on federal warrants. He was on the phone with a scammer. In a Facebook video that's since spread across the Treasure Coast, Arrington describes getting a voicemail from someone claiming to be with the Martin County Sheriff's Office . When he called back, the man on the line told him he had two federal warrants tied to a missed jury summons in a murder case and needed to come in immediately to clear it up. Arrington, a content creator known for videos wrestling alligators and swimming with sharks, said the call still ranks among the most frightening moments of his life. "That dude put the fear of God in me right now," Arrington said. He said thinking of his 16-year-old son is what made him call the blocked number back, and the man who answered used a local 772 area code and identified himself as an officer with the Sheriff's Office. Arrington says the caller kept him on the phone for the entire drive from Central Florida to Martin County, warning him that hanging up would look like he was fleeing. He says the man read back his own personal information without being asked, sent him fake court documents including a warrant and what he was told was a gag order, and told him he'd need to withdraw $32,000 in cash from his bank to post bond once he arrived. Arrington said the caller pinned the warrants to a missed June 8 court date. "I was offshore fishing," Arrington said. "I couldn't sign for anything." The caller told him that proved his point, that he just needed to come in and sign to clear his name. The bond broke down to $16,000 for each of the two warrants, and the caller said he was waiting inside the Sheriff's Office, telling Arrington to check back in every few minutes. "Where am I going to get $32,000 cash on a Saturday morning?" Arrington said. He said the caller grew aggressive when he pushed back, telling him this was standard procedure and that they knew exactly how banks worked. "If I hang up the phone, you're going to think I'm running," Arrington said. "I can't call my parents or my attorney. It was horrifying." "This was the most well-laid-out scam I've ever seen," Arrington said in the video. "He didn't ask me to send the money. He didn't ask me to click on any links. He didn't ask me to do anything other than go to the police station." "I was never going to give him my money," Arrington said. At one point during the drive, he told the caller he had two hunting rifles in his back seat. He said the caller barely reacted, telling him that was fine and he'd make a note of it. Arrington says he only caught on after his fiancée grew suspicious and he noticed a fourth document had been slipped in among the three he'd been told to expect. He hung up and called Martin County dispatch, where he says a 911 operator told him there was no warrant and that the office had already fielded roughly a dozen similar calls that same day. The Martin County Sheriff's Office says Arrington's experience fits a scam that's targeted residents for years and shows no signs of slowing down. In an interview with CBS12, Sheriff John Budensiek said scammers spoof the office's real phone number, use real employees' names pulled from the internet, and lean on the fear of arrest to pressure victims into paying what's framed as a bond before they can be taken into custody. "First and foremost, the Martin County Sheriff's Office or any law enforcement agency is not going to call you and tell you that you have a warrant for your arrest," Budensiek said. "If we're looking for you, we're going to come find you," Budensiek said. Budensiek said the scam has been running for close to a decade and isn't limited to Martin County. He said his office has struggled to track down the people behind it because the calls route through untraceable internet-based phone numbers. In one case, he said, deputies kept a scammer on the line and found he could answer detailed questions about real employees, judges and case numbers, which he said shows how convincing the calls have become. The Sheriff's Office says the impact goes beyond any single case. MCSO confirms Martin County residents have lost at least $6 million to scams of all kinds over the past two years. The calls haven't stopped. Arrington said he's had to freeze his Social Security number and lock down his bank accounts, YouTube channel and Instagram page, after learning the caller also used his brother's and father's names. As of Tuesday, three days after the first call, he said the same operation is still calling. "Same type of voice came on, hey Gabe, is this you? I immediately hung up," Arrington said. He said the number called back three more times and left a voicemail. Budensiek's advice: if a caller says you have a warrant, hang up. Then call the Sheriff's Office back using a number you look up yourself, not one the caller gives you, to confirm whether it's real. Arrington says he wants his story to serve as a warning to anyone who thinks they'd never fall for it. Arrington said he posted the video about 30 minutes after getting back to camp because he makes content for a living and wanted people to hear how scared he sounded. "I made that video hoping to save one person, if not thousands," Arrington said. "You can laugh at me in the comments all you want," Arrington said, "but until you're in my shoes, you will then see how bad it is." Anyone who receives a suspicious call claiming to be from the Sheriff's Office is asked to hang up and contact MCSO directly to verify it before taking any action or sending any money.

Democratic-controlled states on Wednesday filed another lawsuit challenging President Donald Trump’s executive order seeking to limit mail voting in this year's midterm elections.The action, filed by about two dozen states against the U.S. Postal Service, marked a new phase in the high-stakes litigation just two days after the Supreme Court ruled against them in a separate case, but did not say Trump’s order was legal.RELATED STORY | Supreme Court clears the way for Trump mail voting order in advance of midtermsThe high court majority found the Democratic lawsuit was premature, but that was before the Republican administration issued a rule governing U.S. Postal Service delivery of mail ballots. Election officials warn it will be impossible to implement in the days before the first wave of mail ballots are sent out next week.“Across the country, states are already deep into preparations for the 2026 elections. Now, at the last moment, the federal government is attempting to meddle in those preparations and potentially threaten countless Americans’ right to vote,” New York Attorney General Letitia James, one of 25 Democratic attorneys general filing the lawsuit, said in a statement. “USPS has no authority to decide who can and cannot vote by mail.”Trump’s executive order remains barred from taking effect under a separate injunction that the administration argues needs to be immediately rescinded in light of the high court’s ruling in the previous Democratic state lawsuit. It also had succeeded in a third case filed in May in the District of Columbia, convincing a judge that it was too early to prevent its implementation of the executive order.All previous challenges were filed before the administration published its mail ballot rule Friday night. The rule says that if states want their mail ballots delivered, they will need federal approval of the design of their envelopes and must give the Postal Service a list of voters eligible to receive them.National Democrats on Tuesday cited the rule in asking the federal judge in the Washington case to block Trump’s order after he declined to do so last spring, saying the administration at the time had not taken concrete action. District Judge Indira Talwani also found that the administration moving forward with the mail ballot rule had violated a separate injunction she had placed on the Postal Service prohibiting it from enacting Trump’s order, although she did not take any action against the government.IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | USPS proposes rule requiring states to share voter lists for mail-in ballotsTalwani, who was nominated by Democratic President Barack Obama, had issued the injunction against Trump’s executive order in the prior Democratic state case, which is the one the Supreme Court overturned on Monday. She has yet to act on the administration’s urging her to revoke her second injunction. 11 in a case against the executive order and was filed by the League of Women Voters and other voting rights groups while the Supreme Court was considering the administration’s appeal of the judge's first order.Trump has long targeted mail voting, which he falsely blames for his 2020 election loss and is disproportionately used by Democrats as a result of Trump’s condemnations. Since returning to power, Trump has tried to claim authority over election rules, saying he thinks Republicans should “take over” vote counting in Democratic areas.He issued his first election executive order just months after retaking office, attempting to require documentary proof of citizenship to vote, among other changes. The Okeechobee Utility Authority (OUA) has issued a drinking water warning after testing revealed elevated lead levels in some homes and buildings throughout the community.Between June 26 and July 26, OUA collected 70 water samples and found that more than 10% exceeded the EPA's action level for lead, which is set at 0.015 mg/L (15 ppb). This triggered mandatory public notification and additional safety measures."OUA is focused on protecting the health of every household in our community," the utility said in its public notice. While the authority's source water lines do not contain lead, the contamination appears to come from lead plumbing, fixtures, and service lines that can dissolve or break off into the water supply.Greg Kennedy, executive director of the OUA, says that nine homes have been affected.OUA recommends several steps residents can take to minimize lead exposure. Using properly certified water filters can reduce lead levels, but filters must be maintained according to manufacturer instructions and replaced when expired. Hot water should never be used for drinking, cooking, or preparing baby formula since lead dissolves more easily in hot water, and boiling does not remove lead. The Okeechobee County School District is distributing water bottles for students and staff in affected areas.Water testing is available through OUA at 863-763-3239, and the utility recommends parents have their children's blood tested for lead through their family doctor, pediatrician, or local health department. The CDC recommends public health action when children's blood lead levels reach 3.5 micrograms per deciliter or higher.

The city of Fort Pierce is enforcing two-hour parking limits in parts of downtown, with citations now being issued to drivers who exceed the limit. Drivers who stay longer than two hours will receive a $50 citation, which increases to $100 for repeat offenses. The initiative, which began in July, aims to increase parking turnover, improve traffic flow, and make it easier for visitors to find available spaces, according to city officials. Parking downtown can be challenging in any city due to congestion and limited spaces. Owner of Notions Potions, Beryl Muise, spoke about those challenges before the city implemented the parking limit. "You drive around forever, just trying to find a spot just so you can run in," Muise said. Muise said the two-hour parking limit has benefited her business. "I have seen my customers be able to find a parking spot and come into the store, and then get back into their car and be able to leave. They didn't get frustrated driving around in circles looking for a spot," she said. While there are two free parking garages nearby, some businesses have expressed concerns. One restaurant, which declined to comment on camera, said two hours is not long enough for their lunch rush, especially with limited parking in front of the establishment. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Muise acknowledged the parking limit may not work for all businesses but believes it helps certain groups, including those with disabilities. "These spots would be full, and then customers who are handicapped, they can't walk from the garage. I think it's been beneficial to the city," she said. "I think two is OK because it's actually getting people in and out. So, the turnover is higher." The two-hour parking limits are enforced Monday through Friday from 8:30 a.m. Muise said weekends are less congested, benefiting retail and restaurants. "On the weekends, it's better for the retail and the restaurants. You don't have as many offices that are here, you know? Like the public defender's office. Their employees are here, and other businesses like the title company have employees here Monday through Friday. So, on the weekend, I don't think it's as congested," she said. Tornadoes are not uncommon here in South Florida, but depending on the time of year, they can form quickly without much time for notice. The National Weather Service in Melbourne did issue a tornado warning after reports of funnel clouds started to come in Sunday evening. At the point in which the warning was issued, the tornado had already dissipated, leaving residents with questions. Because this tornado featured very shallow circulation, it was not picked up well by the radar. Reports of the funnel cloud are what then prompted the warning of the EF-0 tornado that became a waterspout at a point. Will Ulrich, a meteorologist with NWS Melbourne, said, "What made Sunday's event so unique was that it was on the ground for a little bit. 10-15 minutes is not something that we typically see during the summer months, but it was one of your typical summer afternoon thunderstorms that generated a brief and weak tornado that had winds of 60-70 mph, which is still pretty impactful to communities. And it’s a good reminder that Mother Nature will always throw us curveballs regardless of the time of year." Download the WPBF 25 News app for the most up-to-date weather alerts. The National Weather Service has confirmed that an EF0 tornado touched down Sunday evening in St. Lucie County, damaging about 20 to 30 homes along a 2.1-mile path.WATCH THE FULL PRESS CONFERENCE BELOW:Will Ulrich, warning coordination meteorologist with the National Weather Service Melbourne office, announced the findings Monday morning during a press conference at Jessica Clinton Park following a damage survey of the affected areas.The tornado, classified as a landspout, first touched down around 6:10 p.m. near Southeast Kitching Cove Lane and Southeast Morningside Boulevard, close to the Tarpon Bay Yacht Club. It produced minimal structural damage, including roof damage, soffit damage and pool enclosures lifted from their foundations.The tornado then moved over the St. Lucie River, where it became a waterspout for approximately five to seven minutes, meandering slowly from north to south over the water before moving back onshore in the Bay St. Lucie community around 6:20 p.m."The strongest wind gusts likely occurred in the Bay St. Lucie community," Ulrich said, where the tornado caused numerous downed trees and large branches, along with damage to well-built homes with tile roofs from winds of 65 to 75 mph.The tornado continued west into Port St. Lucie communities near the Southbend area, where it caused discontinuous damage including downed trees, blown-over fences, and damaged or destroyed pool screen enclosures before dissipating.The entire event lasted approximately 14 to 15 minutes, making it unusually long for this type of tornado. Most of the damage was classified as minor, with approximately 20 to 30 percent of roof covers removed from some homes, though no homes were destroyed.No injuries were reported from the tornado, officials confirmed.Ulrich explained that landspouts form differently than traditional tornadoes, developing closer to the surface along the leading edge of thunderstorm updrafts rather than from mesocyclones. Residents reported it wasn't raining during the tornado itself, with heavy rain arriving only after the tornado passed through."This was more of boundary interactions from those daily afternoon showers and thunderstorms that we receive, and lately it has been abnormally warm," Ulrich said. "The more heat you have, the more vigorous those boundary collisions are going to be."While landspouts are more common during summer months in Florida, any one location experiencing a tornado remains historically rare.The National Weather Service worked alongside the City of Port St. Lucie Emergency Management and St. Lucie County Emergency Management to conduct interviews with residents and piece together the timeline of the event.

The National Weather Service confirmed an EF0 tornado with peak winds of 75 mph touched down in Port St. Lucie before becoming a waterspout as it moved over the St. Lucie River Sunday evening. According to Will Ulrich, a warning coordination meteorologist with the National Weather Service, the tornado touched down at 6:10 p.m. near Southeast Kitchen Cove Lane and Southeast Morningside Boulevard, near the Tarpon Bay Club. It traveled a little more than two miles over 14 to 15 minutes. Ulrich said the tornado then moved over the St. Lucie River, where it became a waterspout. "That waterspout meandered very slowly over the St. Lucie River," Ulrich said. Ulrich said the waterspout remained over the St. Lucie River for five to seven minutes, traveling from north to south before moving back onshore near the Bay St. Lucie community at about 6:20 p.m. "We do believe that the strongest wind gusts occurred in the Bay St. Lucie community before the circulation continued west into Port St. Lucie's Southbend area, where we saw a discontinuous damage path of some trees down, along with some homes that had fences blown over and some pool screen enclosures that were damaged or destroyed," Ulrich said. See also: 'I love Mike’: Tracy Caruso defends husband, resigns from public boards Despite the tornado and the strong gusts of wind, no homes were damaged, and there were no injuries. Videos sent to CBS12 News showed funnel clouds in several areas, including Port St. Lucie, as strong winds and storms swept across the Treasure Coast and parts of northern Palm Beach County. The National Weather Service said it is also aware of damage reported in Jensen Beach. Based on preliminary information from Martin County Emergency Management, storm spotter calls and videos submitted to local media, forecasters said a brief landspout or tornado likely developed near the Treasure Coast Square Mall. The weather service said the possible tornado lofted a small amount of debris and caused minor damage. Allison Rogers lives off of Southbend Blvd, across from Jessica Clinton Park. Her fence was blown down during the storm. It sounded really breezy outside, just a little louder than normal. So, I peeked out the window, saw the whole fence come down. The shed was swirling around. It really looked like a tornado. You could see the things spinning. I was born and raised here. I've never seen anything like this, said Rogers. Rogers and her roommate were cleaning up the yard Monday morning when they discovered nails, wood beams, furniture and lawn equipment had been moved. Thankful that our screen enclosure, the house itself, the roof and everything we never lost power. It's just cosmetic fence and shed and things like that. So thankful every day that it did not get worse," said Rogers. Lots of cleanup to do, a run to Home Depot, temporary fence for the dogs, all the things. So, seems like a hurricane cleanup, but no hurricane," said Rogers. Another woman, who lives across the street from where the tornado started, had parts of her roof ripped off. She tells CBS12 News that in her nearly 30 years of living there, this is the first time she's had major damage. The storms also caused problems farther south. "My house is old, but it made it through all the hurricanes. It never lost anything ever. Through all the crazy ones we've had. This was five minutes, and my roof just peeled off like a Band-Aid," said Carol Cadotte. Cadotte voiced her frustration with receiving the alert for the Tornado well after it passed her house. "Our phones went off, and we looked at each other like, you're kidding me, right? 20 minutes later, that's something's wrong with that picture," said Cadotte. Ulrich said this tornado was unique in multiple ways. It wasn't raining when it touched down; the heavy rain came afterward, which he said is typical of how landspouts form. And unlike most tornadoes, it didn't spin out of a rotating supercell thunderstorm; it formed along the leading edge of one. "The problem with landspouts is that the circulations aren't particularly strong, such that we can very easily see it on radar. We know that there's a weak circulation, but we see weak circulations all the time, so that doesn't necessarily always lead to a tornado," Ulrich said. The storm caused problems down south. In Jupiter, a large tree fell across the road near Donald Ross Road and Central Boulevard Sunday night. Jupiter police responded and blocked the area to prevent drivers from hitting the tree. CBS12 News crews were across the Treasure Coast Monday morning as daylight provided a clearer look at the extent of the damage. Martin County commissioners are asking staff to bring back a proposal for a possible one-year pause on large-scale data center development as they examine the potential effects on the community. The discussion was not originally scheduled for Tuesday’s County Commission meeting, but it followed public comments from residents and others who urged commissioners to act. Majority of Commissioners voted to have a moratorium proposal brought back for formal consideration. Former gubernatorial candidate and businessman James Fishback was among those who spoke during public comment, raising concerns about possible effects on electricity costs, water supply and nearby property values. We have to ask ourselves, despite all of the drawbacks of data centers, are there really any upsides? Are there upsides to building a data center that we are now being told the internet won’t work because there’s a two-million-square-foot facility built just outside of our neighborhood? Netflix, email, ChatGPT will suddenly shut down unless Martin County residents accept higher electric bills, lower water pressure and lower property values. Commissioners said they want more information before deciding whether to restrict new applications for hyperscale data centers in unincorporated Martin County. Commissioner Ed Ciampi said the county should study what data centers could mean for the environment, economy and community while allowing residents and experts to weigh in. Commissioner Sarah Heard Vargas said she supports a hard pause while officials continue researching the issue. County staff and the county attorney are expected to return with information about the county’s authority to impose a moratorium, including potential legal questions involving state laws SB 180 and SB 484. During Tuesday night's meeting, the county attorney said the laws create a legal gray area. While SB 180 limits certain local moratoriums, SB 484 i ncludes language encouraging local governments to address data center issues through comprehensive planning and land development regulations. Any proposed ordinance establishing a moratorium would likely require two public hearings. A moratorium is not currently in effect in Martin County, and commissioners have not yet set a date for the proposal to return for a formal vote. This is a developing story.

After two of the largest animal hoarding cases in recent Martin County history, the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast says many of the rescued animals are already beginning to heal.The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast in Palm City is now caring for over 100 animals connected to two separate hoarding investigations in Stuart and Palm City.One case involved 108 cats and dogs rescued from a Stuart home owned by 77-year-old Gail Giustino. WPTV previously reported that deputies found horrific conditions at Giustino's home on Southwest Meadowlark Circle in July, with no working air conditioning, little ventilation and up to a foot of animal feces covering the floor.The second case involved 36 Border Collies rescued from a Palm City home after deputies described severe neglect conditions. Paige O'Donnell was arrested and faces 72 criminal charges after WPTV's investigation helped renew the sheriff's office probe. Deputies found the dogs living in deplorable conditions, with fur matted with feces and debris.Cesar Perea, associate vice president of rescue for American Humane Society, said the emotional and physical recovery process for animals often begins quickly once they are removed from dangerous conditions."As soon as you start providing care, you immediately start to see the animal's personality come out," Perea said. "When they were in that situation, they were completely shut down."Perea said American Humane has been assisting the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast with shelter operations and veterinary support following the rescues.The Border Collies rescued from the Palm City home are undergoing what shelter staff call "medical grooming," a process that involves carefully shaving severely matted fur while checking for injuries and infections underneath. "We shaved 9 pounds off of one dog filled with feces and urine," Sarah Fisher, spokesperson for the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, said.Fisher previously told WPTV that some dogs arrived with metal and glass fragments trapped in their fur. During the initial rescue, she said staff found "lots of pieces of metal — rusted metal, sharp metal — that have been stuck in their fur, along with shards of glass."Perea said trauma in rescued animals can appear as emotional shutdown, inactivity and fear, but he has seen dramatic turnarounds in many hoarding cases across the country."Within two weeks, you wouldn't even recognize that animal," Perea said. "They start getting a little more active and joyful. They start behaving like the pets that they're meant to be."He said even small signs — including a tail wag or playful behavior — can signal major progress."The first little tail wag," Perea said, "is an indication that something's going right."Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said in the Stuart case that investigators believed Giustino thought she was helping animals, despite the dangerous conditions inside the home. In the Palm City case, O'Donnell exhibited deceptive behavior during the investigation, blaming strong odors on "missed trash collection" and "old seafood," according to court documents."It becomes overwhelming very quickly when people feel that compassion to want to help animals, but then they don't have the resources or the ability to continue to manage and provide a level of care that's acceptable," he said.Perea said animal hoarding can still qualify as criminal neglect under the law when animals are denied proper veterinary care, food or safe living conditions. He said there are several warning signs communities should recognize when animal hoarding may be occurring nearby."The smell will probably be your first indicator," Perea said. "If you see a lot of animals, more animals than you usually see people having as pets, that's also a big indicator."The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast has received an outpouring of support from the community following both cases."The community really comes together when it comes to animals," Perea said.However, monetary donations are often more helpful than physical supplies because shelters may already have enough blankets, towels or pet food while urgently needing medications and veterinary resources.The organization told WPTV investigative reporter Jamie Ostroff that as of Friday afternoon, they have received over $44,000 through Facebook donations. Additionally, over 1,000 people have donated through other channels. "To put the need in context, under normal conditions, it costs our Humane Society nearly $12,000 per day to operate the shelter and its programs," said Sarah Fisher, spokesperson for the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast. "We do not yet have an estimate for the additional cost of treating and caring for the 36 border collies because assessments are still underway. We are deeply grateful for the donations already made to our Emergency Medical Fund, and continued support will help us provide the care these animals need during this difficult time.”The cases have prompted legislative action from State Rep. Meg Weinberger, R-Palm Beach Gardens, who is pushing for a mandatory dog breeder registry in Florida following the Palm City rescue.The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is currently encouraging the public to adopt or foster available animals while the rescued Border Collies continue receiving treatment and rehabilitation. The shelter is also asking for donations to its emergency medical fund or through its Amazon Wish List.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Lucie neighborhood are cleaning up after an EF-0 tornado touched down Sunday, and some say the weather alerts meant to warn them either arrived too late — or never came at all.The National Weather Service issued a Tornado Warning for portions of St. after the initial tornado reports in Port St. Lucie.Watch report from Zitali SolacheAron Christiansen said his alert came in at 6:28 p.m., 6 minutes after the tornado had already passed his home."It's crazy like, I got the tornado alert after it hit my house. Was outside looking around and got the alert its like tornado warning, yeah, no kidding," Christiansen said.One day after the storm, Christiansen was already working to clear the damage."Made progress getting some of the lanai down," Christiansen said.He described the difference between preparing for a hurricane versus a tornado."Hurricanes — we get days to prepare, and tornado we had all of 10 seconds," Christiansen said.Neighbor Theresa Garone said she never received an alert."It's scary, it is, cause we don't get any warning for that," Garone said."My nephews phone went off for a tornado, but my phone never went off. so I don't know if it was like — I don't know what happened," Garone said.The NWS said about 145,000 people were in the Tornado Warning area, though the agency does not track how many individuals ultimately received alerts through the various dissemination systems.Once issued, the warning was distributed through multiple channels, including NOAA Weather Radio, the Emergency Alert System on television and radio, Wireless Emergency Alerts on compatible mobile devices, and local notification services such as ALERT St. The NWS said the exact time an individual receives an alert can vary depending on the dissemination system, cellular provider, device settings, and local notification service.The NWS said it had no known technical or dissemination issues with its systems related to this warning. Officials said the tornado was a small, shallow circulation that was not well-sampled by radar. Unlike stronger tornadoes associated with rotating thunderstorms, landspouts typically develop from rotation near the ground that stretches upward beneath a developing thunderstorm. Because these circulations can be very small and short-lived, they can be difficult for radar to detect — particularly at greater distances from the radar site.In comparison, the NWS said radar can often detect tornadoes associated with stronger, deeper rotation within a thunderstorm higher in the atmosphere before a tornado develops at the ground, sometimes providing more advance warning. Atmospheric conditions at the time remained favorable for the development of additional landspouts or waterspouts in the area.Last year, investigative reporter Kate Hussey uncovered flaws in Florida's tornado alert system, where thousands of people received alerts too late as a tornado struck Martin County in October 2024.Resident Scott Appell said timely alerts matter."From what I saw, that is important," Appell said.Appell acknowledged that while improvements could be made, the unpredictable nature of weather presents its own challenges."Technology can always be improved," Appell said. "I just don't know how it's going to be fast enough to relay to people."

Gabriel Arrington says he spent three hours believing he was minutes from being arrested on federal warrants. He was on the phone with a scammer. In a Facebook video that's since spread across the Treasure Coast, Arrington describes getting a voicemail from someone claiming to be with the Martin County Sheriff's Office . When he called back, the man on the line told him he had two federal warrants tied to a missed jury summons in a murder case and needed to come in immediately to clear it up. Arrington, a content creator known for videos wrestling alligators and swimming with sharks, said the call still ranks among the most frightening moments of his life. "That dude put the fear of God in me right now," Arrington said. He said thinking of his 16-year-old son is what made him call the blocked number back, and the man who answered used a local 772 area code and identified himself as an officer with the Sheriff's Office. Arrington says the caller kept him on the phone for the entire drive from Central Florida to Martin County, warning him that hanging up would look like he was fleeing. He says the man read back his own personal information without being asked, sent him fake court documents including a warrant and what he was told was a gag order, and told him he'd need to withdraw $32,000 in cash from his bank to post bond once he arrived. Arrington said the caller pinned the warrants to a missed June 8 court date. "I was offshore fishing," Arrington said. "I couldn't sign for anything." The caller told him that proved his point, that he just needed to come in and sign to clear his name. The bond broke down to $16,000 for each of the two warrants, and the caller said he was waiting inside the Sheriff's Office, telling Arrington to check back in every few minutes. "Where am I going to get $32,000 cash on a Saturday morning?" Arrington said. He said the caller grew aggressive when he pushed back, telling him this was standard procedure and that they knew exactly how banks worked. "If I hang up the phone, you're going to think I'm running," Arrington said. "I can't call my parents or my attorney. It was horrifying." "This was the most well-laid-out scam I've ever seen," Arrington said in the video. "He didn't ask me to send the money. He didn't ask me to click on any links. He didn't ask me to do anything other than go to the police station." "I was never going to give him my money," Arrington said. At one point during the drive, he told the caller he had two hunting rifles in his back seat. He said the caller barely reacted, telling him that was fine and he'd make a note of it. Arrington says he only caught on after his fiancée grew suspicious and he noticed a fourth document had been slipped in among the three he'd been told to expect. He hung up and called Martin County dispatch, where he says a 911 operator told him there was no warrant and that the office had already fielded roughly a dozen similar calls that same day. The Martin County Sheriff's Office says Arrington's experience fits a scam that's targeted residents for years and shows no signs of slowing down. In an interview with CBS12, Sheriff John Budensiek said scammers spoof the office's real phone number, use real employees' names pulled from the internet, and lean on the fear of arrest to pressure victims into paying what's framed as a bond before they can be taken into custody. "First and foremost, the Martin County Sheriff's Office or any law enforcement agency is not going to call you and tell you that you have a warrant for your arrest," Budensiek said. "If we're looking for you, we're going to come find you," Budensiek said. Budensiek said the scam has been running for close to a decade and isn't limited to Martin County. He said his office has struggled to track down the people behind it because the calls route through untraceable internet-based phone numbers. In one case, he said, deputies kept a scammer on the line and found he could answer detailed questions about real employees, judges and case numbers, which he said shows how convincing the calls have become. The Sheriff's Office says the impact goes beyond any single case. MCSO confirms Martin County residents have lost at least $6 million to scams of all kinds over the past two years. The calls haven't stopped. Arrington said he's had to freeze his Social Security number and lock down his bank accounts, YouTube channel and Instagram page, after learning the caller also used his brother's and father's names. As of Tuesday, three days after the first call, he said the same operation is still calling. "Same type of voice came on, hey Gabe, is this you? I immediately hung up," Arrington said. He said the number called back three more times and left a voicemail. Budensiek's advice: if a caller says you have a warrant, hang up. Then call the Sheriff's Office back using a number you look up yourself, not one the caller gives you, to confirm whether it's real. Arrington says he wants his story to serve as a warning to anyone who thinks they'd never fall for it. Arrington said he posted the video about 30 minutes after getting back to camp because he makes content for a living and wanted people to hear how scared he sounded. "I made that video hoping to save one person, if not thousands," Arrington said. "You can laugh at me in the comments all you want," Arrington said, "but until you're in my shoes, you will then see how bad it is." Anyone who receives a suspicious call claiming to be from the Sheriff's Office is asked to hang up and contact MCSO directly to verify it before taking any action or sending any money.

All 36 Border Collies removed from a Palm City home earlier this month have now been legally surrendered to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast , clearing the way for medical evaluations and eventual adoptions. "They've come a very, very long way. I can't believe from when they've started to where they are now," said Sarah Fisher, Humane Society of the Treasure Coast Spokesperson. The dogs were rescued Aug. 10 from a home on Southwest Alligator Street, where investigators said they found them living without air conditioning and surrounded by feces, urine-soaked materials and debris. Many arrived at the shelter dirty, severely matted and covered in dried waste. "You know, when they came in, they were very, very terrified. They were saturated in urine and feces," said Lori Tucker, Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, Director of Operations. Since then, shelter staff have removed the dogs’ matted fur and cleaned away the layers of dried feces as the animals begin their recovery. They've received several baths, vaccinations and veterinary care. Some have been treated for skin infections, body sores, eye infections and intestinal parasites. Tucker says two of the Border Collies are still struggling, are very withdrawn and don't make eye contact. Others are perking up already and appear to be super friendly. "I distinctly remember the second day that I came in and the first dog wagged its tail at me and for me, that was, I'll never forget that moment. I will never forget that moment. It was amazing," Tucker said as she fought back tears. Paige O’Donnell, 62, was arrested in the case. She faces 72 charges 36 third-degree felony counts of animal cruelty and 36 misdemeanor counts alleging animals were kept without sufficient exercise and air. Her bond was set at $270,000, and a judge ordered that she not have pets if released. See also: Stuart shakeup, Mayor removed, city manager fired in dramatic end to commission meeting The Humane Society said it will complete medical testing and behavioral evaluations so potential adopters have clear information about each dog’s needs. The dogs will also be spayed or neutered, microchipped and vaccinated on a phased schedule. Some of the Border Collies will need additional veterinary care in the months ahead. "We've seen a lot of organ abnormalities and we think they're just like, defects from probably inbreeding. So we think that it's going to be a long road ahead of them," Fisher said. Adoption applications for the Border Collies, including applications from nonprofit rescue groups, will be available beginning Sept. 1 through the Humane Society’s website and Facebook page . The shelter said applicants will be carefully screened to find appropriate placements. Adoption fees will be $140 for adult Border Collies and $175 for puppies. The shelter is asking people not to call about the dogs so its phone lines remain available for urgent needs. While it does not need pet food or supplies at this time, it is accepting donations to its Emergency Medical Fund to help cover veterinary care for the Border Collies and other shelter animals.
