Darline Graham won the Republican nomination to replace her late brother Lindsey Graham on South Carolina’s general election ballot.Darline Graham defeated U.S. Ralph Norman in Tuesday’s special Republican primary runoff, two weeks after they were the top two finishers in a 10-way primary.Despite being a political unknown, Darline Graham bested some of South Carolina’s top political names in the special election spun up after her brother’s sudden death last month. Henry McMaster to serve out the remaining months of her late brother’s current term and swiftly notched an endorsement from President Donald Trump, who encouraged her to enter the race for a full term and campaigned for her in the state last week.Graham will face Democratic nominee Annie Andrews in November.On Monday, MAGA Inc., the super PAC that supports Trump and aligned Republicans — but that has spent little thus far on Trump's picks in this year's midterms — infused nearly $830,000 into Graham's campaign for voter calls and text message blasts.Among the unknowns going into Tuesday was whether Trump's backing would be enough to boost the novice candidate with the famous last name, but whose political positions were previously unknown, across the finish line to the nomination.After losing a top Senate advocate when Lindsey Graham died July 11, Trump angled to play a role in picking his successor.Trump heralded the selection of Darline Graham to serve as her brother’s interim replacement as “a fabulous tribute.” He also urged her to run in the special primary, endorsing her before she’d made her candidacy official.On Friday in Myrtle Beach, Trump reiterated that sentiment to a crowd of several thousand, encouraging people to vote for Graham to preserve tax cuts, among other things.“I want it to happen,” he said. “Good luck, Darline.”In forging a relationship with her, Trump could be angling to develop another ally to help steer his agenda through the Senate.Throughout her brief campaign, Graham did just that. She repeatedly stressed to voters her intent to support Trump’s policy positions and often referenced in particular her co-sponsorship of a voting bill that’s become a key priority for the president.Casting his ballot for Graham at an early voting location near Trump's rally site, Robert Tropiano said Friday that the president's backing for the candidate was enough to win his support.“Trump wants her, he's doing a great job and I believe we should give him what he wants,” Tropiano said.RELATED STORY | Aisha Wahab becomes first Afghan American elected to CongressNorman promoted legislative know-how over Graham's inexperienceFresh off his unsuccessful primary run for governor, Norman entered the Senate contest as one of several politicians more familiar to South Carolina voters. He snapped up endorsements from the likes of Sens. Rick Scott of Florida and Mike Lee of Utah, as well as former South Carolina Sen. Jim DeMint and Turning Point Action, the conservative youth movement founded by the late Charlie Kirk.During the sprint to the runoff, Norman — one of the most conservative U.S. House members — frequently touted his experience in Washington and willingness to take unpopular stances. That includes at times challenging Trump, whose policies Norman has routinely supported in Congress. But Norman campaigned against Trump in the early part of the 2024 presidential primary, siding instead with former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley.A wealthy developer before he entered politics, Norman put some of his own fortune toward the campaign, including more than $1 million in the closing week.RELATED STORY | Poll: El Sayed holds slight edge in Michigan Senate race, but struggles with older swing votersGraham overcomes debate flubGraham and Norman met for a single runoff debate, and there was one moment from the hourlong face-off that lived on.Graham stumbled over a question about foreign policy — a signature issue of her late brother — when asked whether the U.S. has a national security interest in Taiwan and the South China Sea, a longstanding contention of both Democratic and Republican administrations.She struggled to answer before admitting “national security is not my thing” and “I’m not that informed on national security.”Graham avoided a direct response and instead mentioned her brother’s wealth of experience and her desire to focus on more domestic issues like affordability. Norman called Taiwan “a definite ally” when posed the same question, applauding Trump for “enabling Taiwan to defend themselves against China.” Afterward, he suggested Graham's answer showed her lack of qualifications for the office.Some of that argument landed with Rock Hill voter Mike Sellers, who said that he voted Tuesday for Norman in part because Graham's experience level “wasn't really cutting it for me."Sellers also said he wasn't swayed by the notion of supporting Graham as a tribute to her late brother.“Just because her brother was senator doesn’t give her an easy pass in,” Sellers said. "If she wants to come next time around — maybe challenge (Sen.) Tim Scott — we’ll look at it then.”No Democrat has won a U.S. Senate seat in South Carolina in decades. When Graham last ran in 2020, he defeated his Democratic opponent by a 10 percentage point margin.That contest was the most expensive in state history and among the country’s most expensive congressional races ever.

Lucie residents spent Monday cleaning up after a storm tore through the area Sunday night, leaving behind damaged structures, debris-filled pools and downed foliage.The National Weather Service determined it was an EF-0 tornado, with 65-75 mph winds.WATCH BELOW: Port St. Lucie tornado: 75 mph winds leave trail of damageAron Christiansen spent the morning pulling debris out of his pool after already retrieving furniture from the bottom. Lucie neighborhood are cleaning up after an EF-0 tornado touched down Sunday, and some say the weather alerts meant to warn them either arrived too late — or never came at all.The National Weather Service issued a Tornado Warning for portions of St. after the initial tornado reports in Port St. Lucie.Watch report from Zitali SolacheAron Christiansen said his alert came in at 6:28 p.m., 6 minutes after the tornado had already passed his home."It's crazy like, I got the tornado alert after it hit my house. Was outside looking around and got the alert its like tornado warning, yeah, no kidding," Christiansen said.One day after the storm, Christiansen was already working to clear the damage."Made progress getting some of the lanai down," Christiansen said.He described the difference between preparing for a hurricane versus a tornado."Hurricanes — we get days to prepare, and tornado we had all of 10 seconds," Christiansen said.Neighbor Theresa Garone said she never received an alert."It's scary, it is, cause we don't get any warning for that," Garone said."My nephews phone went off for a tornado, but my phone never went off. so I don't know if it was like — I don't know what happened," Garone said.The NWS said about 145,000 people were in the Tornado Warning area, though the agency does not track how many individuals ultimately received alerts through the various dissemination systems.Once issued, the warning was distributed through multiple channels, including NOAA Weather Radio, the Emergency Alert System on television and radio, Wireless Emergency Alerts on compatible mobile devices, and local notification services such as ALERT St. The NWS said the exact time an individual receives an alert can vary depending on the dissemination system, cellular provider, device settings, and local notification service.The NWS said it had no known technical or dissemination issues with its systems related to this warning. Officials said the tornado was a small, shallow circulation that was not well-sampled by radar. Unlike stronger tornadoes associated with rotating thunderstorms, landspouts typically develop from rotation near the ground that stretches upward beneath a developing thunderstorm. Because these circulations can be very small and short-lived, they can be difficult for radar to detect — particularly at greater distances from the radar site.In comparison, the NWS said radar can often detect tornadoes associated with stronger, deeper rotation within a thunderstorm higher in the atmosphere before a tornado develops at the ground, sometimes providing more advance warning. Atmospheric conditions at the time remained favorable for the development of additional landspouts or waterspouts in the area.Last year, investigative reporter Kate Hussey uncovered flaws in Florida's tornado alert system, where thousands of people received alerts too late as a tornado struck Martin County in October 2024.Resident Scott Appell said timely alerts matter."From what I saw, that is important," Appell said.Appell acknowledged that while improvements could be made, the unpredictable nature of weather presents its own challenges."Technology can always be improved," Appell said. "I just don't know how it's going to be fast enough to relay to people."

Corbin, a popular choral teacher at Martin County High School for 34 years, died Saturday. He began his teaching career at Bartow High School in Polk County, and in 1980 came to the school in Stuart. He led OPUS, which stands for Outstanding People United to Sing, until he retired in 2014 "after dedicating his career to helping students find their voices and discover the joy of music," the school district posted on Instagram. "Our thoughts and hearts go to the family, friends, and generations of Martin County students who had the privilege of knowing Mr. Ron Corbin." He was known for more than being a choir teacher. Corbin volunteered as a scorekeeper for basketball and volleyball, and traveled across the state to support Martin County High School athletics. Corbin gave so much of his life to our students, our schools and our community," the district said. "His impact cannot be measured in years or accolades—it lives on in the countless students he encouraged, the music he helped create and the memories shared by those who knew him. "We are deeply grateful for the life he shared with Martin County, and we will carry his memory with us, forever in our hearts. Once a Tiger, always a Tiger." The Florida Vocal Association also noted his passing. "His choirs consistently earned superior ratings at district and state performance assessments and were recognized as Choirs of Distinction by FVA. Corbin was added to the Roll of Distinction in 2014," the FVA wrote on Facebook. Corbin was added to the Roll of Distinction in 2014. In 2017, he received the R. Wayne Hugoboom Distinguished Service Award from the Florida chapter of the American Choral Directors Association. Corbin Musical Arts Center at Martin County High School was dedicated in his name in 2015. "We remember Ron with gratitude for his years of service, his passion for choral music, his mentorship, and the countless students and educators whose lives were enriched by his presence," FVA posted. "Our deepest condolences go to Ron's family, friends, former students, and the many members of FVA and the choral communities who loved and respected him." Corbin received a scholarship to attend Florida A M University, where he studied music. After ending his 40-plus years of teaching, he remained a familiar face and voice at the Stuart school. Last March, alumni gathered to honor Corbin in song. New kidney In 2018 at Cleveland Clinic in Weston, he received a new kidney from his daughter, Candice Corbin, who also was one of his former students. "I was walking down the street and suddenly, I felt like I was inebriated," Ronald said in an article by the Cleveland Clinic. "That's when I said, whoa, something is wrong." A follow-up appointment with his primary care doctor led to a visit with a nephrologist, who told him he had chronic kidney disease and would need to begin dialysis treatment immediately. Candice, an accomplished singer who lives in New York, began thinking about what she could do to support her dad. "I was shocked when he told me he needed to go on dialysis," Candice said. "I remember thinking, I need to learn more and figure out what happens next." She continued to monitor her dad’s health over the next three years, knowing that one day, she would undergo testing to determine whether she was a successful match. After completing initial testing in New York, Candice called her dad to share the news. "When I told him I was a match, I think we were both shocked," Candice said. "And I said, wow, this is really happening." "It just took my breath away that she would want to give me her kidney," Ronald said. Candice then began traveling to Florida to meet with Cleveland Clinic Florida's multidisciplinary transplant team to prepare herself and her dad for surgery. He received his new kidney from his daughter a few weeks before Father's Day. "I'm blessed to have her in my life, that she would think enough of me to do this for me," he said. "I don’t think there's anything I can think of that would be a better gift than the one I got." A GoFundMe fundraising effort raised more than $23,000, including members of his Tiger community. Safe after being missing In March 2023, he was found safe after going missing for almost 24 hours. Corbin was found along Interstate 95 and was taken to the hospital. He was last seen driving his gray Honda CRV heading west on St. Lucie Boulevard in Port St. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

Applications to adopt or rescue 36 border collies rescued from a Palm City home will open Sept. 1, the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast announced Tuesday.Martin County sheriff's deputies and animal control officers removed the dogs from a Palm City home on Aug. 10, following an investigation into neighbors' concerns about a suspected hoarding situation. "Underneath the coats have been skin infections, body sores, we found wounds."Tucker said the dogs are being treated for intestinal parasites, and many are still being spayed or neutered."So far, all of them have had something abnormal with their reproductive anatomy… Some have been attached almost near the spinal column. Gabriel Arrington says he spent three hours believing he was minutes from being arrested on federal warrants. He was on the phone with a scammer. In a Facebook video that's since spread across the Treasure Coast, Arrington describes getting a voicemail from someone claiming to be with the Martin County Sheriff's Office . When he called back, the man on the line told him he had two federal warrants tied to a missed jury summons in a murder case and needed to come in immediately to clear it up. Arrington, a content creator known for videos wrestling alligators and swimming with sharks, said the call still ranks among the most frightening moments of his life. "That dude put the fear of God in me right now," Arrington said. He said thinking of his 16-year-old son is what made him call the blocked number back, and the man who answered used a local 772 area code and identified himself as an officer with the Sheriff's Office. Arrington says the caller kept him on the phone for the entire drive from Central Florida to Martin County, warning him that hanging up would look like he was fleeing. He says the man read back his own personal information without being asked, sent him fake court documents including a warrant and what he was told was a gag order, and told him he'd need to withdraw $32,000 in cash from his bank to post bond once he arrived. Arrington said the caller pinned the warrants to a missed June 8 court date. "I was offshore fishing," Arrington said. "I couldn't sign for anything." The caller told him that proved his point, that he just needed to come in and sign to clear his name. The bond broke down to $16,000 for each of the two warrants, and the caller said he was waiting inside the Sheriff's Office, telling Arrington to check back in every few minutes. "Where am I going to get $32,000 cash on a Saturday morning?" Arrington said. He said the caller grew aggressive when he pushed back, telling him this was standard procedure and that they knew exactly how banks worked. "If I hang up the phone, you're going to think I'm running," Arrington said. "I can't call my parents or my attorney. It was horrifying." "This was the most well-laid-out scam I've ever seen," Arrington said in the video. "He didn't ask me to send the money. He didn't ask me to click on any links. He didn't ask me to do anything other than go to the police station." "I was never going to give him my money," Arrington said. At one point during the drive, he told the caller he had two hunting rifles in his back seat. He said the caller barely reacted, telling him that was fine and he'd make a note of it. Arrington says he only caught on after his fiancée grew suspicious and he noticed a fourth document had been slipped in among the three he'd been told to expect. He hung up and called Martin County dispatch, where he says a 911 operator told him there was no warrant and that the office had already fielded roughly a dozen similar calls that same day. The Martin County Sheriff's Office says Arrington's experience fits a scam that's targeted residents for years and shows no signs of slowing down. In an interview with CBS12, Sheriff John Budensiek said scammers spoof the office's real phone number, use real employees' names pulled from the internet, and lean on the fear of arrest to pressure victims into paying what's framed as a bond before they can be taken into custody. "First and foremost, the Martin County Sheriff's Office or any law enforcement agency is not going to call you and tell you that you have a warrant for your arrest," Budensiek said. "If we're looking for you, we're going to come find you," Budensiek said. Budensiek said the scam has been running for close to a decade and isn't limited to Martin County. He said his office has struggled to track down the people behind it because the calls route through untraceable internet-based phone numbers. In one case, he said, deputies kept a scammer on the line and found he could answer detailed questions about real employees, judges and case numbers, which he said shows how convincing the calls have become. The Sheriff's Office says the impact goes beyond any single case. MCSO confirms Martin County residents have lost at least $6 million to scams of all kinds over the past two years. The calls haven't stopped. Arrington said he's had to freeze his Social Security number and lock down his bank accounts, YouTube channel and Instagram page, after learning the caller also used his brother's and father's names. As of Tuesday, three days after the first call, he said the same operation is still calling. "Same type of voice came on, hey Gabe, is this you? I immediately hung up," Arrington said. He said the number called back three more times and left a voicemail. Budensiek's advice: if a caller says you have a warrant, hang up. Then call the Sheriff's Office back using a number you look up yourself, not one the caller gives you, to confirm whether it's real. Arrington says he wants his story to serve as a warning to anyone who thinks they'd never fall for it. Arrington said he posted the video about 30 minutes after getting back to camp because he makes content for a living and wanted people to hear how scared he sounded. "I made that video hoping to save one person, if not thousands," Arrington said. "You can laugh at me in the comments all you want," Arrington said, "but until you're in my shoes, you will then see how bad it is." Anyone who receives a suspicious call claiming to be from the Sheriff's Office is asked to hang up and contact MCSO directly to verify it before taking any action or sending any money.

Lucie High School senior and star athlete is in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody. Eighteen-year-old Emmanuel Nelson is a football player, a wrestler and a friend to many at the school, and Tuesday makes almost a week since the student has been in ICE’s custody following a traffic stop on his way to school. Lucie police report, police stopped Nelson Wednesday around 8:30 a.m. for traveling 45 miles per hour in an active school zone, which had a speed limit of 20 miles per hour. The reporting officer said they ran Nelson’s information through D.A.V.I.D., a Driver and Vehicle Information Database, which showed the student as a non-U.S. The officer then contacted ICE, arrested Nelson and placed him on ICE detainer. The senior is now at an ICE detention center in Broward County. An ICE spokesperson sent WPBF 25 a statement saying in part: Nelson legally entered the United States Jan. 16, 2016, but failed to comply with the terms of his admission and is now in violation of immigration law. He will remain in ice custody pending removal proceedings. A family spokesperson said ever since Nelson was lawfully allowed into the country under the Haitian Family Reunification Program, he’s been being petitioned for by a U.S. citizen step-parent and the appropriate documentation was submitted for permanent residency. The spokesperson said that the application is pending, stating that it sometimes takes years because there are millions of applications. During that time, Nelson was issued a valid employment authorization document and a Social Security number. As a result, he was enrolled in school and had a valid driver’s license while waiting for the application to be approved. The spokesperson added that people are considered minors until the age of 21 for immigration purposes. Lucie County School District released this statement: St. Lucie Public Schools does not comment on immigration enforcement matters, as they fall under the authority of federal agencies and are outside the school district’s jurisdiction. There's been an outpouring of support for Nelson on social media from the Port St. Lucie High School community.

Applications to adopt or rescue 36 border collies rescued from a Palm City home will open Sept. 1, the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast announced Tuesday.Martin County sheriff's deputies and animal control officers removed the dogs from a Palm City home on Aug. 10, following an investigation into neighbors' concerns about a suspected hoarding situation. All 36 Border Collies removed from a Palm City home earlier this month have now been legally surrendered to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast , clearing the way for medical evaluations and eventual adoptions. The dogs were rescued Aug. 10 from a home on Southwest Alligator Street, where investigators said they found them living without air conditioning and surrounded by feces, urine-soaked materials and debris. Many arrived at the shelter dirty, severely matted and covered in dried waste. Since then, shelter staff have removed the dogs’ matted fur and cleaned away the layers of dried feces as the animals begin their recovery. Paige O’Donnell, 62, was arrested in the case. She faces 72 charges 36 third-degree felony counts of animal cruelty and 36 misdemeanor counts alleging animals were kept without sufficient exercise and air. Her bond was set at $270,000, and a judge ordered that she not have pets if released. The Humane Society said it will complete medical testing and behavioral evaluations so potential adopters have clear information about each dog’s needs. The dogs will also be spayed or neutered, microchipped and vaccinated on a phased schedule. Adoption applications for the Border Collies, including applications from nonprofit rescue groups, will be available beginning Sept. 1 through the Humane Society’s website and Facebook page . The shelter said applicants will be carefully screened to find appropriate placements. Adoption fees will be $140 for adult Border Collies and $175 for puppies. The shelter is asking people not to call about the dogs so its phone lines remain available for urgent needs. While it does not need pet food or supplies at this time, it is accepting donations to its Emergency Medical Fund to help cover veterinary care for the Border Collies and other shelter animals.

Gabriel Arrington says he spent three hours believing he was minutes from being arrested on federal warrants. He was on the phone with a scammer. In a Facebook video that's since spread across the Treasure Coast, Arrington describes getting a voicemail from someone claiming to be with the Martin County Sheriff's Office . When he called back, the man on the line told him he had two federal warrants tied to a missed jury summons in a murder case and needed to come in immediately to clear it up. Arrington says the caller kept him on the phone for the entire drive from Central Florida to Martin County, warning him that hanging up would look like he was fleeing. He says the man read back his own personal information without being asked, sent him fake court documents including a warrant and what he was told was a gag order, and told him he'd need to withdraw $32,000 in cash from his bank to post bond once he arrived. "If I hang up the phone, you're going to think I'm running," Arrington said. "I can't call my parents or my attorney. It was horrifying." "This was the most well laid out scam I've ever seen," Arrington said in the video. "He didn't ask me to send the money. He didn't ask me to click on any links. He didn't ask me to do anything other than go to the police station." Arrington says he only caught on after his fiancée grew suspicious and he noticed a fourth document had been slipped in among the three he'd been told to expect. He hung up and called Martin County dispatch, where he says a 911 operator told him there was no warrant and that the office had already fielded roughly a dozen similar calls that same day. The Martin County Sheriff's Office says Arrington's experience fits a scam that's targeted residents for years and shows no signs of slowing down. In an interview with CBS12, Sheriff John Budensiek said scammers spoof the office's real phone number, use real employees' names pulled from the internet, and lean on the fear of arrest to pressure victims into paying what's framed as a bond before they can be taken into custody. "First and foremost, the Martin County Sheriff's Office or any law enforcement agency is not going to call you and tell you that you have a warrant for your arrest," Budensiek said. "If we're looking for you, we're going to come find you," Budensiek said. Budensiek said the scam has been running for close to a decade and isn't limited to Martin County. He said his office has struggled to track down the people behind it because the calls route through untraceable internet-based phone numbers. In one case, he said, deputies kept a scammer on the line and found he could answer detailed questions about real employees, judges and case numbers, which he said shows how convincing the calls have become. The Sheriff's Office says the impact goes beyond any single case. MCSO confirms Martin County residents have lost at least $6 million to scams of all kinds over the past two years. Budensiek's advice: if a caller says you have a warrant, hang up. Then call the Sheriff's Office back using a number you look up yourself, not one the caller gives you, to confirm whether it's real. Arrington says he wants his story to serve as a warning to anyone who thinks they'd never fall for it. "You can laugh at me in the comments all you want," Arrington said, "but until you're in my shoes, you will then see how bad it is." Anyone who receives a suspicious call claiming to be from the Sheriff's Office is asked to hang up and contact MCSO directly to verify it before taking any action or sending any money.

Florida chef Elijah Button was chopping onions in June when his knife slipped and sliced his middle finger to the bone.It was his worst kitchen accident to date. But having given up his Affordable Care Act health insurance plan in January because of a $100 monthly premium hike he couldn't afford, the 21-year-old in St. Cloud didn't have the money for emergency care."Going to the hospital for it wasn't even an option," he said, gesturing toward his finger before preparing a pot roast for his aunt and uncle in their suburban home. "My first thought was, 'how am I going to fix this?'"After Republicans in Congress let enhanced federal subsidies for Affordable Care Act health plans expire in January, millions of Americans, including Button, had to decide whether to keep insurance that often doubled or tripled in cost — or risk going without it.Months later, with no action from lawmakers to replace the lost funds, they're facing the consequences. Some are dealing with strained budgets and exorbitant medical bills, while others avoid the doctor in fear of the cost.Florida, whose large population of gig workers, entrepreneurs and small business owners relies heavily on the federal health insurance marketplace, has become one of the nation's most visible epicenters of that impact.Figures first reported by The Associated Press showed that about 440,000 Floridians dropped their Affordable Care Act plans this year — more than in any other state. Thousands more who kept coverage are struggling to get by, as prices of necessities like groceries and gasoline remain steep, and health insurers project another year of double-digit premium hikes.While Florida had the most affected residents, its struggles are reflective of broader nationwide concerns over rising healthcare costs and a lack of meaningful policy to address them.In the deep-red state where congressional districts were recently redrawn to strongly favor Republicans, the cost of healthcare is a major campaign issue. Republican midterm candidates have been promoting fraud crackdowns to protect federal health programs, while Democrats have been urging voters to help Congress change hands so they can restore subsidies.Button, who is estranged from his parents, asked his uncle for help with his bloodied finger. With a butterfly bandage, splint and daily cleanings and dressings, it healed. But the scar still gnaws at Button as a symbol of what else could go wrong."It just feels like I'm living in a house of cards," he said.Last fall, debate over the expiring subsidies consumed Congress, resulting in a record 43-day government shutdown as Democrats insisted on extending the COVID-era assistance and most Republicans refused.Fast forward almost a year and lawmakers rarely reference the topic anymore. The administration says it is addressing affordability with fraud-busting efforts and deals with drug companies, but Congress hasn't passed any significant legislation to lower health costs.In part due to its large number of construction, hospitality and small business workers — and also because its Republican-led legislature never expanded the Medicaid safety-net health program — Florida has the largest Affordable Care Act enrollment in the country. At just over 3.8 million enrollees, it represents about a fifth of the nation's total enrolled population.Of the roughly 443,000 Floridians who left the marketplace, most are likely going without insurance, according to Cynthia Cox, a vice president at the healthcare research nonprofit KFF. She said that's because it is typically a "place of last resort" to get coverage.The data doesn't tell the stories of those who kept insurance. Tracy Rand, a licensed mental health counselor in Leesburg, Florida, is one of them.Ever since getting her ovaries removed last year due to benign but painful tumors, she has had severe menopause symptoms that require medication, including an overactive bladder and hot flashes that cause piercing headaches.She uses clear plastic containers to organize the more than 30 medicines and supplements she takes daily, their bottles crammed into a living-room drawer and a tray on her kitchen counter.The 51-year-old's Affordable Care Act plan was going to surge in price this year from $55 a month to $1,100 a month, so she downgraded. Her new plan, with higher deductibles and copays, costs $160 a month.To make that work in her budget, Rand quit a doctoral program she was working toward, started buying groceries at cheaper stores, gave up once-monthly dinners out with her husband and stopped meeting friends regularly at a paint-your-own pottery studio.It's been a difficult adjustment, but a necessary one for her health.Rand said the prospect of insurers raising rates again fills her with dread."I don't know what else we can get rid of," she said, covering her face with her hands. "I don't know if we're going to have to file bankruptcy."In Orlando's leafy, brick-paved neighborhood of Colonialtown South, Tarsha Watson found her lifeline. A clinic there called Grace Medical Home provides low-income, uninsured Floridians with comprehensive care for a $5 per-visit fee.Watson, 54, has a master's degree in business administration, but she hasn't been able to find work since losing her job two years ago. That means she doesn't have health insurance. When she explored Affordable Care Act coverage, she was quoted $600 per month, far out of her reach.At Grace, Watson learned her blood sugar is high and that she needed to lose weight. Now, she walks laps around her backyard pool and does Tai Chi YouTube tutorials to focus on fitness. She said she wishes everyone could have her experience."It's very hard out here," she said. "It's not enough."At the clinic, patients cycle in and out of a wide hallway lined with appointment rooms as doctors scan supply shelves for complimentary over-the-counter medications. The expansive building has separate areas for dental, mental health, vision and pediatric care.CEO Stephanie Garris said it's one of 110 free or charitable clinics in Florida, but that's not enough to handle demand. To treat more people in response to the Affordable Care Act changes, it recently started hosting a mobile acute care clinic for walk-in patients.Garris said Grace Medical Home treated about 1,350 people last year. Every year, they take about 350 new patients."Would I love to double that, triple that? "I just think in the reality, with the huge number of uninsured that we have, it's just not possible."For U.S. Darren Soto, a Democrat defending his seat in a sprawling — and now much redder — redrawn district south of Orlando, health costs are a campaign focal point.He said his district, which is near various theme parks, had the second-largest Affordable Care Act enrollment in the nation, in part because many small tourism businesses can't offer employees health insurance."I just hear it everywhere I go," he said. His Republican opponent, Navy veteran and former Trump administration official Dan Green, did not answer emailed questions about the subsidies but has emphasized affordability of groceries and property insurance as campaign priorities.Soto voted with Democrats and some Republicans — including a few from Florida — to save the subsidies last year. The Republican majority declined and suggested other ideas, including funding Americans' health savings accounts. No law along those lines has passed yet.Button, a Democrat in Soto's district, said he is open to different reforms for health costs, but said politicians aren't acting fast enough."They keep trying to make excuse after excuse," he said. "I don't have six months to a year to wait for you guys to pass this through the hoops that you need to."

A new dance festival is set to debut in West Palm Beach this summer, bringing together nationally recognized choreographers, aspiring dancers and community arts programming across Palm Beach County.The inaugural Banyan Dance Festival will take place Aug. 3-8 throughout West Palm Beach, according to organizers Natural Movers Foundation and Grounded WPB. The weeklong event will feature performances, professional dance training, public classes, artist talkbacks and community experiences designed to strengthen South Florida’s dance community.Festival founders Ericka Squire of Natural Movers Foundation and Branndi Lewis of Grounded WPB said the event was created to expand opportunities for dancers and choreographers while positioning Palm Beach County as a destination for dance.“At its core, Banyan is about creating opportunities for artists,” Squire said in a statement. “Palm Beach County is Florida’s Cultural Capital®, and we wanted to create an opportunity for audiences to experience high-quality dance performances while also creating real pathways for dancers and choreographers to train, work, create, and be seen right here in Palm Beach County.”Festival organizers said the event will bring together professional artists, students and community members through performances, creative development and educational programming hosted at venues throughout the city.Featured artists include internationally recognized choreographers and educators Sean Aaron Carmon, Babatunji and Loni Landon, along with local, national and international performers participating throughout the week.Carmon, a former dancer with Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater, will create an original work for the Banyan Dance Company. Babatunji, a former member of Alonzo King LINES Ballet, will choreograph a new piece for the Banyan Dance Ensemble.Landon, a Princess Grace Choreography Fellowship Award winner and Guggenheim fellow, will teach during the festival and create a featured solo work for a dancer participating in the Banyan Dance Intensive.The festival’s inaugural Banyan Choreography Fellowship was awarded to Betty Garcia Diaz, a Cuban-born dancer and choreographer who has performed with companies including Northwest Dance Project, Malpaso Dance Company and Boston Dance Theater. Organizers said Garcia Diaz will create a newly commissioned work during the festival.Programming throughout the week includes:Youth Artist Program classes for dancers ages 9-15A pre-professional dance intensive for dancers ages 16-25Community dance classes sponsored by the Downtown Development AuthorityA Banyan Silent Disco at Nora DistrictRehearsal observations and artist talkbacks at Ballet FloridaThe Banyan Gala at the Community Foundation for Palm Beach and Martin CountiesThe Banyan Dance Festival Concert at the Norton Museum of ArtLewis said the festival is designed to create opportunities for dancers who previously may have needed to leave South Florida to pursue professional growth.“Banyan Dance Festival is building something that doesn’t currently exist in South Florida,” Lewis said in a statement. “Together, Grounded WPB and Natural Movers Foundation have created a platform that expands the local dance ecosystem while investing in artists through paid opportunities, professional training, and a full creative pipeline.”More information and a full schedule can be found at banyandancefestival.com or on Instagram at @banyandancefestival.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Thompson makes no secret about how much he loves the water and boating; the Heat play their home games at the edge of Biscayne Bay. He's of Bahamian heritage; the island nation is a short flight from Miami and is home to a sizable base of Heat fans. And, perhaps most importantly, the Heat knew they wanted to add shooting to surround the newly acquired Giannis Antetokounmpo and incumbent center Bam Adebayo."Klay is one of the most iconic players to ever suit up in the NBA," Heat President Pat Riley said. "A four-time battle tested World Champion who will fit perfectly into his role as an all-around player at both ends of the court. We all talk about his shooting skill, but there is so much more he brings to the game. We are blessed that Klay chose the Heat in our quest to challenge for championships."Thompson, a 36-year-old about to enter his 14th season (not counting two missed because of injury) fits that bill perfectly. The National Weather Service has confirmed that an EF0 tornado touched down Sunday evening in St. Lucie County, damaging about 20 to 30 homes along a 2.1-mile path.WATCH THE FULL PRESS CONFERENCE BELOW:Will Ulrich, warning coordination meteorologist with the National Weather Service Melbourne office, announced the findings Monday morning during a press conference at Jessica Clinton Park following a damage survey of the affected areas.The tornado, classified as a landspout, first touched down around 6:10 p.m. near Southeast Kitching Cove Lane and Southeast Morningside Boulevard, close to the Tarpon Bay Yacht Club. It produced minimal structural damage, including roof damage, soffit damage and pool enclosures lifted from their foundations.The tornado then moved over the St. Lucie River, where it became a waterspout for approximately five to seven minutes, meandering slowly from north to south over the water before moving back onshore in the Bay St. Lucie community around 6:20 p.m."The strongest wind gusts likely occurred in the Bay St. Lucie community," Ulrich said, where the tornado caused numerous downed trees and large branches, along with damage to well-built homes with tile roofs from winds of 65 to 75 mph.The tornado continued west into Port St. Lucie communities near the Southbend area, where it caused discontinuous damage including downed trees, blown-over fences, and damaged or destroyed pool screen enclosures before dissipating.The entire event lasted approximately 14 to 15 minutes, making it unusually long for this type of tornado. Most of the damage was classified as minor, with approximately 20 to 30 percent of roof covers removed from some homes, though no homes were destroyed.No injuries were reported from the tornado, officials confirmed.Ulrich explained that landspouts form differently than traditional tornadoes, developing closer to the surface along the leading edge of thunderstorm updrafts rather than from mesocyclones. Residents reported it wasn't raining during the tornado itself, with heavy rain arriving only after the tornado passed through."This was more of boundary interactions from those daily afternoon showers and thunderstorms that we receive, and lately it has been abnormally warm," Ulrich said. "The more heat you have, the more vigorous those boundary collisions are going to be."While landspouts are more common during summer months in Florida, any one location experiencing a tornado remains historically rare.The National Weather Service worked alongside the City of Port St. Lucie Emergency Management and St. Lucie County Emergency Management to conduct interviews with residents and piece together the timeline of the event.

Gabriel Arrington says he spent three hours believing he was minutes from being arrested on federal warrants. He was on the phone with a scammer. In a Facebook video that's since spread across the Treasure Coast, Arrington describes getting a voicemail from someone claiming to be with the Martin County Sheriff's Office . When he called back, the man on the line told him he had two federal warrants tied to a missed jury summons in a murder case and needed to come in immediately to clear it up. Arrington says the caller kept him on the phone for the entire drive from Central Florida to Martin County, warning him that hanging up would look like he was fleeing. He says the man read back his own personal information without being asked, sent him fake court documents including a warrant and what he was told was a gag order, and told him he'd need to withdraw $32,000 in cash from his bank to post bond once he arrived. "If I hang up the phone, you're going to think I'm running," Arrington said. "I can't call my parents or my attorney. It was horrifying." "This was the most well laid out scam I've ever seen," Arrington said in the video. "He didn't ask me to send the money. He didn't ask me to click on any links. He didn't ask me to do anything other than go to the police station." Arrington says he only caught on after his fiancée grew suspicious and he noticed a fourth document had been slipped in among the three he'd been told to expect. He hung up and called Martin County dispatch, where he says a 911 operator told him there was no warrant and that the office had already fielded roughly a dozen similar calls that same day. The Martin County Sheriff's Office says Arrington's experience fits a scam that's targeted residents for years and shows no signs of slowing down. In an interview with CBS12, Sheriff John Budensiek said scammers spoof the office's real phone number, use real employees' names pulled from the internet, and lean on the fear of arrest to pressure victims into paying what's framed as a bond before they can be taken into custody. "First and foremost, the Martin County Sheriff's Office or any law enforcement agency is not going to call you and tell you that you have a warrant for your arrest," Budensiek said. "If we're looking for you, we're going to come find you," Budensiek said. Budensiek said the scam has been running for close to a decade and isn't limited to Martin County. He said his office has struggled to track down the people behind it because the calls route through untraceable internet-based phone numbers. In one case, he said, deputies kept a scammer on the line and found he could answer detailed questions about real employees, judges and case numbers, which he said shows how convincing the calls have become. The Sheriff's Office says the impact goes beyond any single case. MCSO confirms Martin County residents have lost at least $6 million to scams of all kinds over the past two years. Budensiek's advice: if a caller says you have a warrant, hang up. Then call the Sheriff's Office back using a number you look up yourself, not one the caller gives you, to confirm whether it's real. Arrington says he wants his story to serve as a warning to anyone who thinks they'd never fall for it. "You can laugh at me in the comments all you want," Arrington said, "but until you're in my shoes, you will then see how bad it is." Anyone who receives a suspicious call claiming to be from the Sheriff's Office is asked to hang up and contact MCSO directly to verify it before taking any action or sending any money.

Lucie residents will pay more for trash service after the City Council approved an increase to the annual solid waste assessment Monday night. The council approved Resolution 26-R70, raising the annual assessment by $14.83 per dwelling unit, from $467.33 to $482.16 for the fiscal year beginning Oct. There was no public comment or council discussion before the item was read and approved. The assessment pays for garbage collection, disposal services, facilities and related solid waste programs. It is collected through residents' property tax bills. See also: Florida tourism dips again as Canadian visitors continue to stay away The increase amounts to about $1.24 more per month for residential properties. City officials previously said the increase is required under Port St. Lucie's solid waste franchise agreement with FCC Environmental Service and reflects rising costs for labor, equipment, vehicle maintenance and fuel. The new $482.16 assessment remains below the city's previously established maximum rate of $513.70. The increase comes as Port St. Lucie's trash service remains a major issue for residents. The city previously reached a $24 million settlement with Waste Pro over poor service, and voters are expected to decide in November whether to bring back twice-weekly garbage pickup.

An EF0 tornado with peak winds of 75 mph left a trail of damage through Port St. Lucie neighborhoods Sunday evening, damaging roofs, fences, pool enclosures and yards. The National Weather Service said the tornado touched down around 6:10 p.m. near Southeast Kitchen Cove Lane and Southeast Morningside Boulevard, near the Tarpon Bay Club. It traveled a little more than two miles over about 14 to 15 minutes. The tornado crossed the St. Lucie River as a waterspout before moving back onshore near the Bay St. Lucie community and continuing west into Port St. Crews estimate 20 to 30 homes were damaged. At Charity Smith’s home on Stow Terrace, off Southbend Boulevard, part of the roof paneling blew off and through the pool screen enclosure. Backyard furniture was also blown into the pool. "It's one of the things about tornadoes that are scary for people," said Smith. Smith said conditions changed quickly as she watched the storm from inside her home. So, I look out and when I turn to my husband, I'm like, babe, it's gonna rain, and I'm like, babe, the wind just took direction, and then part of the roof came off, came through my screen, and I was like, Trinity, fine cover. Somebody get the cats, Smith said. Smith, who is from Kansas, said she immediately recognized the danger as the wind shifted. And then, as quickly as it came, it was gone, Smith said. Nearby, residents found fence panels, nails, wood beams, furniture and lawn equipment scattered across their properties. Video captured in one Southbend neighborhood showed winds tearing down a fence and sending debris through a yard. Smith said her home remains livable, but her family plans to cover the missing shingles with a tarp while waiting for repairs. We did not lose any fence or any trees, thank goodness. But all the stuff in the Lanai kind of blew into the pool, and then of course the screen has got a giant mosquito horn, Smith said. No injuries were reported across the city. "Thankfully, my home is totally livable. My husband's going to put a tarp up where the big piece of shingles is gone, and we're just waiting on the interns to come through and let us know when we can get it fixed," said Smith. The National Weather Service said the tornado began as a landspout, which can form quickly and be difficult to detect on radar. The storm later became a waterspout as it crossed the St. Lucie River before returning to land.

At least 1 in 4 former National Football League players who died between 2016 and 2021 had chronic traumatic encephalopathy, according to a study released on Tuesday in the journal BMJ.The study is “one of the most informative estimates to date of CTE burden among former NFL players,” an editorial that was published along with the study said.CTE is a neurodegenerative disease associated with repeated blows to the head. It can only be diagnosed after death, although symptoms can include memory loss, impulse control problems, anxiety, depression and anger issues. RELATED STORY | Former NFL QB Matt Hasselbeck is part of the latest CTE frontierIt’s most often seen in people who play sports such as football, hockey and soccer, but it has also been detected in the brains of soldiers who have been injured in explosions and in some people who experienced domestic violence. In the brain, it is marked by an abnormal buildup of the protein tau.A separate recent analysis detected the disease in 99% of former NFL players who had donated their brains for research. However, a significant limitation of that study was that it was done in a population of people who were potentially biased because their brains had been donated by family members who may have noticed symptoms while their family members were living.For this new study, researchers from Mass General Brigham, Boston University and the Concussion & CTE Foundation — many of whom had been involved in the previous CTE research — set to overcome that limitation by analyzing the total number of NFL deaths between 2008 and 2021. The researchers used death certificate data and compared it to the number of brain donors with confirmed CTE. The researchers further narrowed the time period down to 2016 and 2021, when the highest number of brain donations had been received.Of the 878 former players who died in the time frame, 235 had donated their brains for research. Among them, 215 had been diagnosed with CTE. Many of the brain donations analyzed had been done at brain banks at Boston University and the University of California, San Francisco.An NFL spokesperson said: “The NFL continuously strives to make the game of football safer, including by implementing strategies to reduce concussions and head impacts.“The NFL remains committed to ensuring that the NFL community has access to a robust – and expanding – set of resources to enhance their physical and mental well being.“We encourage former players to utilize these ⁠resources to identify and seek treatment when they are concerned about their health.”The study’s lead author Dr. Daniel Daneshvar, the chair of physical medicine and rehabilitation at Mass General Brigham and an associate professor at Harvard Medical School, said that repeated traumatic brain injuries are a known factor in elevated rates of neurodegenerative disease.“Similarly, we and others have shown that in NFL players, specifically, there is about a four times higher rate of death from neurodegenerative disease than the general population,” he added.The study also found dementia was common among brain donors, with researchers urging prevention measures that focus on cutting down on repetitive head impacts across all levels of the sport.“The ‌bulk ⁠of the head impacts that these former NFL players experienced didn’t occur at the NFL level. They occurred at the collegiate level … and at the high school level and in many cases the youth level. And all of those cumulative hits to the head added up to result in an increased risk,” said Daneshvar.The NFL’s 2011 Collective Bargaining Agreement limited the number of contact practices during the ⁠season. The current CBA was ratified in 2020 and runs through March 2031.FROM THE ARCHIVES | 1 in 3 retired professional football players believe they have CTE, study findsThe Ivy League banned full-contact tackling during practices five years later.The Supreme Court cleared the way for the NFL’s settlement of concussion-related lawsuits with thousands of retired players in 2016.“If the changes that have been implemented at the NFL level, including reducing the amount of ⁠contact in sports practices to less than one per week, were propagated at the collegiate, high school, and youth levels, athletes would be better off,” said Daneshvar, who urged current and former athletes experiencing cognitive symptoms to seek a neurodegenerative ⁠disease expert evaluation.“We know that nearly 70% of head impacts are occurring in practice. So without changing a single minute of game time at any of those levels, we can be substantially reducing the cumulative head impact burden that these individuals are experiencing throughout their lives.”The-CNN-Wire™ & © 2026 Cable News Network, Inc., a Warner Bros.

A Florida state representative is proposing new legislation to require timely elevator repairs in condominium buildings after a 99-year-old Boca Raton woman was trapped in her home for three weeks due to a broken elevator.WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW:State Rep. Peggy Gossett-Seidman, R-Boca Raton, announced her legislative push last week following WPTV's reporting about Norma Schweitzer, an elderly resident who couldn't leave her condo unit because her building's elevator remained out of service for weeks. The state lawmaker said she'd been working to come up with legislative solutions for months.Florida's Elevator Safety Act mandates annual elevator inspections, but Gossett-Seidman said the law contains a critical loophole that leaves condo residents vulnerable."So, I started doing a deep dive and it turns out our state statutes do not really fully cover this issue," Gossett-Seidman told WPTV.When elevators fail inspection, building management must take them out of service, but state law includes no requirement to actually repair the equipment."You can let it languish there and keep people not able to leave their units -- their home — and that has been the problem statewide," Gossett-Seidman said.The issue has gained urgency as Florida's aging condo population continues to grow, with many elderly residents dependent on elevators for basic mobility and access to essential services."They put these condos up sometimes 40 years ago — who knows who was inspecting them," Gossett-Seidman said. "So we've got the tropical climate, we've got the erosion, the rust, the rebar that rusts mixed with concrete and water — boom. It's a perfect scenario for failure."While federal laws including the Americans with Disabilities Act and Fair Housing Act provide civil protections, Gossett-Seidman said federal litigation isn't practical for residents needing immediate access to their homes."I mean, all of the condo could join together and file a class action. We just need to get the elevator fixed," she said.Gossett-Seidman plans to model her proposal on Florida's Building Safety Act, legislation passed after the 2021 Surfside condominium collapse that killed 98 people. That law requires building inspections, reserve funds and certain repairs for multi-story condo buildings.The representative wants to expand the act's repair requirements beyond structural integrity to include elevator maintenance and timely repairs.WATCH BELOW: 99-year-old trapped in 4th-floor home during elevator outagesThe Building Safety Act has faced criticism from condo owners who say required financial assessments have created unaffordable costs. However, Gossett-Seidman doesn't expect similar opposition to elevator repair requirements."What's the cost to not being able to leave your condo?" she said. "When you add up everyone having to order DoorDash, because they can't go to the grocery store, would be your argument there."The lawmaker emphasized her goal isn't to penalize building management but to provide resources ensuring repairs happen quickly. She said she has already worked in recent months with the Department of Business and Professional Regulation and more than a dozen condo buildings in Palm Beach County to get broken elevators fixed in a timely manner."DBPR has a great way of putting pressure and making sure that (condo associations) know that this is way more serious than just some broken mechanics," Gossett-Seidman said.Gossett-Seidman said she plans to introduce the legislation during the upcoming Florida legislative session, which begins in March.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A Martin County Sheriff’s Office helicopter crew is being credited with spotting a large fire late Sunday night and helping get firefighters to the scene before the flames spread to a nearby home. The MCSO Air One pilot and tactical flight observer were on patrol around 10:30 p.m. when they noticed flames coming from a detached garage along Southwest Martin Highway, according to the sheriff’s office. The crew immediately alerted deputies and Martin County Fire Rescue. Firefighters arrived to find the roughly 1,600-square-foot structure engulfed in flames, with its roof already gone. The sheriff’s office said the fire was threatening the main home on the property. See also: Funnel cloud spotted above Port St. Lucie neighborhood amid tornado warning Crews were able to contain the blaze before it reached the house. The homeowners were not home at the time, according to MCSO. Firefighters found a Class C motorhome and a Jeep inside the structure. The sheriff’s office said the garage and both vehicles were completely destroyed. MCSO praised the Air One crew and responding deputies and firefighters, saying the helicopter crew’s discovery allowed emergency crews to reach the property in time to keep the flames from spreading to the home. The question mark is not.Florida Lt. Jay Collins (R) says he is focused on finishing his current job and helping reunite Republicans following a bruising primary for governor. What comes after January, however, remains undecided.Watch report from Forrest SaundersCollins finished second to U.S. Byron Donalds (R-FL19) in the Republican primary, receiving about 25% of the vote compared with Donalds' nearly 48%. Collins carried 17 counties, most of them across North Florida, giving him a regional political footprint despite the decisive statewide loss."Byron and I have spoken. We're good," Collins said in an interview following the primary.Donalds, who was endorsed by President Donald Trump, will face Democratic nominee David Jolly in the Nov. The winner will succeed term-limited Gov. Ron DeSantis.The truce comes after a contentious Republican contest in which Collins and Donalds traded attacks over their records and conservative credentials."I think this was a pretty nasty primary," Collins said. "There was a lot of misinformation, a lot of bad polling and a lot of things that I think we should learn from as a party. But this is what happens in elections. You’ve got to come together."Collins said he hopes Donalds succeeds and argued that Republicans must put their primary differences aside to defeat Jolly.The lieutenant governor is not entirely abandoning his case about how the primary unfolded. Collins said consolidating the field around his campaign could have produced "a different outcome," but added that candidates must own their decisions and move forward.DeSantis appointed Collins as Florida's lieutenant governor in August 2025, filling the vacancy left by Jeanette Nuñez. At the time, DeSantis called the Army Special Forces veteran "the Chuck Norris of Florida politics."Collins had served in the Florida Senate since 2022 and emerged as a reliable ally of the governor. He sponsored the 2023 law allowing eligible Floridians to carry concealed weapons without a state permit and later championed legislation expanding required public-school instruction on the history of communism.Collins entered the governor’s race promising to preserve the DeSantis administration’s conservative agenda. DeSantis, however, stopped short of endorsing Collins or any other candidate in the primary.Collins now says he will spend the administration’s closing months traveling the state, working with communities and making the lieutenant governor's office more visible.He is not announcing another campaign, but he is not closing the door on politics either. Another bid for office and a return to the private sector are both possibilities."Do I think I'll stay in politics? "Maybe it's time to go back to the private sector. I’ve always said I don't have to be a politician. I don't have to be in politics to be a leader."For now, the immediate future for Florida’s number two is making his current post a number one priority. What comes after that is the one contest Collins is not ready to call.

Ralph Norman face South Carolina voters yet again Tuesday in a special Republican primary runoff to replace the late Lindsey Graham in the Senate, one month after his sudden death.The two-week runoff window since the two Republicans were the top vote-getters in an Aug. 11 primary has been a slugfest. Darline Graham — a political newcomer serving as interim replacement for her late brother — has struggled to define herself to voters who routinely backed Lindsey Graham in the heavily Republican state. Norman, who's served the better part of two decades in state and federal elected office, has stressed his experience to voters already aware of him from his years in Congress, plus an unsuccessful run for governor earlier this year.In the background of all of this is President Donald Trump, the longtime Lindsey Graham ally who endorsed Darline Graham's candidacy to replace her brother in the November general election before she even entered the race, stumped for her in the state days ahead of the runoff and held a runoff-eve tele-rally with Graham.On Monday, MAGA Inc., the super PAC that supports Trump and aligned Republicans — but has spent little thus far on Trump's picks in this year's midterms — infused nearly $830,000 into Graham's campaign for voter calls and text message blasts.Among the unknowns is whether Trump's backing is enough to boost the novice candidate with the famous last name, but whose political positions were previously unknown, across the finish line to the nomination. Also yet to be determined is whether Norman's hard-line conservatism has an appeal statewide, two months after he finished third in the Republican governor's primary.Will Trump's backing be enough for Graham?After losing a top Senate advocate when Lindsey Graham died July 11, Trump has angled to play a role in picking his successor.Trump heralded the selection of Darline Graham to serve as her brother’s interim replacement as “a fabulous tribute.” He also urged her to run in the special primary, endorsing her before she’d made her candidacy official.RELATED STORY | Darline Graham advances to GOP runoff to replace late Sen. Lindsey GrahamOn Friday in Myrtle Beach, Trump reiterated that sentiment to a crowd of several thousand, encouraging people to vote for Graham to preserve tax cuts, among other things.“I want it to happen,” he said. “Good luck, Darline.”In forging a relationship with her, Trump could be angling to develop another ally to help steer his agenda through the Senate.Throughout her brief campaign, Graham did just that. She repeatedly stressed to voters her intent to support Trump’s policy positions and often referenced in particular her co-sponsorship of a voting bill that’s become a key priority for the president.Casting his ballot for Graham at an early voting location near Trump's rally site, Robert Tropiano said Friday that the president's backing for the candidate was enough to win his support.“Trump wants her, he's doing a great job and I believe we should give him what he wants,” Tropiano said.In the primary's opening days, when she was largely absent from candidate events due to her obligations as a sitting senator, Graham reminded voters via video messages that she remained in Washington “working hard for you” and decried the notion of congressional recess breaks.Norman promotes legislative know-how over Graham's inexperienceFresh off his unsuccessful primary run for governor, Norman entered the Senate contest as one of several politicians more familiar to South Carolina voters. He snapped up endorsements from the likes of Sens. Rick Scott of Florida and Mike Lee of Utah, as well as former South Carolina Sen. Jim DeMint and Turning Point Action, the conservative youth movement founded by the late Charlie Kirk.During the sprint to the runoff, Norman — one of the most conservative U.S. House members — frequently touted his experience in Washington and willingness to take unpopular stances. That includes at times challenging Trump, whose policies Norman has routinely supported in Congress. But Norman campaigned against Trump in the early part of the 2024 presidential primary, siding instead with former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley.A wealthy developer before he entered politics, Norman has put some of his own fortune toward the campaign, including more than $1 million in the closing week.In the head-to-head with Graham, he's stressed what he characterized as the highly managed nature of Graham's campaign. He portrayed her during an interview with The Associated Press as beholden to “Washington elite” special interests that, by way of funneling money to her campaign, were “dictating the terms and giving her the political answers.”Will Graham's debate flub come back to haunt her?Graham and Norman met for a single runoff debate, and there was one moment from the hourlong face-off that lived on.Graham stumbled over a question about foreign policy — a signature issue of her late brother — when asked whether the U.S. has a national security interest in Taiwan and the South China Sea, a longstanding contention of both Democratic and Republican administrations.She struggled to answer before admitting “national security is not my thing” and “I’m not that informed on national security.”Graham avoided a direct response and instead mentioned her brother’s wealth of experience and her desire to focus on more domestic issues like affordability. Norman called Taiwan “a definite ally” when posed the same question, applauding Trump for “enabling Taiwan to defend themselves against China.” Afterward, he suggested Graham's answer showed her lack of qualifications for the office.The Democratic nominee was chosen months agoAnnie Andrews, a Charleston physician, won her party’s primary in June outright. Having set up her entire campaign based around challenging Lindsey Graham, Andrews has been forced to pivot to a broader critique of the Republican contenders.No Democrat has won a U.S. Senate seat in South Carolina in decades. When Graham last ran in 2020, he defeated his Democratic opponent by a 10 percentage point margin.RELATED STORY | Darline Graham to run for late brother Lindsey Graham's South Carolina Senate seatThat contest was the most expensive in state history, and among the country’s most expensive congressional races ever.

An EF0 tornado touched down in a Port St. Lucie neighborhood, leaving some homes damaged and residents recounting the frightening experience. A viewer shared Ring camera footage showing the tornado in the background, while another video captured the strong winds and the sounds that accompanied them. Resident Allison Rogers described the terrifying noises she heard during the storm. "It sounded like there was a hurricane outside the window, right, because I've heard those noises before and things like that, but it was just a swoosh, and it was just so scary to hear," Rogers said. "It was just this 'swoosh,' and it just was so scary to hear, and that's when I was like, I got to get up and look at what's happening because it wasn't normal, no." Rogers admitted she was scared as she watched the twister from her home. "Absolutely, I stood there for a good minute before I even thought about grabbing my phone because you could see the twister in the street. Is it going to hit the windows? There's metal everywhere; it was pretty scary," Rogers said. VIDEO BELOW: NWS CONFIRMS EF-0 TORNADO IN PORT ST. LUCIE Her home lost its fence and shed but never lost power. Another resident, Debbie Mastrolillo, said her home was untouched by the storm. "Our house, it's 637, did not even get touched. Nothing!" Mastrolillo said. Aron Christiansen, who lives around the corner, said his roof was damaged during the tornado. "I looked out my window and we had a bunch of dark clouds over there and I saw a bunch of white and I thought that's a lot of birds and I look closer and it's debris and I'm trying to hustle my dogs into my bedroom and ten seconds later it went through and what we're left with is a big mess," Christiansen said. The tornado also moved over the St. Lucie River, where one viewer captured video of it as a waterspout. Even though most homes were spared, some residents said the experience was unsettling. You could see it coming, and it was really, really frightening," Mastrolillo said. While some residents are still clearing debris, many are relieved that no one was injured. Some residents say their phones didn’t alert them until after a tornado had already hit Sunday evening. The confirmed EF-0 tornado touched down in Port St. Lucie just after 6 p.m., bringing winds of up to 75 mph and damaging several homes. Carol Cadotte, who lives in Port St. Lucie, said she quickly went inside her home after hearing a strange noise. I just felt like a suction and a really strange noise, Cadotte said. The storm peeled roofs from homes, scattered debris across yards and damaged fences, boats and a pool gazebo. The National Weather Service says the tornado first touched down around 6:10 p.m. and traveled a little more than two miles over roughly 15 minutes. It then moved across the St. Lucie River, where it became a waterspout, before moving back onto land around 6:20 p.m. The tornado warning wasn’t issued until 6:28 p.m. See also: Fire crews contain Fort Pierce structure blaze before it spreads to mobile homes That means the warning came about 18 minutes after the tornado first touched down. Our phones went off and we looked at each other like, you’re kidding me, right? Twenty minutes later, that’s something’s wrong with that picture. Why was the warning delayed? CBS12 News StormTrac Chief Meteorologist Greg Rule says radar limitations made it difficult for forecasters to immediately identify a tornado threat. Basically the radar beam was flying up and over the storm system, so it didn’t really have a clear defined rotation, Rule said. When we were looking at it on radar yesterday, it didn’t scream out, Hey, this has potential for a tornado.’ That’s part of what makes tornadoes so difficult to predict. They can form quickly, and sometimes the warning signs aren’t immediately obvious on radar. There are ways to make sure you know when severe weather is moving in. Because tornadoes can develop rapidly, meteorologists say residents should not rely on just one source for severe weather information. Rule recommends keeping Wireless Emergency Alerts turned on through your phone. He also recommends having a NOAA Weather Radio programmed for your county and downloading the CBS12 Weather app for additional weather information and alerts. And if a tornado warning is issued for your area, don’t wait to see the tornado before taking action. Get inside and take shelter immediately.

Lucie neighborhood are cleaning up after an EF-0 tornado touched down Sunday, and some say the weather alerts meant to warn them either arrived too late — or never came at all.The National Weather Service issued a Tornado Warning for portions of St. after the initial tornado reports in Port St. Lucie.Watch report from Zitali SolacheAron Christiansen said his alert came in at 6:28 p.m., 6 minutes after the tornado had already passed his home."It's crazy like, I got the tornado alert after it hit my house. Was outside looking around and got the alert its like tornado warning, yeah, no kidding," Christiansen said.One day after the storm, Christiansen was already working to clear the damage."Made progress getting some of the lanai down," Christiansen said.He described the difference between preparing for a hurricane versus a tornado."Hurricanes — we get days to prepare, and tornado we had all of 10 seconds," Christiansen said.Neighbor Theresa Garone said she never received an alert."It's scary, it is, cause we don't get any warning for that," Garone said."My nephews phone went off for a tornado, but my phone never went off. so I don't know if it was like — I don't know what happened," Garone said.The NWS said about 145,000 people were in the Tornado Warning area, though the agency does not track how many individuals ultimately received alerts through the various dissemination systems.Once issued, the warning was distributed through multiple channels, including NOAA Weather Radio, the Emergency Alert System on television and radio, Wireless Emergency Alerts on compatible mobile devices, and local notification services such as ALERT St. The NWS said the exact time an individual receives an alert can vary depending on the dissemination system, cellular provider, device settings, and local notification service.The NWS said it had no known technical or dissemination issues with its systems related to this warning. Officials said the tornado was a small, shallow circulation that was not well-sampled by radar. Unlike stronger tornadoes associated with rotating thunderstorms, landspouts typically develop from rotation near the ground that stretches upward beneath a developing thunderstorm. Because these circulations can be very small and short-lived, they can be difficult for radar to detect — particularly at greater distances from the radar site.In comparison, the NWS said radar can often detect tornadoes associated with stronger, deeper rotation within a thunderstorm higher in the atmosphere before a tornado develops at the ground, sometimes providing more advance warning. Atmospheric conditions at the time remained favorable for the development of additional landspouts or waterspouts in the area.Last year, investigative reporter Kate Hussey uncovered flaws in Florida's tornado alert system, where thousands of people received alerts too late as a tornado struck Martin County in October 2024.Resident Scott Appell said timely alerts matter."From what I saw, that is important," Appell said.Appell acknowledged that while improvements could be made, the unpredictable nature of weather presents its own challenges."Technology can always be improved," Appell said. "I just don't know how it's going to be fast enough to relay to people."
