A woman was arrested for using counterfeit currency to pay for her meal in St. Lucie County, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office . SLCSO says that on August 22, deputies responded to a reported theft involving a food delivery in which the customer used two counterfeit $50 bills as payment for the $83.90 order. On Monday, deputies learned that the individual who used the counterfeit money was staying at a residence on Miramar Avenue in Fort Pierce. Upon arrival, they quickly identified Adrianna Marie Sheppard, 19, as the person who provided the fake money. See also: PSL neighbors fight Riverland sports complex over noise ahead of council vote She was promptly arrested and charged with fraud utter bank bill, note, check or draft, as well as possession of counterfeited bank bill, note, check or draft and larceny.

The National Weather Service confirmed an EF0 tornado with peak winds of 75 mph touched down in Port St. Lucie before becoming a waterspout as it moved over the St. Lucie River Sunday evening. According to Will Ulrich, a warning coordination meteorologist with the National Weather Service, the tornado touched down at 6:10 p.m. near Southeast Kitchen Cove Lane and Southeast Morningside Boulevard, near the Tarpon Bay Club. It traveled a little more than two miles over 14 to 15 minutes. Ulrich said the tornado then moved over the St. Lucie River, where it became a waterspout. "That waterspout meandered very slowly over the St. Lucie River," Ulrich said. Ulrich said the waterspout remained over the St. Lucie River for five to seven minutes, traveling from north to south before moving back onshore near the Bay St. Lucie community at about 6:20 p.m. "We do believe that the strongest wind gusts occurred in the Bay St. Lucie community before the circulation continued west into Port St. Lucie's Southbend area, where we saw a discontinuous damage path of some trees down, along with some homes that had fences blown over and some pool screen enclosures that were damaged or destroyed," Ulrich said. See also: 'I love Mike’: Tracy Caruso defends husband, resigns from public boards Despite the tornado and the strong gusts of wind, no homes were damaged, and there were no injuries. Videos sent to CBS12 News showed funnel clouds in several areas, including Port St. Lucie, as strong winds and storms swept across the Treasure Coast and parts of northern Palm Beach County. The National Weather Service said it is also aware of damage reported in Jensen Beach. Based on preliminary information from Martin County Emergency Management, storm spotter calls and videos submitted to local media, forecasters said a brief landspout or tornado likely developed near the Treasure Coast Square Mall. The weather service said the possible tornado lofted a small amount of debris and caused minor damage. Allison Rogers lives off of Southbend Blvd, across from Jessica Clinton Park. Her fence was blown down during the storm. It sounded really breezy outside, just a little louder than normal. So, I peeked out the window, saw the whole fence come down. The shed was swirling around. It really looked like a tornado. You could see the things spinning. I was born and raised here. I've never seen anything like this, said Rogers. Rogers and her roommate were cleaning up the yard Monday morning when they discovered nails, wood beams, furniture and lawn equipment had been moved. Thankful that our screen enclosure, the house itself, the roof and everything we never lost power. It's just cosmetic fence and shed and things like that. So thankful every day that it did not get worse," said Rogers. Lots of cleanup to do, a run to Home Depot, temporary fence for the dogs, all the things. So, seems like a hurricane cleanup, but no hurricane," said Rogers. Another woman, who lives across the street from where the tornado started, had parts of her roof ripped off. She tells CBS12 News that in her nearly 30 years of living there, this is the first time she's had major damage. The storms also caused problems farther south. "My house is old, but it made it through all the hurricanes. It never lost anything ever. Through all the crazy ones we've had. This was five minutes, and my roof just peeled off like a Band-Aid," said Carol Cadotte. Cadotte voiced her frustration with receiving the alert for the Tornado well after it passed her house. "Our phones went off, and we looked at each other like, you're kidding me, right? 20 minutes later, that's something's wrong with that picture," said Cadotte. Ulrich said this tornado was unique in multiple ways. It wasn't raining when it touched down; the heavy rain came afterward, which he said is typical of how landspouts form. And unlike most tornadoes, it didn't spin out of a rotating supercell thunderstorm; it formed along the leading edge of one. "The problem with landspouts is that the circulations aren't particularly strong, such that we can very easily see it on radar. We know that there's a weak circulation, but we see weak circulations all the time, so that doesn't necessarily always lead to a tornado," Ulrich said. The storm caused problems down south. In Jupiter, a large tree fell across the road near Donald Ross Road and Central Boulevard Sunday night. Jupiter police responded and blocked the area to prevent drivers from hitting the tree. CBS12 News crews were across the Treasure Coast Monday morning as daylight provided a clearer look at the extent of the damage. If you have photos or videos of storm damage in your neighborhood, you can safely upload them to CBS12 News through our Chime In page .

Lucie residents are cleaning up after a possible tornado or landspout hit their neighborhood near Southbend Boulevard and Southeast Navy Ave on Sunday.Aaron Christiansen said he was home around 6 p.m. when he noticed something strange through his window. He immediately took cover, and moments later found significant damage in his backyard."Looked across, and I saw dark clouds and I saw a bunch of white. I said that looks like a lot of birds, and I went and got closer, I'm like, that's not birds, that's debris. And tried to hustle my dogs into my bedroom so we could all take cover. We had about 10 seconds to react before the storm hit," Christiansen said.His patio furniture was submerged in his pool, his pool fence was blown toward his home, debris was scattered across the ground and plants were blown away.Christiansen, originally from Minnesota, said his experience with tornado-like weather helped him know what precautions to take. He and his family and pets were not injured."I've seen them before," Christiansen said. "I'm just grateful that all of us are okay."Christiansen said he received the emergency alert after the storm had already hit. Christiansen said he plans to begin cleanup efforts Monday and will also have his roof inspected.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A Martin County Sheriff’s Office helicopter crew is being credited with spotting a large fire late Sunday night and helping get firefighters to the scene before the flames spread to a nearby home. The MCSO Air One pilot and tactical flight observer were on patrol around 10:30 p.m. when they noticed flames coming from a detached garage along Southwest Martin Highway, according to the sheriff’s office. The crew immediately alerted deputies and Martin County Fire Rescue. Firefighters arrived to find the roughly 1,600-square-foot structure engulfed in flames, with its roof already gone. The sheriff’s office said the fire was threatening the main home on the property. See also: Funnel cloud spotted above Port St. Lucie neighborhood amid tornado warning Crews were able to contain the blaze before it reached the house. The homeowners were not home at the time, according to MCSO. Firefighters found a Class C motorhome and a Jeep inside the structure. The sheriff’s office said the garage and both vehicles were completely destroyed. MCSO praised the Air One crew and responding deputies and firefighters, saying the helicopter crew’s discovery allowed emergency crews to reach the property in time to keep the flames from spreading to the home. Martin County Fire Rescue said the State Fire Marshal was notified. The cause of the fire remains under investigation.

Paige O'Donnell has legally surrendered the 36 Border Collies rescued from her Palm City home, the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast confirmed with WPTV on Friday, clearing the way for the dogs to be adopted.Staff will complete thorough medical testing and evaluations so adopters receive clear information about any long-term needs before placement decisions are made, the organization said. The dogs also will be prepared for spay/neuter services, microchipping and vaccinations on a phased schedule alongside animals already in the shelter’s care.Adoption applications will be available here and the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast's Facebook page beginning Sept. Applicants will be highly vetted to ensure appropriate matches, and applications for 501(c)(3) rescue groups also will be available beginning Sept. 1.To keep phone lines available for urgent shelter needs and services, the shelter is asking the public not to call about the Border Collies at this time.WATCH BELOW: Healing begins for animals rescued in Martin County hoarding casesO'Donnell faces 72 charges in what the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast calls the worst animal hoarding case it has ever seen. The dogs were rescued from her hoarded home in Palm City earlier this month. A WPTV investigation helped renew the sheriff's office probe into the case.Deputies found the dogs living in deplorable conditions, with fur matted with feces and debris. Court documents show O'Donnell exhibited deceptive behavior during the investigation, blaming strong odors on "missed trash collection" and "old seafood."The rescued Border Collies underwent what shelter staff call "medical grooming," a process that involves carefully shaving severely matted fur while checking for injuries and infections underneath."We shaved 9 pounds off of one dog filled with feces and urine," Sarah Fisher, spokesperson for the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, said.Fisher previously told WPTV that some dogs arrived with metal and glass fragments trapped in their fur. During the initial rescue, she said staff found "lots of pieces of metal — rusted metal, sharp metal — that have been stuck in their fur, along with shards of glass."WATCH BELOW: Deputies describe 'the filth' involved in rescuing 36 neglected dogsThe Humane Society of the Treasure Coast says many of the rescued animals are already beginning to heal.Cesar Perea, associate vice president of rescue for American Humane Society, said the emotional and physical recovery process for animals often begins quickly once they are removed from dangerous conditions."As soon as you start providing care, you immediately start to see the animal's personality come out," Perea said. "When they were in that situation, they were completely shut down."Perea said trauma in rescued animals can appear as emotional shutdown, inactivity and fear, but he has seen dramatic turnarounds in many hoarding cases across the country."Within two weeks, you wouldn't even recognize that animal," Perea said. "They start getting a little more active and joyful. They start behaving like the pets that they're meant to be."WATCH BELOW: 'Worst case we've ever seen': Humane Society caring for 36 rescued dogsPerea said animal hoarding can still qualify as criminal neglect under the law when animals are denied proper veterinary care, food or safe living conditions. He said communities should watch for several warning signs that animal hoarding may be occurring nearby."The smell will probably be your first indicator," Perea said. "If you see a lot of animals, more animals than you usually see people having as pets, that's also a big indicator."Perea said the situation can escalate when people feel compassion for animals but lack the resources to properly care for them."It becomes overwhelming very quickly when people feel that compassion to want to help animals, but then they don't have the resources or the ability to continue to manage and provide a level of care that's acceptable," Perea said.The case has prompted legislative action from State Rep. Meg Weinberger, R-Palm Beach Gardens, who is pushing for a mandatory dog breeder registry in Florida following the Palm City rescue.The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is encouraging the public to adopt or foster available animals while the rescued Border Collies continue receiving treatment and rehabilitation. The shelter is also asking for donations to its emergency medical fund or through its Amazon Wish List.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Lucie County Fire District Board meeting turned into a show of support for three firefighters who were fired following an investigation into hazing allegations, with nearly every public speaker urging district leaders to reinstate them. The packed meeting lasted about three hours Wednesday. While board members spent part of the meeting discussing the district's upcoming budget, much of the public comment period focused on criticism of Fire Chief Jeff Lee and the controversy surrounding the firefighters' terminations. Several speakers called on the board to bring the terminated firefighters back. "I'm asking you respectfully to bring these firefighters home," one speaker told the board. Others questioned the district's handling of the investigation. "I think you've made a mockery of these three men," another speaker said. "It seems like you retaliated against these guys." See also: Deputies arrest man, 27, accused of traveling to meet 14-year-old in Hallandale Beach Another commenter said to the chief, "I don't know how you sleep at night." Last month, the St. Lucie County Fire District fired three senior firefighters and suspended two others over hazing allegations after videos surfaced showing rookie firefighters being shocked with a modified bug zapper. Two of the terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin, addressed the board publicly for the first time since their firings. Both questioned the integrity of the investigation that led to the disciplinary action. "We were held accountable. They need to be held accountable," Hutchinson said. The former firefighters alleged district leadership retaliated against them after they raised concerns with the Board of Commissioners and filed internal grievances months before they were fired. "There is absolutely a culture problem, and ultimately we were trying to address a problem, and in doing so this is what's happened to us," Baldwin said. Fire Chief Jeff Lee also addressed the crowd, saying he has been trying for weeks to reinstate the terminated firefighters but is currently unable to do so. "For anybody to assume, or make assumption that I don't care about the people of this fire district, they're wrong," Lee said. Lee also acknowledged that the district does not currently have a formal process for handling internal complaints involving the fire chief. "I can't fix that problem. The board has to fix that problem," Lee said. Hutchinson and Baldwin said they want their jobs back but are not willing to withdraw their complaints against the fire district and the chief. "All we've been trying to do is make sure nobody else in this fire department ends up where we are right now," Hutchinson said. "We've been trying to fix the process the entire time, and even after being fired, we're still here today trying to fix the process." The dispute is now in arbitration. During the meeting, a motion was also made to suspend both Fire Chief Lee and the district's attorney, but the motion failed. Fire Board Chair and Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin was absent from Wednesday's meeting . Board members did not provide a reason for her absence. CBS12 reached out to Martin for comment but had not received a response.

A Martin County Sheriff’s Office helicopter crew is being credited with spotting a large fire late Sunday night and helping get firefighters to the scene before the flames spread to a nearby home. The MCSO Air One pilot and tactical flight observer were on patrol around 10:30 p.m. when they noticed flames coming from a detached garage along Southwest Martin Highway, according to the sheriff’s office. The crew immediately alerted deputies and Martin County Fire Rescue. Firefighters arrived to find the roughly 1,600-square-foot structure engulfed in flames, with its roof already gone. The sheriff’s office said the fire was threatening the main home on the property. See also: Funnel cloud spotted above Port St. Lucie neighborhood amid tornado warning Crews were able to contain the blaze before it reached the house. The homeowners were not home at the time, according to MCSO. Firefighters found a Class C motorhome and a Jeep inside the structure. The sheriff’s office said the garage and both vehicles were completely destroyed. MCSO praised the Air One crew and responding deputies and firefighters, saying the helicopter crew’s discovery allowed emergency crews to reach the property in time to keep the flames from spreading to the home. Martin County Fire Rescue said the State Fire Marshal was notified. The cause of the fire remains under investigation.

New York Liberty star Breanna Stewart has always seen the WNBA as an inclusive place that has served as a safe space for both its fans and the players. That’s been challenged lately.The WNBA has been the subject of recent debates on whether transgender women — people assigned male at birth who transition to align with their gender identity — should be allowed to participate in the league. There has never been such a player in the WNBA. Although the league’s collective bargaining agreement says the WNBA is restricted to women, it contains no more specific language about gender identity or sex assigned at birth.RELATED STORY | WNBA to discuss transgender athlete policies at league meetingsThere have been small rallies and protests outside Indiana Fever games after the issue came to a head when Sophie Cunningham of the Fever said in an ESPN profile published last month that she was opposed to transgender girls and women competing in girls’ and women’s sports. There are rallies planned before the Liberty face the Fever on Saturday night in Brooklyn.“Knowing that rallies are happening on both sides shows the platform that the W has and the stunts for attention are just continuing to try and ride the wave that we have,” Stewart told a small group of reporters Saturday morning. “I want Liberty fans and even Indy fans that are going to come here tonight to be able to have this arena be a safe space.”At least three fans were asked by WNBA security personnel to cover shirts that had messages about transgender women participating in women’s sports during last Sunday’s game at Atlanta between the Dream and the Fever. The league later said the fans should have been free to wear those shirts.Stewart said Liberty fans specifically, but WNBA fans in general, come to games because “they can feel like they can be themselves in whatever capacity that is and we don’t want to lose sight of that."RELATED STORY | WNBA growth amplifies longstanding debates over race, gender and powerThe Liberty forward said everyone is entitled to their own opinion and if that stops being allowed there are much bigger issues. However, she said, trying to divide teams and players shouldn't be tolerated.“If we don’t allow (free speech), we need to like really kind of go back and look at more things. I think the bigger thing is people are trying to divide us as teams, but also as teammates or as opponents," she said. "This league is incredibly inclusive and what we continue to fight for and stand up against. So, we don’t want to take that platform away.”

Coast Guard veteran James Martin has secured the Democratic nomination for Florida's 21st Congressional District after a razor-close primary victory over challenger Bernard Taylor. Martin captured 50.4% of the vote compared to Taylor's 49.6%, according to election results from NBC News Friday afternoon.The narrow margin underscores the competitive nature of the Democratic race in a district that includes St. Lucie County, Martin County and portions of northern Palm Beach County. Martin will now face incumbent Republican Rep. Brian Mast in November's general election.Taylor conceded the race Thursday night on social media, acknowledging the outcome while emphasizing the importance of democratic processes."The voters have spoken, and while this isn't the outcome we hoped for, we respect their decision," Taylor wrote on X. "Democracy only works when we respect the voice of the people, even when the result isn't the one we wanted."Martin posted on Facebook Thursday evening that he was "honored to be the nominee" and congratulated Taylor on a "hard-fought race."The Democratic primary results set up a November contest between Martin and Rep. Brian Mast, an Army veteran who has represented the district since 2017. Mast ran unopposed in the Republican primary.Florida's 21st Congressional District spans a significant portion of the Treasure Coast, encompassing communities from northern Palm Beach County through Martin County and into St. The narrow primary victory highlights the competitive political landscape ahead of November's general election. With both major party nominees now confirmed, voters in St. Lucie, Martin and northern Palm Beach counties can expect an active campaign season as Martin challenges the incumbent Republican.Both Martin and Mast bring military backgrounds to their campaigns, with Martin's Coast Guard service and Mast's Army experience potentially resonating with the significant veteran population throughout the Treasure Coast region.A Democrat has not represented this area of Florida in a decade.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A woman was arrested for using counterfeit currency to pay for her meal in St. Lucie County, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office . SLCSO says that on August 22, deputies responded to a reported theft involving a food delivery in which the customer used two counterfeit $50 bills as payment for the $83.90 order. On Monday, deputies learned that the individual who used the counterfeit money was staying at a residence on Miramar Avenue in Fort Pierce. Upon arrival, they quickly identified Adrianna Marie Sheppard, 19, as the person who provided the fake money. An EF0 tornado touched down in a Port St. Lucie neighborhood, leaving some homes damaged and residents recounting the frightening experience. A viewer shared Ring camera footage showing the tornado in the background, while another video captured the strong winds and the sounds that accompanied them. Resident Allison Rogers described the terrifying noises she heard during the storm. "It sounded like there was a hurricane outside the window, right, because I've heard those noises before and things like that, but it was just a swoosh, and it was just so scary to hear," Rogers said. "It was just this 'swoosh,' and it just was so scary to hear, and that's when I was like, I got to get up and look at what's happening because it wasn't normal, no." Rogers admitted she was scared as she watched the twister from her home. "Absolutely, I stood there for a good minute before I even thought about grabbing my phone because you could see the twister in the street. Is it going to hit the windows? There's metal everywhere; it was pretty scary," Rogers said. Her home lost its fence and shed but never lost power. Another resident, Debbie Mastrolillo, said her home was untouched by the storm. "Our house, it's 637, did not even get touched. Nothing!" Mastrolillo said. Aron Christiansen, who lives around the corner, said his roof was damaged during the tornado. "I looked out my window and we had a bunch of dark clouds over there and I saw a bunch of white and I thought that's a lot of birds and I look closer and it's debris and I'm trying to hustle my dogs into my bedroom and ten seconds later it went through and what we're left with is a big mess," Christiansen said. The tornado also moved over the St. Lucie River, where one viewer captured video of it as a waterspout. Even though most homes were spared, some residents said the experience was unsettling. You could see it coming, and it was really, really frightening," Mastrolillo said. While some residents are still clearing debris, many are relieved that no one was injured. The National Weather Service confirmed an EF0 tornado with peak winds of 75 mph touched down in Port St. Lucie before becoming a waterspout as it moved over the St. Lucie River Sunday evening. According to Will Ulrich, a warning coordination meteorologist with the National Weather Service, the tornado touched down at 6:10 p.m. near Southeast Kitchen Cove Lane and Southeast Morningside Boulevard, near the Tarpon Bay Club. It traveled a little more than two miles over 14 to 15 minutes. Ulrich said the tornado then moved over the St. Lucie River, where it became a waterspout. "That waterspout meandered very slowly over the St. Lucie River," Ulrich said. Ulrich said the waterspout remained over the St. Lucie River for five to seven minutes, traveling from north to south before moving back onshore near the Bay St. Lucie community at about 6:20 p.m. "We do believe that the strongest wind gusts occurred in the Bay St. Lucie community before the circulation continued west into Port St. Lucie's Southbend area, where we saw a discontinuous damage path of some trees down, along with some homes that had fences blown over and some pool screen enclosures that were damaged or destroyed," Ulrich said. See also: 'I love Mike’: Tracy Caruso defends husband, resigns from public boards Despite the tornado and the strong gusts of wind, no homes were damaged, and there were no injuries. Videos sent to CBS12 News showed funnel clouds in several areas, including Port St. Lucie, as strong winds and storms swept across the Treasure Coast and parts of northern Palm Beach County. The National Weather Service said it is also aware of damage reported in Jensen Beach. Based on preliminary information from Martin County Emergency Management, storm spotter calls and videos submitted to local media, forecasters said a brief landspout or tornado likely developed near the Treasure Coast Square Mall. The weather service said the possible tornado lofted a small amount of debris and caused minor damage. Allison Rogers lives off of Southbend Blvd, across from Jessica Clinton Park. Her fence was blown down during the storm. It sounded really breezy outside, just a little louder than normal. So, I peeked out the window, saw the whole fence come down. The shed was swirling around. It really looked like a tornado. You could see the things spinning. I was born and raised here. I've never seen anything like this, said Rogers. Rogers and her roommate were cleaning up the yard Monday morning when they discovered nails, wood beams, furniture and lawn equipment had been moved. Thankful that our screen enclosure, the house itself, the roof and everything we never lost power. It's just cosmetic fence and shed and things like that. So thankful every day that it did not get worse," said Rogers. Lots of cleanup to do, a run to Home Depot, temporary fence for the dogs, all the things. So, seems like a hurricane cleanup, but no hurricane," said Rogers. Another woman, who lives across the street from where the tornado started, had parts of her roof ripped off. She tells CBS12 News that in her nearly 30 years of living there, this is the first time she's had major damage. The storms also caused problems farther south. "My house is old, but it made it through all the hurricanes. It never lost anything ever. Through all the crazy ones we've had. This was five minutes, and my roof just peeled off like a Band-Aid," said Carol Cadotte. Cadotte voiced her frustration with receiving the alert for the Tornado well after it passed her house. "Our phones went off, and we looked at each other like, you're kidding me, right? 20 minutes later, that's something's wrong with that picture," said Cadotte. Ulrich said this tornado was unique in multiple ways. It wasn't raining when it touched down; the heavy rain came afterward, which he said is typical of how landspouts form. And unlike most tornadoes, it didn't spin out of a rotating supercell thunderstorm; it formed along the leading edge of one. "The problem with landspouts is that the circulations aren't particularly strong, such that we can very easily see it on radar. We know that there's a weak circulation, but we see weak circulations all the time, so that doesn't necessarily always lead to a tornado," Ulrich said. The storm caused problems down south. In Jupiter, a large tree fell across the road near Donald Ross Road and Central Boulevard Sunday night. Jupiter police responded and blocked the area to prevent drivers from hitting the tree. CBS12 News crews were across the Treasure Coast Monday morning as daylight provided a clearer look at the extent of the damage. If you have photos or videos of storm damage in your neighborhood, you can safely upload them to CBS12 News through our Chime In page .

If you’re a football fan, and call Palm Beach County home, let's say we're spoiled."It's just super competitive. We're in South Florida, it's probably one of the most competitive parts of the country, and we've got a good team to compete with everybody,” said Ty Kirkpatrick, Cardinal Newmans, edge rusher and tight end.That great team that can compete with the best of them is Cardinal Newman, the 2025 1A FHSAA State Champs - the first in school history."It was a great experience, coming over from Benjamin; that was our goal the whole year. It was just a great experience, something I'll never forget,” said Kirkpatrick.A year to never forget indeed; the team went 12-3 and featured several Division I prospects like quarterback Jyron Hughley, who is playing for West Virginia, who they’ve now replaced with the dual-threat QB Pedro Martinez."It's a lot of pressure for sure, replacing a quarterback like they had last year. I was at Atlantic, so it was a big step up for sure, but it's the same thing I've been doing all my life - playing good,” said Martinez.That confidence and poise have the Crusaders among the favorites to repeat.But the guys know, they have a tough road ahead."We're going to put up a fight in every game, win or lose; we're going to win more than we lose, though,” said Kirkpatrick."A lot of electric plays and a lot of wins,” said Martinez.I love the energy, and after a Week 1 30-0 win - now the Crusaders turn their eyes to a trip to Sarasota for a matchup against Cardinal Mooney.

License plate reader cameras are drawing attention on the Treasure Coast after Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers credited the technology with leading to an arrest in a homicide case. Flowers said the Flock Safety system, a nationwide network of cameras connected to a searchable law enforcement database, played a key role in tracking a suspect to a West Virginia motel. The arrest came after what Flowers described as a cold-blooded murder in Vero Beach that triggered a multi-state manhunt. WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW: "We got a murderer behind bars because of this. We got this guy off the streets because of the Flock system," Flowers said. Many residents welcomed the technology's role in catching a suspected killer. "I think that's a good thing if we can keep criminals out of our lives, we're doing a justice to the people," Larry, a Treasure Coast resident, said. Meghan Ford, a Treasure Coast visitor, said she sees value in the system for serious cases. "I think it's great for finding people that have committed horrible crimes, maybe missing children, I think it's a great idea to do that," Ford said. But as the system's use expands, unease is growing among some community members. "We don't have that much privacy anymore, so where do you draw the line?" Michael Maslak, a Stuart resident, said. "I feel like it's a little invasion of privacy for those of us that are doing the right thing in life, so it's good and bad," Ford said. Recent reports indicate some officers have misused the Flock Safety system to track romantic partners, fueling controversy around the technology. In response, Flock Safety announced changes requiring searches to include a case number and mandating that all agencies use a new audit system designed to flag suspicious activity. For Maslak, the key is keeping the technology in check. "You can't just let it run wild the way they're kind of starting to do right now. I think it's a great idea but let's keep it under control," Maslak said. Treasure Coast residents say they hope regulations will continue to evolve alongside the technology's expanding uses. Lucie residents spent Monday cleaning up after a storm tore through the area Sunday night, leaving behind damaged structures, debris-filled pools and downed foliage.The National Weather Service determined it was an EF-0 tornado, with 65-75 mph winds.Aron Christiansen spent the morning pulling debris out of his pool after already retrieving furniture from the bottom. Video from a neighbor's camera captured the moment his patio broke apart during the storm. Half of the patio is now out on the curb, set to be salvaged for recycling."I looked out the windows last night, saw a bunch of debris flying. I thought it was birds at first; they were white, [so I] thought they might be ibises. [I looked] closer, and there's debris, and had about 10 seconds before it hit our house," Christiansen said.Janelle Pierre-Louis said she was surprised by the amount of damage to her backyard foliage after dealing with damage at the front of her house first."My front door caved in; our door is kind of old. Dirt came through the cracks. It was a hot mess," Pierre-Louis said. "We've got to clean up and start all over."Around the corner, Mitch Brewer had debris piled out front — most of it from a shed he had tied down."It looks like it caught some heavy updrafts and left," Brewer said.Brewer said he had been thinking about demolishing the old shed at some point, but Mother Nature beat him to it. He said living in the mid-South made him familiar with tornadoes.Florida sees about 65 to 70 tornadoes a year, according to the Florida Climate Center, and has a higher frequency per 10,000 square miles than any other state, including Oklahoma.Marlene Torres was in a good mood Sunday night before returning home to find the storm had moved through her neighborhood."I had just come back from Jensen Beach celebrating my birthday, which is today," Torres said. "I came home and witnessed the tornado."Her home was not damaged, but she needed an electrician to fix her meter."I'm the only one with no electricity because my power was more damaged than other folks in the area, so that is the situation, but I can't complain; it could be worse," Torres said.Monday, August 24, is also the anniversary of Hurricane Andrew. Torres said she was living in Miami when the historic hurricane hit the region."You can't compare Andrew to this. It was life-altering for the longest time. The repairs took months and months and months," Torres said.Torres said she is thankful not to have to go through that again."Here I am picking up sticks and stones," Torres said while laughing.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. For once, things were moving fast in the nation's capital.Washington was hosting an IndyCar race through its streets Sunday, with President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump kicking off the Freedom 250 Grand Prix by leading a slow lap in the presidential limousine through the course. Soon after, the president waved the green flag to start the race and drivers began whipping through downtown, including a stretch along Pennsylvania Avenue not too far from the White House.“I’m going to make a little circle in a nice, secure car, slightly slower than the ones we’re going to witness, but we’re going to have fun,” Trump said in an interview on Fox shortly before the ride.The open-wheel race, with cars whizzing past Washington’s monuments at speeds approaching 200 mph, is the latest of Trump’s celebrations this year to mark America’s 250th birthday.Trump’s other events to mark the semiquincentennial of the Declaration of Independence’s signing have included a UFC fight on the White House lawn, military aircraft flyovers, a massive July Fourth fireworks show on the National Mall and a Great American State Fair that the president headlined after scores of ’90s-era musical acts dropped out. The events have all had a Trumpian flair, featuring appearances from his friends and the aim of showcasing spectacle, Americana and power.In this latest case, it was be horsepower.Racing day brings out some of Trump's favoritesSunday included some of Trump's favorite flourishes. One of his favorite singers, tenor Christopher Macchio, performed, “The Star-Spangled Banner.” A trained bald eagle was dramatically released near the start line, and it swooped and flew overhead before returning to its handler.There were flyovers of military aircraft, which have boomed over the city during the July Fourth celebrations, among other events. One flyover Sunday involved a formation featuring a B-2 stealth bomber, which Trump frequently boasts about for its role in dropping massive bunker-buster bombs on Iranian nuclear facilities last year.Air Force One, escorted by four fighter jets, flew overhead as Trump did his lap. The jet was the Qatar-gifted aircraft that the president has been using as Air Force One, which has attracted scrutiny not only for Trump’s acceptance of the luxury gift but because it is not equipped with some of the same missile detection and countermeasure systems found on older presidential jets.The IndyCar race took place Trump has struggled to resolve the war he started nearly six months ago with Iran, a conflict that has driven up gasoline prices and exacerbated worries from officials in his Republican Party that voters in this November’s midterm elections see the president as distracted and not focused enough on cost-of-living concerns.Trump in his second term has increasingly seemed to focus on relishing the presidency’s ceremonial aspects. That's included a healthy dose of visits to sporting events — including an appearance last month at the World Cup final, where he presented the trophy to winner Spain and lingered onstage with the team as its members jumped in a hail of confetti.Bringing Indy to DC was a longtime quest for racing series ownerFrom his viewing box, Trump had the honor of waving the green flag to kick off the race.Before the race, Trump and his wife met and chatted with some of the race drivers. They then took a slow drive through the course in a small motorcade and could be seen waving at the crowd as a Marine Corps band played “Stars and Stripes Forever."IndyCar series owner Roger Penske, a longtime friend of Trump’s who received the Presidential Medal of Freedom from him in 2019, helped lead the effort to bring the race to Washington.Trump told Fox on Sunday that Penske told him that he had been trying to bring the race to Washington for 20 years.“When he came to see Trump it got done in about 15 minutes and it’s turned out to be much bigger than we ever even thought possible,” the president said, referring to himself in the third person.Penske met Trump when he arrived at the course and later joined him in his viewing box, as did the president’s friend and UFC CEO Dana White, who helped put on the fight at the White House in June.An executive order Trump signed earlier this year calling for the Freedom 250 Grand Prix declared that the “cars and drivers inspire awe and respect in all who watch this quintessentially American sport,” and the event will “showcase the majesty of our great city as drivers navigate a track around our iconic national monuments in celebration of America’s 250th birthday.”Trump wanted to hear ‘freedom roar’ from the powerful racing machines“Their beautiful cars are going to make freedom roar. This will be a freedom that’s roaring like never before,” Trump said at the White House earlier this month as he promoted the event.Bud Denker, president of Penske Corporation and the race’s chair, said that Penske is paying for the “vast majority” of the race, including building the track and road improvements, while the District of Columbia handled some repaving.Among the changes needed on the city’s streets for the Indycar race was the welding of more than 200 maintenance hole covers to ensure the race cars don’t suck them up off the road.Sunday’s festivities were also the latest opportunity for Trump to revel in the way he’s putting his mark on the nation’s capital, including large banners showing his face on government buildings, the construction of a massive White House ballroom, a gold-adorned Oval Office and botched repairs at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

Fort Pierce's city commission held a heated special meeting Monday after nearly the city's entire legal team resigned. This is leaving the city with no attorneys and forcing officials to spend $31,000 in taxpayer money to find a permanent replacement.The mass departure followed the city's decision not to renew the current city attorney's contract, which expires Sept. City staff confirmed that aside from one paralegal, the entire legal department has left."The entire staff left. There's no city attorneys right now, none," City Commissioner Michael Broderick told WPTV. In the meeting, Broderick called the situation a "self-inflicted wound" and said he isn't aware of any complaints, disciplinary action or poor performance reviews that would lead to her leaving. "And I've asked the question over and over and over: 'Why was she terminated? Why was she terminated by a majority vote of the commission?' I've yet to get an answer on that other than to say, 'Well, her contract was over,'" Broderick told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey. Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky suggested the resignations were not spontaneous."I think this was orchestrated in which the members of the city attorney's office chose not to renew contracts, to resign," Dzadovsky said.Dzadovsky did not say who he believed orchestrated the mass resignation; however, Broderick said the departures included at least three city attorneys. Broderick expressed his concern that the lack of legal representation could make it easier for developers to push projects through — particularly on South Hutchinson Island, where a 900-unit residential project is already pending at Causeway Cove."Allowing the developers to build as high as they want to build out there," Broderick said.Dzadovsky disagreed, arguing the absence of legal staff would actually slow development down."It's going to slow things down," Dzadovsky said. "It's going to take longer to have a city attorney legal review."The commission's decision to spend $31,000 on an outside search firm drew sharp criticism from both Broderick and a taxpayer who spoke during public comment."This is a substantial cost now being presented after the city had advanced notice the city would become vacant and nevertheless failed to orderly execute a succession process," taxpayer Kevin Keene said."I share the taxpayer's concern. I think this is a complete waste of taxpayer money," Broderick said.City Human Resources Manager Jared Sorenson defended the decision, saying an outside firm was needed to keep the process impartial."The independence is really what we were looking for," Sorenson said."More assets are available. More time can be spent doing it," Dzadovsky added. The commission ultimately approved the $31,000 contract. It also appointed Deputy City Manager Camille Wallace as interim city attorney while the permanent search is conducted.WPTV has asked the city why the city attorney's contract was not reviewed. We are still waiting on an answer. This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Congressman Brian Mast is pointing to progress on some of the Treasure Coast’s biggest issues as he campaigns for a sixth term, while laying out what he says still needs to be done on taxes, transportation, water quality, and health concerns. In a wide-ranging one-on-one interview with CBS12 News, the Republican congressman discussed everything from Lake Okeechobee and Brightline to Florida’s rapid growth and concerns about a possible cancer cluster in St. The interview is part of CBS12 News’ continuing coverage of the race for Florida’s 21st Congressional District . CBS12 News had hoped to bring voters a debate between the Republican and Democratic nominees, but the Democratic primary remained too close to call for days. It was not until Friday that the Associated Press declared James Martin the winner by a little more than 300 votes. CBS12 News will sit down one-on-one with Martin next Friday to give voters a chance to hear directly from Mast’s Democratic opponent ahead of the November election. See also: James Martin wins Democratic primary, will face Brian Mast in Florida’s 21st District Mast, who has represented the area since 2017, said one of the accomplishments he is most proud of is the progress made toward reducing harmful Lake Okeechobee discharges into the St. He pointed to changes in the way the Army Corps of Engineers manages Lake Okeechobee, the construction of the Everglades Agricultural Area reservoir, and increased federal funding for Everglades restoration. Mast said federal funding for ecosystem restoration has grown from roughly $60 million to $65 million a year when he entered office to hundreds of millions of dollars annually. He said those projects have helped dramatically reduce the threat of damaging discharges into the Treasure Coast’s waterways. I hope they look at it and they say, you know what? In 2016, when Brian Mast came into office, or before he came into office, we couldn't go and sit on our dock in our backyard because there were toxic algal blooms all around St. Lucie, all across the Treasure Coast, Mast said. Brightline station on the Treasure Coast Mast also said he wants Treasure Coast residents to get more benefit from Brightline trains that currently travel through the region without stopping. Absolutely, Mast said when asked whether he would like to see a Brightline presence on the Treasure Coast. If they're going to be instead of just a pass through through our community, a place where people can get on and get off, that would be a benefit. But Mast questioned whether taxpayers should be expected to shoulder the full cost of a new station. He said Brightline has sought public funding for a station that could cost tens of millions of dollars and suggested a less expensive passenger platform should at least be considered. Mast also highlighted roughly $220 million in funding for replacement of the aging Florida East Coast Railway bridge over the St. The new bridge is expected to provide significantly more clearance for boats, reducing conflicts between rail and marine traffic. Renewed push for cancer cluster investigation Mast also told CBS12 News he has asked the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to take another look at concerns about glioblastoma cases in St. The aggressive form of brain cancer has raised concerns among some families who believe the number of cases in the area warrants additional investigation. Previous state and federal reviews did not determine that a cancer cluster existed. Mast said the emergence of additional cases deserves another examination. I have requested again that the CDC come in, Mast said. We're seeing more instances of this aggressive brain tumor. You need to come in and you need to take a look. Mast said he wants federal health officials to provide residents with detailed data explaining how the cases were evaluated and whether there is any connection between them. Supporting Amendment 3 Mast also gave his full support to Amendment 3, which would increase Florida’s homestead exemption and reduce property taxes for qualifying homeowners. For Mast, the issue comes down to allowing Floridians to keep more of their money. I fully support reducing the tax burden, Mast said. Every dollar that we spend in government, at any level of government, federal or local, it comes out of your pocket. Cities, counties, and some public safety agencies have warned the amendment could reduce the money available to provide local services. Mast acknowledged there could be an impact on local budgets but said governments should also examine their own spending and look for places to cut. There are absolutely places that our cities and our counties can cut, Mast said. Growth and data centers With Port St. Lucie County experiencing explosive population growth, Mast said federal infrastructure funding will be an important part of keeping up. As a member of the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, Mast said his role allows him to advocate for federal dollars for roads, bridges, airports and other major projects in the district. He also weighed in on the growing debate over massive data centers needed to power artificial intelligence and other technology. Mast acknowledged the country needs data centers but said that does not mean they need to be built in South Florida. Do they need to be in your backyard or in the 21st congressional district? Absolutely not, Mast said. He said those decisions ultimately belong to local communities, which have to weigh potential jobs and tax revenue against demands on electricity, water and the character of the community. Health care and affordability On health care, Mast said he does not support bringing back enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies that were tied to the COVID-19 pandemic. Instead, he pointed to efforts to reduce prescription drug prices and said consumers should have more flexibility to choose health plans based on what they actually need. Mast also argued that reducing taxes is one of the most effective ways Washington can address affordability, pointing to tax reductions involving tips, overtime and Social Security. Iran and gas prices As chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Mast also defended the U.S. Mast argued Iran has targeted American interests and service members for years and said preventing the country from obtaining a nuclear weapon is critical to U.S. He acknowledged that instability in the Middle East has contributed to higher gas prices and said he supports eliminating the federal gasoline and diesel taxes as another way to lower prices at the pump. Term limits Despite seeking a sixth term himself, Mast said he supports congressional term limits and has signed a pledge committing to vote for them if legislation reaches the House floor. If he were writing the proposal, Mast said he would limit House members to three terms, or six years, while allowing one or possibly two Senate terms. Mast said his own record is what he wants voters to consider as he asks them for another term particularly his work on the Treasure Coast’s waterways, veterans, and taxes. I hope they say, you know what, Brian does what he says, Mast said.

The National Weather Service has confirmed that an EF0 tornado touched down Sunday evening in St. Lucie County, damaging about 20 to 30 homes along a 2.1-mile path.WATCH THE FULL PRESS CONFERENCE BELOW:Will Ulrich, warning coordination meteorologist with the National Weather Service Melbourne office, announced the findings Monday morning during a press conference at Jessica Clinton Park following a damage survey of the affected areas.The tornado, classified as a landspout, first touched down around 6:10 p.m. near Southeast Kitching Cove Lane and Southeast Morningside Boulevard, close to the Tarpon Bay Yacht Club. It produced minimal structural damage, including roof damage, soffit damage and pool enclosures lifted from their foundations.The tornado then moved over the St. Lucie River, where it became a waterspout for approximately five to seven minutes, meandering slowly from north to south over the water before moving back onshore in the Bay St. Lucie community around 6:20 p.m."The strongest wind gusts likely occurred in the Bay St. Lucie community," Ulrich said, where the tornado caused numerous downed trees and large branches, along with damage to well-built homes with tile roofs from winds of 65 to 75 mph.The tornado continued west into Port St. Lucie communities near the Southbend area, where it caused discontinuous damage including downed trees, blown-over fences, and damaged or destroyed pool screen enclosures before dissipating.The entire event lasted approximately 14 to 15 minutes, making it unusually long for this type of tornado. Most of the damage was classified as minor, with approximately 20 to 30 percent of roof covers removed from some homes, though no homes were destroyed.No injuries were reported from the tornado, officials confirmed.Ulrich explained that landspouts form differently than traditional tornadoes, developing closer to the surface along the leading edge of thunderstorm updrafts rather than from mesocyclones. Residents reported it wasn't raining during the tornado itself, with heavy rain arriving only after the tornado passed through."This was more of boundary interactions from those daily afternoon showers and thunderstorms that we receive, and lately it has been abnormally warm," Ulrich said. "The more heat you have, the more vigorous those boundary collisions are going to be."While landspouts are more common during summer months in Florida, any one location experiencing a tornado remains historically rare.The National Weather Service worked alongside the City of Port St. Lucie Emergency Management and St. Lucie County Emergency Management to conduct interviews with residents and piece together the timeline of the event.

The National Weather Service confirmed an EF0 tornado with peak winds of 75 mph touched down in Port St. Lucie before becoming a waterspout as it moved over the St. Lucie River Sunday evening. According to Will Ulrich, a warning coordination meteorologist with the National Weather Service, the tornado touched down at 6:10 p.m. near Southeast Kitchen Cove Lane and Southeast Morningside Boulevard, near the Tarpon Bay Club. It traveled a little more than two miles over 14 to 15 minutes. Ulrich said the tornado then moved over the St. Lucie River, where it became a waterspout. "That waterspout meandered very slowly over the St. Lucie River," Ulrich said. Ulrich said the waterspout remained over the St. Lucie River for five to seven minutes, traveling from north to south before moving back onshore near the Bay St. Lucie community at about 6:20 p.m. "We do believe that the strongest wind gusts occurred in the Bay St. Lucie community before the circulation continued west into Port St. Lucie's Southbend area, where we saw a discontinuous damage path of some trees down, along with some homes that had fences blown over and some pool screen enclosures that were damaged or destroyed," Ulrich said. See also: 'I love Mike’: Tracy Caruso defends husband, resigns from public boards Despite the tornado and the strong gusts of wind no homes were damaged and there were no injuries. Videos sent to CBS12 News showed funnel clouds in several areas, including Port St. Lucie, as strong winds and storms swept across the Treasure Coast and parts of northern Palm Beach County. The National Weather Service said it is also aware of damage reported in Jensen Beach. Based on preliminary information from Martin County Emergency Management, storm spotter calls and videos submitted to local media, forecasters said a brief landspout or tornado likely developed near the Treasure Coast Square Mall. The weather service said the possible tornado lofted a small amount of debris and caused minor damage. Allison Rogers lives off of Southbend Blvd, across from Jessica Clinton Park. Her fence was blown down during the storm. It sounded really breezy outside, just a little louder than normal. So, I peeked out the window, saw the whole fence come down. The shed was swirling around. It really looked like a tornado. You could see the things spinning. I was born and raised here. I've never seen anything like this, said Rogers. Rogers and her roommate were cleaning up the yard Monday morning when they discovered nails, wood beams, furniture and lawn equipment had been moved. Thankful that our screen enclosure, the house itself, the roof and everything we never lost power. It's just cosmetic fence and shed and things like that. So thankful every day that it did not get worse," said Rogers. Lots of cleanup to do, a run to Home Depot, temporary fence for the dogs, all the things. So, seems like a hurricane cleanup, but no hurricane," said Rogers. The storms also caused problems farther south. San Francisco 49ers owner Jed York was arrested over the weekend in Ohio and pleaded no contest to misdemeanor charges of disorderly conduct and possessing criminal tools.York was arrested Sunday in East Palestine, Ohio, and was released after posting a $5,000 bond. He was sentenced to one day in jail for both offenses to be served concurrently and was credited with one day served when he pleaded no contest Monday morning. He also was fined $1,150.Court records show that York initially was charged with engaging in prostitution, but prosecutors amended that to disorderly conduct. Records also show that York had a cellphone returned to him and that $160 that was seized was to be given to the Mahoning Valley Human Trafficking Task Force as part of the plea agreement. York also completed an online course.FROM THE ARCHIVES | New England Patriots owner officially charged in prostitution caseThe 49ers and the NFL didn't immediately respond to requests for comment.The 46-year-old York took over day-to-day control of the 49ers from his parents in 2008. He became the team's principal owner in 2024. After some initial struggles under York's leadership, the team has been a consistent contender since hiring coach Kyle Shanahan and general manager John Lynch in 2017.The Niners have made the Super Bowl three times under York's leadership, losing in the 2012 season under coach Jim Harbaugh and the 2019 and '23 seasons under Shanahan and Lynch.York also oversaw the building of Levi's Stadium in Santa Clara, California. The team moved from San Francisco to the new stadium in 2014. The stadium has hosted two Super Bowls, a World Cup and a College Football Playoff title game.

A Florida state representative is proposing new legislation to require timely elevator repairs in condominium buildings after a 99-year-old Boca Raton woman was trapped in her home for three weeks due to a broken elevator.WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW:State Rep. Peggy Gossett-Seidman, R-Boca Raton, announced her legislative push last week following WPTV's reporting about Norma Schweitzer, an elderly resident who couldn't leave her condo unit because her building's elevator remained out of service for weeks.Florida's Elevator Safety Act mandates annual elevator inspections, but Gossett-Seidman said the law contains a critical loophole that leaves condo residents vulnerable."So, I started doing a deep dive and it turns out our state statutes do not really fully cover this issue," Gossett-Seidman told WPTV.When elevators fail inspection, building management must take them out of service, but state law includes no requirement to actually repair the equipment."You can let it languish there and keep people not able to leave their units -- their home — and that has been the problem statewide," Gossett-Seidman said.The issue has gained urgency as Florida's aging condo population continues to grow, with many elderly residents dependent on elevators for basic mobility and access to essential services.While federal laws including the Americans with Disabilities Act and Fair Housing Act provide civil protections, Gossett-Seidman said federal litigation isn't practical for residents needing immediate access to their homes."I mean, all of the condo could join together and file a class action. We just need to get the elevator fixed," she said.Gossett-Seidman plans to model her proposal on Florida's Building Safety Act, legislation passed after the 2021 Surfside condominium collapse that killed 98 people. That law requires building inspections, reserve funds and certain repairs for multi-story condo buildings.The representative wants to expand the act's repair requirements beyond structural integrity to include elevator maintenance and timely repairs.WATCH BELOW: 99-year-old trapped in 4th-floor home during elevator outagesThe Building Safety Act has faced criticism from condo owners who say required financial assessments have created unaffordable costs. However, Gossett-Seidman doesn't expect similar opposition to elevator repair requirements."What's the cost to not being able to leave your condo?" she said. "When you add up everyone having to order DoorDash, because they can't go to the grocery store, would be your argument there."The lawmaker emphasized her goal isn't to penalize building management but to provide resources ensuring repairs happen quickly.Gossett-Seidman said she plans to introduce the legislation during the upcoming Florida legislative session, which begins in March.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Lucie City Council is set to hold a public hearing Monday night before voting on a proposed increase to the annual solid waste assessment charged to residential properties. The assessment would rise $14.83 per dwelling unit, from $467.33 to $482.16 for the fiscal year beginning Oct. That works out to about $1.24 more per month. The non-ad valorem assessment pays for solid waste and recycling collection, disposal services, facilities, and related programs. It is collected through property tax bills. City officials said the increase is required under Port St. Lucie’s solid waste franchise agreement with FCC Environmental Service . Public Information Officer Scott Samples said the adjustment reflects inflationary costs for labor, equipment, vehicle maintenance and fuel. This is standard for most solid waste contracts throughout the country, Samples said. The proposed increase arrives after years of frustration over trash service in Port St. The city won a $24 million settlement with Waste Pro over poor service, but residents received a tax credit rather than refund checks. Lucie mayor's race is tied to lingering trash problems Trash collection also became a central issue in this year’s mayoral campaign , with residents and candidates debating the reliability of service and whether the city should restore twice-weekly garbage pickup. Voters are expected to weigh in on that question on the November ballot . The city adopted a preliminary rate resolution in July and mailed notices to affected residential property owners, according to the proposed final rate resolution. Council members will hear public comments and objections before considering the final rate. The proposed $482.16 annual assessment remains below the city’s previously established maximum rate of $513.70. If approved, the new assessment would take effect Oct.

Lucie man faces multiple charges involving a minor after officers served a search warrant at a home Thursday morning, authorities said. Lucie Police Department's SWAT team executed the warrant around 6 a.m. at a residence in the 900 block of Southwest Jaslo Avenue. During the operation, officers arrested 48-year-old Virgil Jason Vinz without incident Police said Vinz is charged with five counts of sexual activity with a minor, a second-degree felony under Florida law, and six counts of contributing to the delinquency or dependency of a child, a first-degree misdemeanor. The response drew attention from neighbors, several of whom reported hearing loud booms before seeing officers outside the home. Authorities said the sounds were not gunshots but Noise Flash Diversionary Devices used during the SWAT team's entry into the home. "It's a diversion to either make entry. When conducting a high-risk operation, these are utilized just for the safety of both the officers and the individual," police spokesperson Brandon Martinez said. Authorities have not said what evidence was recovered from the home or what prompted the investigation and say they are limited in what they can discuss while the case remains active. "As a father of three myself, we take it very serious anytime there is a child involved," Martinez said. Martinez said officers are familiar with Vinz from previous encounters but emphasized the current case is separate from any prior incidents. Court records show Vinz pleaded no contest and was adjudicated guilty in 2023 on charges of battery on a law enforcement officer and contributing to the delinquency of a child. Records also show he later violated probation before completing Mental Health Court in October 2024. Jail records show Vinz remained in the St. Lucie County Jail as of Thursday night, with bond pending. A Palm Beach County restaurant had a decade of loyal customers, award-worthy barbecue and a reputation built one brisket at a time — and still, it wasn't enough to keep the doors open.Pigsty Barbecue recently closed its original South Florida location in Boynton Beach after years of mounting financial pressure, becoming one of the latest casualties in a wave of neighborhood restaurant closures sweeping Palm Beach County and the broader South Florida region.WATCH: How Palm Beach County restaurant owners are fighting backOwner and Pigsty Tom Rhodemeyer said the decision came after costs climbed from nearly every direction."It's been a whirlwind, that's for sure. A lot of different things played into having to close that location. By the time you're done checking all the boxes, you've got to decide: Can I take a paycheck this week?" Rhodemeyer said.Road construction outside the restaurant hurt customer traffic while operating costs continued to rise. Nationally, restaurant operating costs have increased about 36% since before the pandemic — a figure Rhodemeyer said reflects what owners across South Florida are experiencing firsthand."It's not just the rent. It's everything from the cost of containers, souffle cups and to-go boxes. Everything has a dollar sign on it, and they're all getting bigger," Rhodemeyer said.Industry leaders say Pigsty's experience is becoming increasingly common across Florida.Samantha Padgett, vice president of government relations and general counsel for the Florida Restaurant and Lodging Association, said rising lease costs and longer lease commitments are pushing many longtime operators toward the exit."It has to do with both the cost of their leases and the length of their leases. You have individuals that have had restaurants for a very long time. They may be getting to a point in their lives where they're not sure how many more years they want to stay open," Padgett said.Many landlords are raising rents while requiring restaurant owners to commit to 10-year leases or longer — a risk some operators are no longer willing to take."They're making the decision of, do they want to pay that much for the commercial rent, and do they want to make the commitment for 10 more years?" Padgett said.Some closures happen with little warning. One Palm Beach County tea shop that operated for nearly 3 decades recently received an eviction notice after its landlord decided not to renew the lease. In other cases, property owners see greater profit in redeveloping land for commercial or residential use."There's always the possibility that they've decided that there is another, a higher and better and more profitable use for the land," Padgett said.For Rhodemeyer, closing the original Pigsty location did not mean giving up on barbecue — it meant reinventing how he serves it.After announcing the closure on Facebook, he was contacted by partners at Bungalow Bar and Grill, who invited him to bring Pigsty's barbecue operation into their existing venue. The partnership combines barbecue, drinks and live entertainment under one roof while allowing both businesses to share overhead costs."We were contacted by the partners here at the Bungalow Bar and Grill, and we started a conversation, and it's been fantastic. I think it's the direction a lot of small businesses are going in — partnerships and collaborations," Rhodemeyer said.The new setup creates what Rhodemeyer describes as a "synergy" between different customer groups."It allows us to bring our barbecue people to the Bungalow's bar people, and we've got a new guy coming in that's going to do all the entertainment. It's all of us bringing the lanes together," he said.The revamped venue will feature barbecue alongside bands, karaoke, DJ dance parties and other events designed to create a more social, entertainment-driven atmosphere.Padgett said that kind of adaptation is exactly what many restaurants across Florida are now being forced to pursue. Operators are simplifying menus, emphasizing takeout and delivery, restructuring operations and sharpening their brand identities to survive."Sometimes we see restaurants do things like simplify their menus. They may focus their menus, which can lower their food costs, and it can also give their customers a different choice and kind of cement their identity," Padgett said.Pigsty has already embraced those changes. Rhodemeyer redesigned the menu to include lower-cost "bar bites," baskets and appetizers better suited for outdoor dining and entertainment crowds — while keeping the traditional Texas-style barbecue sold by the pound."We reinvented and restructured the menu. You'll still be able to get your meat by the half pound, by the pound, good old Texas-style barbecue. But we've also introduced some basket options that will be friendly to a nice outdoor venue like this," Rhodemeyer said.He also raised prices."I'll tell you straight out: to buy the pound, the price went up. I had hundreds and hundreds of people tell me on my Facebook page, 'Just raise the prices, we'll keep coming.' Well, I did, so come on down," Rhodemeyer said.Even loyal customer support, however, does not erase the financial realities restaurants face. Padgett said operators are battling labor shortages, inflation,rising food and transportation costs, credit card processing fees and shifting consumer behavior simultaneously."At every turn, the cost of doing business is going up," Padgett said.Consumers are under pressure too. Rising housing costs, property taxes and everyday expenses are forcing many families to cut back on dining out."They are having to make hard decisions about how they allocate their resources. Do we eat out tonight or do we eat home? And we're not always on the winning side of that," Padgett said.Rhodemeyer believes local governments also play a role in the struggles facing independent restaurants. He said municipalities often prioritize large national chains — which can commit to expensive build-outs and long-term leases —over smaller local businesses."A lot of the municipalities really want the big national brands. Everything is going corporate, and that's just not the way we roll," Rhodemeyer said.He argued cities should offer more support, grants or incentives for independent operators trying to stay afloat."That's what we need in our local government — to partner with the small businesses and give them some incentives, give them some help. Trust me, I've looked," Rhodemeyer said.Despite the challenges, both Rhodemeyer and Padgett said neighborhood restaurants remain vital community gathering places worth preserving."We hope that people will continue to seek their neighborhood restaurants because without our customers, we can't continue to operate," Padgett said.Rhodemeyer still drives past his former restaurant location every day, but he said he sees it as part of the past."It's a chapter that's closed, and this is a new chapter that's opening. Let's just hope for the best on it," Rhodemeyer said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI.
