cards.headline: 2 arrested in string of firearm burglaries across Martin County neighborhoods
cards.teaser: Two 19-year-old men face charges after a nearly monthlong investigation into firearm burglaries affecting multiple Martin County neighborhoods, including gated communities.
cards.body:
Stephen Ivan Morris and Shaun Alexander Bilbrey were arrested following a nearly monthlong investigation into a string of firearm burglaries across neighborhoods in Martin County. Both men, 19, face charges of grand theft, armed burglary, larceny and traveling to commit a burglary. Both were booked into the Martin County Jail on Tuesday.

The investigation into burglaries affecting multiple neighborhoods, including gated communities, began in early August. With assistance from the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office SWAT team and Criminal Investigations Division, Martin County detectives served warrants at the St. Lucie County homes of Morris and Bilbrey.

Multiple guns were recovered, allowing Martin County Sheriff's Office detectives to close about 13 cases and move forward with charges against the suspects.

cards.headline: All 36 Border Collies surrendered after Palm City rescue; adoption applications open Sept. 1
cards.teaser: All 36 Border Collies removed from a Southwest Alligator Street home in Palm City have been legally surrendered to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, and adoption applications will be available starting Sept. 1.
cards.body:
All 36 Border Collies removed from a Palm City home on Southwest Alligator Street earlier this month have been legally surrendered to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast. The dogs were rescued Aug. 10 from the home, where investigators said they found them living without air conditioning and surrounded by feces, urine-soaked materials and debris. Many arrived at the shelter dirty, severely matted and covered in dried waste.

Shelter staff have removed the dogs' matted fur and cleaned away the layers of dried feces as the animals begin their recovery. They've received several baths, vaccinations and veterinary care. Some have been treated for skin infections, body sores, eye infections and intestinal parasites. Two of the Border Collies are still struggling, are very withdrawn and don't make eye contact. Others are perking up already and appear to be super friendly.

Paige O'Donnell, 62, was arrested in the case. She faces 72 charges: 36 third-degree felony counts of animal cruelty and 36 misdemeanor counts alleging animals were kept without sufficient exercise and air. Her bond was set at $270,000, and a judge ordered that she not have pets if released. Adoption applications for the Border Collies, including applications from nonprofit rescue groups, will be available beginning Sept. 1 through the Humane Society's website and Facebook page. Adoption fees will be $140 for adult Border Collies and $175 for puppies.
cards.article_text: All 36 Border Collies removed from a Palm City home earlier this month have now been legally surrendered to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast , clearing the way for medical evaluations and eventual adoptions. "They've come a very, very long way. I can't believe from when they've started to where they are now," said Sarah Fisher, Humane Society of the Treasure Coast Spokesperson. The dogs were rescued Aug. 10 from a home on Southwest Alligator Street, where investigators said they found them living without air conditioning and surrounded by feces, urine-soaked materials and debris. Many arrived at the shelter dirty, severely matted and covered in dried waste. "You know, when they came in, they were very, very terrified. They were saturated in urine and feces," said Lori Tucker, Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, Director of Operations. Since then, shelter staff have removed the dogs’ matted fur and cleaned away the layers of dried feces as the animals begin their recovery. They've received several baths, vaccinations and veterinary care. Some have been treated for skin infections, body sores, eye infections and intestinal parasites. Tucker says two of the Border Collies are still struggling, are very withdrawn and don't make eye contact. Others are perking up already and appear to be super friendly. "I distinctly remember the second day that I came in and the first dog wagged its tail at me and for me, that was, I'll never forget that moment. I will never forget that moment. It was amazing," Tucker said as she fought back tears. Paige O’Donnell, 62, was arrested in the case. She faces 72 charges 36 third-degree felony counts of animal cruelty and 36 misdemeanor counts alleging animals were kept without sufficient exercise and air. Her bond was set at $270,000, and a judge ordered that she not have pets if released. See also: Stuart shakeup, Mayor removed, city manager fired in dramatic end to commission meeting The Humane Society said it will complete medical testing and behavioral evaluations so potential adopters have clear information about each dog’s needs. The dogs will also be spayed or neutered, microchipped and vaccinated on a phased schedule. Some of the Border Collies will need additional veterinary care in the months ahead. "We've seen a lot of organ abnormalities and we think they're just like, defects from probably inbreeding. So we think that it's going to be a long road ahead of them," Fisher said. Adoption applications for the Border Collies, including applications from nonprofit rescue groups, will be available beginning Sept. 1 through the Humane Society’s website and Facebook page . The shelter said applicants will be carefully screened to find appropriate placements. Adoption fees will be $140 for adult Border Collies and $175 for puppies. The shelter is asking people not to call about the dogs so its phone lines remain available for urgent needs. While it does not need pet food or supplies at this time, it is accepting donations to its Emergency Medical Fund to help cover veterinary care for the Border Collies and other shelter animals.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce man charged with manslaughter after fatal BB gun shooting near elementary school
cards.teaser: A 36-year-old Fort Pierce man faces manslaughter charges after fatally shooting a 34-year-old man with a BB gun on Saturday near an elementary school.
cards.body:
Fort Pierce police arrested Jabari Cowart, 36, after he fatally shot a 34-year-old man with a BB gun on Saturday in the 2900 block of Avenue G. The incident occurred near an elementary school where a group of men in their 30s had been shooting a BB gun at trees. Investigators believe Cowart asked to use the BB gun and later pointed it at one of the men before pulling the trigger.

The victim fell to the ground, and officers were called to the scene. Cowart is being held at the St. Lucie County Jail. Ken Noble, marketing manager at The Tactical Store in Fort Pierce, said BB guns can be extremely dangerous. He explained that BB guns, while often considered less harmful than traditional firearms, can still cause serious injury or death.

Noble said anything with a projectile can be a weapon and advised people not to point anything at anyone. He said following safety procedures is critical when handling firearms, including BB guns.

hero.teaser: The National Weather Service issued a tornado warning after reports of funnel clouds came in Sunday evening, but the tornado had already dissipated by that point.
hero.body:
The National Weather Service in Melbourne issued a tornado warning after reports of funnel clouds started coming in Sunday evening in Port St. Lucie, but the tornado had already dissipated at the point the warning was issued. The EF-0 tornado featured very shallow circulation that was not picked up well by radar. Reports of the funnel cloud prompted the warning for the tornado that also became a waterspout at one point.

Will Ulrich, a meteorologist with NWS Melbourne, said what made Sunday's event unique was that it was on the ground for 10 to 15 minutes, which is not typical during summer months. The tornado came from a typical summer afternoon thunderstorm and was brief and weak with winds of 60 to 70 mph, which Ulrich said is still impactful to communities. He said the event is a reminder that Mother Nature will always throw curveballs regardless of the time of year.

The National Weather Service issues a tornado warning once it is able to detect a tornado. The agency says people should have multiple ways to receive warnings to keep themselves and loved ones safe. WPBF 25 News is on-air and streaming live online when a tornado warning is issued in the area.

hero.headline: Woman pleads no contest in Martin County animal hoarding case that rescued 108 animals near Hobe Sound
hero.body:
Gail Giustino pleaded no contest Tuesday to two animal abuse charges stemming from the rescue of 108 animals from a property near Hobe Sound in what officials call Martin County's worst animal hoarding case. Giustino, a 77-year-old mail carrier, will serve two years of probation and is prohibited from having any contact with animals. A no-contest plea means she did not admit guilt but chose not to fight the charges at trial.

Attorney Josh Deckard addressed the sentence outside the Stuart courthouse. "While there was no jail time imposed, my client is required to be on probation for a period of two years. The most important caveat that she has to follow is that she has no contact with any animals," Deckard said. The judge also ordered Giustino to undergo a mental health evaluation and follow any recommended treatment. Violating probation could mean up to two years in county jail.

Tish Ott adopted one of the rescued animals, a dog named Gracie Anne, and described the conditions at the property. "No air conditioning, bad ventilation, lots of fecal matter everywhere," Ott said. Ott has since nursed Gracie Anne back to health and documented the recovery on Facebook. "When I saw her, she had such a look of hopelessness in her eyes, and the moment that I saw that, I just felt that I needed to step up," Ott said. "Now she sleeps in my bed, she's carried around in a snuggle bag 20 hours a day, and as you can see, she's got hope, and she's gorgeous."

Ott reflected on what the animals endured. "No animal deserves to ever, ever live in a situation like that," Ott said. All 108 animals were removed from the property during the rescue operation that led to the charges against Giustino.

"They've come a very, very long way. I can't believe from when they've started to where they are now," said Sarah Fisher, Humane Society of the Treasure Coast Spokesperson. The dogs were rescued Aug. 10 from a home on Southwest Alligator Street, where investigators said they found them living without air conditioning and surrounded by feces, urine-soaked materials and debris. Many arrived at the shelter dirty, severely matted and covered in dried waste. "You know, when they came in, they were very, very terrified. They were saturated in urine and feces," said Lori Tucker, Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, Director of Operations. Since then, shelter staff have removed the dogs’ matted fur and cleaned away the layers of dried feces as the animals begin their recovery. They've received several baths, vaccinations and veterinary care. Some have been treated for skin infections, body sores, eye infections and intestinal parasites. Tucker says two of the Border Collies are still struggling, are very withdrawn and don't make eye contact. Others are perking up already and appear to be super friendly. "I distinctly remember the second day that I came in and the first dog wagged its tail at me and for me, that was, I'll never forget that moment. I will never forget that moment. It was amazing," Tucker said as she fought back tears. Paige O’Donnell, 62, was arrested in the case. She faces 72 charges 36 third-degree felony counts of animal cruelty and 36 misdemeanor counts alleging animals were kept without sufficient exercise and air. Her bond was set at $270,000, and a judge ordered that she not have pets if released. See also: Stuart shakeup, Mayor removed, city manager fired in dramatic end to commission meeting The Humane Society said it will complete medical testing and behavioral evaluations so potential adopters have clear information about each dog’s needs. The dogs will also be spayed or neutered, microchipped and vaccinated on a phased schedule. Some of the Border Collies will need additional veterinary care in the months ahead. "We've seen a lot of organ abnormalities and we think they're just like, defects from probably inbreeding. So we think that it's going to be a long road ahead of them," Fisher said. Adoption applications for the Border Collies, including applications from nonprofit rescue groups, will be available beginning Sept. 1 through the Humane Society’s website and Facebook page . The shelter said applicants will be carefully screened to find appropriate placements. Adoption fees will be $140 for adult Border Collies and $175 for puppies. The shelter is asking people not to call about the dogs so its phone lines remain available for urgent needs. While it does not need pet food or supplies at this time, it is accepting donations to its Emergency Medical Fund to help cover veterinary care for the Border Collies and other shelter animals.

hero.headline: Gov. DeSantis orders Florida flags to half-staff through Sept. 1 following Dolly Parton's death
hero.body:
Gov. Ron DeSantis on Tuesday ordered flags across Florida lowered to half-staff following the death of country music icon Dolly Parton. The directive applies to U.S. and Florida flags at all state and local government buildings, installations and grounds through sunset Sept. 1.

The governor's office said the order follows a directive from the president. Parton died peacefully Tuesday in Nashville at age 80, according to her publicist. The Tennessee native became one of the most recognizable figures in country music during a career that spanned decades.

Parton wrote hundreds of songs, including Jolene, Coat of Many Colors and I Will Always Love You, while also building a career in film, business and philanthropy. She founded the Imagination Library, which provides free books to children, and opened Dollywood in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee.

The governor's office released a statement saying the flags will be flown at half-staff as a mark of respect pursuant to the president's order. The flag directive covers all state and local government facilities throughout Florida until the end of the day Sept. 1.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds selects Miami-Dade Sen. Bryan Avila as running mate in Florida governor's race
cards.teaser: Republican gubernatorial nominee Byron Donalds selected Miami-Dade state Sen. Bryan Avila as his running mate Tuesday, adding a Cuban-American lawmaker and Florida Army National Guard captain to the GOP ticket.
cards.body:
Republican gubernatorial nominee Byron Donalds selected Miami-Dade state Sen. Bryan Avila as his running mate Tuesday, adding a Cuban-American lawmaker, educator and Florida Army National Guard captain to the GOP ticket. Donalds announced the pick at Miami's Freedom Tower, a landmark closely tied to South Florida's Cuban exile community.

Avila was born and raised in Hialeah after his parents, Adrian and Rosa Maria Avila, fled Cuba. He now lives in Miami Springs with his wife, Cindy, and their two children. Avila was first elected to the Florida House in 2014 and eventually rose to speaker pro tempore. He won election to the Senate in 2022 and currently chairs the Finance and Tax Committee.

Donalds and Avila will campaign on affordability, lower taxes, public safety, parental rights and school choice. They face Democratic nominee David Jolly and his running mate, former Democratic Congresswoman Gwen Graham, in the November general election. Jolly congratulated Avila on the selection but argued the race will remain centered on Donalds' close political alliance with President Donald Trump.
cards.article_text: Republican gubernatorial nominee Byron Donalds selected Miami-Dade state Sen. Bryan Avila as his running mate Tuesday, adding a Cuban-American lawmaker, educator and Florida Army National Guard captain to the GOP ticket.Donalds announced the pick at Miami’s Freedom Tower, a landmark closely tied to South Florida’s Cuban exile community. He framed the partnership around their families’ pursuit of opportunity and a shared commitment to conservative policies.“I came to Florida at 17 years old with a trunk full of clothes, chasing a dream. Bryan Avila is the son of Cuban exiles who fled communism so their children could live in freedom,” Donalds said. “We didn’t inherit political names. We didn’t inherit political birthrights, but what we inherited was the responsibility to fight for the state that gave our families everything.”Avila was born and raised in Hialeah after his parents, Adrian and Rosa Maria Avila, fled Cuba. He now lives in Miami Springs with his wife, Cindy, his high school sweetheart, and their two children.The selection gives Donalds, a Southwest Florida congressman, a running mate with deep political and personal ties to Miami-Dade and its influential Cuban-American community.Avila was first elected to the Florida House in 2014 and eventually rose to speaker pro tempore. He won election to the Senate in 2022 and currently chairs the Finance and Tax Committee.Donalds praised Avila as a “proven warrior,” pointing to his work on property taxes, toll relief, human trafficking, conservation and a new law intended to protect utility customers and water supplies as large-scale data centers expand in Florida.Avila also sponsored the Stop WOKE Act, one of Gov. Ron DeSantis’ signature culture-war measures. The law restricts certain instruction and training involving race, discrimination and privilege in schools and workplaces. Critics called it an attack on free speech, and parts of the law have been blocked by federal courts.Avila used his first speech as Donalds’ running mate to focus on his parents’ experience under communism and draw a contrast with Democrats he accused of embracing socialism.“My parents fled communist Cuba and left behind their home and their business because they knew what happens when government takes over, when freedom disappears and when socialism turns opportunity into misery,” Avila said.“So when I hear Democrats casually embracing socialism, I know where that road leads,” he added. “Our families have lived it. I can assure you this: with Byron Donalds as governor and me as your lieutenant governor, socialism will never find a home in the great state of Florida.”Democratic nominee David Jolly congratulated Avila on the selection but argued the race will remain centered on Donalds’ close political alliance with President Donald Trump.“I wish him well,” Jolly said. “But, let’s be honest: this race won’t come down to Byron Donalds’ relationship with Avila, it will come down to Byron’s relationship with Donald Trump.”Beyond politics, Avila serves as a captain in the Florida Army National Guard. His service has included hurricane response missions, command of military units and support for Florida’s COVID-19 response. He also works as an academic dean at the Doral College School of Criminal Justice.Donalds and Avila will campaign on affordability, lower taxes, public safety, parental rights and school choice. They face Jolly and his running mate, former Democratic Congresswoman Gwen Graham, in the November general election.

hero.headline: Martin County PAL Jeep Duck Scavenger Hunt fundraiser set for Sept. 19
hero.body:
Martin County Police Athletic League is hosting a Jeep Duck Scavenger Hunt on Sept. 19 to raise money for youth mentorship, leadership and athletics programs in Martin County. Registration costs $25 per Jeep, and participants can purchase a $10 clue sheet that includes hints and a map to help teams navigate the scavenger hunt route. Participants must complete the scavenger hunt in a Jeep.

Martin County PAL Executive Director Noel DelValle said the nonprofit works closely with children and teens throughout the community through leadership and athletic programming. The organization also partners with schools and the court system through intervention and diversion programs aimed at helping children stay on a positive path. DelValle said Martin County Police Athletic League works with youth in Martin County and develops kids into healthy, productive leaders of the future.

The fundraiser centers around Jeep culture and the popular ducking tradition, where Jeep owners exchange decorative rubber ducks as a way to recognize customized vehicles and fellow Jeep enthusiasts. Director of Strategic Growth Meg Shirey said the event has become one of the organizations signature fundraisers. Shirey said the event helps showcase both local businesses and the nonprofits community programs while bringing Jeep owners together from across Martin County.

Program Manager Kim Zimmerman said the scavenger hunt includes themed awards and unique Jeep duck trophies for participants. Zimmerman said each duck is given to the most unique Jeep in different categories. Proceeds from the fundraiser directly support programs that provide mentorship opportunities, athletics and leadership development for local children and teens. Registration information is available at martincountypal.org.

hero.headline: Woman pleads no contest in Martin County's worst animal hoarding case involving 108 animals near Hobe Sound
hero.body:
Gail Giustino, a 77-year-old mail carrier arrested after more than 100 animals were rescued from a property near Hobe Sound, pleaded no contest Tuesday to two animal abuse charges in what officials call Martin County's worst animal hoarding case. Giustino will serve two years of probation and is prohibited from having any contact with animals. A no-contest plea means she did not admit guilt but chose not to fight the charges at trial.

Attorney Josh Deckard addressed the sentence outside the Stuart courthouse. The judge also ordered Giustino to undergo a mental health evaluation and follow any recommended treatment. Violating probation could mean up to two years in county jail.

A total of 108 animals were rescued from the property. Tish Ott, who adopted one of those animals, a dog named Gracie Anne, described the conditions the animals were living in as having no air conditioning, bad ventilation, and fecal matter everywhere. Ott said when she first met Gracie at the rescue, the dog had a look of hopelessness in her eyes.

Ott has since nursed Gracie Anne back to health and documented every step on Facebook. Gracie now sleeps in her bed and is carried around in a snuggle bag 20 hours a day. Ott said no animal deserves to ever live in a situation like that.

cards.headline: Two St. Lucie County men arrested in Martin County burglary spree targeting firearms
cards.teaser: Stephen Ivan Morris and Shaun Alexander Bilbrey, both 19, face multiple charges after detectives recovered stolen firearms and closed at least 13 burglary cases.
cards.body:
Stephen Ivan Morris, 19, and Shaun Alexander Bilbrey, 19, both of St. Lucie County, were arrested on multiple charges after Martin County Sheriff's Office detectives solved an ongoing burglary case involving the theft of multiple firearms from several neighborhoods, including gated communities. The burglaries began in early August and as detectives worked to piece the cases together, they identified commonalities that ultimately led them to Morris and Bilbrey.

With assistance from the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office SWAT Team and the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Criminal Investigations Division, Martin County detectives served simultaneous search warrants early Wednesday morning at the homes of both men. Multiple stolen firearms were recovered and detectives were able to close at least 13 cases.

Morris and Bilbrey face multiple charges, including grand theft, armed burglary, larceny and traveling to commit burglary. They are being held at Martin County Jail.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce man charged with manslaughter after fatal BB gun shooting near elementary school
cards.teaser: Jabari Cowart, 36, is accused of fatally shooting a 34-year-old man with a BB gun on Saturday in the 2900 block of Avenue G.
cards.body:
Jabari Cowart, 36, has been charged with manslaughter after Fort Pierce police say he fatally shot a 34-year-old man with a BB gun on Saturday near an elementary school. The incident happened in the 2900 block of Avenue G, where a group of men in their 30s had been shooting a BB gun at trees. Investigators believe Cowart asked to use the BB gun and later pointed it at one of the men before pulling the trigger. The victim fell to the ground, and officers were called to the scene.

Ken Noble, marketing manager at The Tactical Store in Fort Pierce, said BB guns can be extremely dangerous because they involve a piece of metal moving really fast. Noble explained that anything with a projectile can be a weapon and that anything moving fast enough can penetrate skin, hit vital spots, and be very lethal.

Fort Pierce police said Cowart is being held at the St. Lucie County Jail. Noble shared safety advice for handling firearms, including BB guns, saying you should not point anything at anyone and that following safety procedures prevents problems.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie approves $14.83 annual trash fee increase despite ongoing service complaints
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie residents will pay $482.16 annually for trash service after the City Council approved a $14.83 increase to the solid waste assessment Monday night. The council approved Resolution 26-R70, raising the fee from $467.33 per dwelling unit for the fiscal year beginning in October. The increase amounts to about $1.24 more per month for residential properties.

City officials said the increase is required under Port St. Lucie's solid waste franchise agreement with FCC Environmental Service and reflects rising costs for labor, equipment, vehicle maintenance and fuel. The new $482.16 assessment remains below the city's previously established maximum rate of $513.70. cards.headline: National Weather Service confirms EF0 tornado touched down in Port St. Lucie
cards.teaser: An EF0 tornado damaged 20 to 30 homes along a 2.1-mile path through Port St. Lucie Sunday evening, the National Weather Service confirmed Monday.
cards.body:
The National Weather Service confirmed that an EF0 tornado touched down Sunday evening in St. Lucie County, damaging about 20 to 30 homes along a 2.1-mile path. Will Ulrich, warning coordination meteorologist with the National Weather Service Melbourne office, announced the findings Monday morning during a press conference at Jessica Clinton Park following a damage survey of the affected areas.

The tornado, classified as a landspout, first touched down around 6:10 p.m. near Southeast Kitching Cove Lane and Southeast Morningside Boulevard, close to the Tarpon Bay Yacht Club. It produced minimal structural damage, including roof damage, soffit damage and pool enclosures lifted from their foundations. The tornado then moved over the St. Lucie River, where it became a waterspout for approximately five to seven minutes before moving back onshore in the Bay St. Lucie community around 6:20 p.m.

The strongest wind gusts occurred in the Bay St. Lucie community, where the tornado caused numerous downed trees and large branches, along with damage to well-built homes with tile roofs from winds of 65 to 75 mph. The tornado continued west into Port St. Lucie communities near the Southbend area, where it caused discontinuous damage including downed trees, blown-over fences, and damaged or destroyed pool screen enclosures before dissipating. The entire event lasted approximately 14 to 15 minutes. No injuries were reported.

The National Weather Service in Melbourne issued a tornado warning after reports of funnel clouds started to come in Sunday evening in Port St. Lucie, though at the point the warning was issued, the tornado had already dissipated. Because the tornado featured very shallow circulation, it was not picked up well by radar. Reports of the funnel cloud are what prompted the warning for the EF-0 tornado that became a waterspout at one point.

Will Ulrich, a meteorologist with NWS Melbourne, said what made Sunday's event unique was that it was on the ground for 10 to 15 minutes, which is not typical during summer months. The tornado was one of the typical summer afternoon thunderstorms that generated a brief and weak tornado with winds of 60 to 70 mph, which is still impactful to communities. Ulrich said the event is a reminder that Mother Nature will always throw curveballs regardless of the time of year.

The National Weather Service is in charge of issuing tornado warnings. Once the agency is able to detect a tornado, it will always issue a tornado warning. The National Weather Service says residents should make sure they have multiple ways to receive warnings to keep themselves and their loved ones safe.

hero.headline: Martin County commissioners move toward one-year pause on large data center development
hero.body:
Martin County commissioners voted Tuesday to direct staff to prepare a proposal for a one-year moratorium on large-scale data center development while the county examines potential effects on the community. The discussion followed public comments from residents and others who raised concerns about electricity costs, water supply and nearby property values during the County Commission meeting.

Former gubernatorial candidate and businessman James Fishback spoke during public comment, questioning whether data centers provide any benefits to Martin County residents. He asked commissioners to consider whether accepting higher electric bills, lower water pressure and lower property values is justified for a two-million-square-foot facility.

Commissioner Ed Ciampi said the county should study what data centers could mean for the environment, economy and community while allowing residents and experts to weigh in. Commissioner Sarah Heard Vargas said she supports a hard pause while officials continue researching the issue. County staff and the county attorney are expected to return with information about the county's authority to impose a moratorium, including potential legal questions involving state laws SB 180 and SB 484. The county attorney said Tuesday that the laws create a legal gray area.

A moratorium is not currently in effect in Martin County. Any proposed ordinance establishing a moratorium would likely require two public hearings. Commissioners have not yet set a date for the proposal to return for a formal vote.

hero.teaser: A 19-year-old woman faces fraud charges after deputies say she used two fake $50 bills to pay for an $83.90 food delivery order in Fort Pierce on August 22.
hero.body:
A 19-year-old woman was arrested Monday after she allegedly used counterfeit currency to pay for a food delivery order in Fort Pierce on August 22, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office. Adrianna Marie Sheppard faces multiple charges after a delivery driver reported receiving two fake $50 bills as payment for an $83.90 meal order.

Deputies initially responded to the theft report on August 22 involving the food delivery transaction where the customer paid with counterfeit bills. On Monday, law enforcement learned that the individual who used the fake money was staying at a residence on Miramar Avenue in Fort Pierce. Upon arriving at the location, deputies quickly identified Sheppard as the person who provided the counterfeit currency to the delivery driver.

Sheppard was promptly arrested at the Miramar Avenue residence. She was charged with fraud utter bank bill, note, check or draft, possession of counterfeited bank bill, note, check or draft, and larceny. The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office handled the investigation into the counterfeit currency incident.

The arrest came nearly two weeks after the initial theft report was filed by the food delivery driver who discovered the bills were fake. Law enforcement did not release additional details about how authorities tracked Sheppard to the Fort Pierce residence or whether other counterfeit bills were recovered during the arrest.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie High School senior in ICE custody after traffic stop on way to school
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie High School senior Emmanuel Nelson, an 18-year-old football player and wrestler, has been held in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody since last Wednesday following a traffic stop on his way to school. Port St. Lucie police stopped Nelson around 8:30 a.m. on Wednesday for traveling 45 miles per hour in an active school zone with a 20-mile-per-hour speed limit. The officer ran Nelson's information through D.A.V.I.D., a Driver and Vehicle Information Database, which showed the student as a non-U.S. citizen. The officer contacted ICE, arrested Nelson and placed him on ICE detainer.

Nelson is now at an ICE detention center in Broward County. An ICE spokesperson said Nelson legally entered the United States on Jan. 16, 2016, but failed to comply with the terms of his admission and is now in violation of immigration law. He will remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings.

A family spokesperson said Nelson entered the country under the Haitian Family Reunification Program and has been petitioned for by a U.S. citizen step-parent. The spokesperson said the appropriate documentation was submitted for permanent residency and the application is pending. During that time, Nelson was issued a valid employment authorization document and a Social Security number. He was enrolled in school and had a valid driver's license while waiting for the application to be approved. The spokesperson added that people are considered minors until the age of 21 for immigration purposes.

The St. Lucie County School District released a statement saying St. Lucie Public Schools does not comment on immigration enforcement matters, as they fall under the authority of federal agencies and are outside the school district's jurisdiction. The Port St. Lucie High School community has shown an outpouring of support for Nelson on social media.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie approves $14.83 trash fee increase for residents
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie residents will pay $482.16 annually for trash service starting in October after the City Council approved a $14.83 increase Monday night.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie residents will pay more for trash service after the City Council approved an increase to the annual solid waste assessment Monday night. The council approved Resolution 26-R70, raising the annual assessment by $14.83 per dwelling unit, from $467.33 to $482.16 for the fiscal year beginning in October. There was no public comment or council discussion before the item was read and approved.

The assessment pays for garbage collection, disposal services, facilities and related solid waste programs. It is collected through residents' property tax bills. The increase amounts to about $1.24 more per month for residential properties. City officials previously said the increase is required under Port St. Lucie's solid waste franchise agreement with FCC Environmental Service and reflects rising costs for labor, equipment, vehicle maintenance and fuel. The new $482.16 assessment remains below the city's previously established maximum rate of $513.70.

The increase comes as Port St. Lucie's trash service remains a major issue for residents. The city previously reached a $24 million settlement with Waste Pro over poor service, and voters are expected to decide in November whether to bring back twice-weekly garbage pickup.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie residents clean up debris, damaged structures after Sunday tornado
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie residents spent Monday cleaning up after an EF0 tornado tore through the area Sunday night with 65 to 75 mph winds, leaving behind damaged structures, debris-filled pools and downed foliage.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie residents spent Monday cleaning up after a storm tore through the area Sunday night, leaving behind damaged structures, debris-filled pools and downed foliage. The National Weather Service determined it was an EF0 tornado, with 65 to 75 mph winds. Aron Christiansen spent the morning pulling debris out of his pool after already retrieving furniture from the bottom. Video from a neighbor's camera captured the moment his patio broke apart during the storm. Half of the patio is now out on the curb, set to be salvaged for recycling. Christiansen said he looked out the windows and saw debris flying, thinking it was birds at first. He had about 10 seconds before it hit his house.

Janelle Pierre-Louis said she was surprised by the amount of damage to her backyard foliage after dealing with damage at the front of her house first. Her front door caved in and dirt came through the cracks. Around the corner, Mitch Brewer had debris piled out front, most of it from a shed he had tied down. He said it looked like it caught some heavy updrafts and left. Brewer said he had been thinking about demolishing the old shed at some point, but Mother Nature beat him to it.

Florida sees about 65 to 70 tornadoes a year, according to the Florida Climate Center, and has a higher frequency per 10,000 square miles than any other state, including Oklahoma. Marlene Torres had just come back from Jensen Beach celebrating her birthday Sunday night before returning home to find the storm had moved through her neighborhood. Her home was not damaged, but she needed an electrician to fix her meter. Torres said she is the only one with no electricity because her power was more damaged than other folks in the area.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie resident takes cover as possible tornado hits neighborhood Sunday
cards.teaser: Aaron Christiansen was home around 6 p.m. Sunday when he noticed strange weather through his window near Southbend Boulevard and Southeast Navy Avenue in Port St. Lucie and immediately took cover.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie residents are cleaning up after a possible tornado or landspout hit their neighborhood near Southbend Boulevard and Southeast Navy Avenue on Sunday. Aaron Christiansen said he was home around 6 p.m. when he noticed something strange through his window. He immediately took cover, and moments later found significant damage in his backyard. Christiansen said he saw dark clouds and a bunch of white objects that he thought looked like birds. He got closer and realized it was debris. He tried to hustle his dogs into his bedroom so they could all take cover. He had about 10 seconds to react before the storm hit.

His patio furniture was submerged in his pool, his pool fence was blown toward his home, debris was scattered across the ground and plants were blown away. Christiansen, originally from Minnesota, said his experience with tornado-like weather helped him know what precautions to take. He and his family and pets were not injured. Christiansen said he received the emergency alert after the storm had already hit. He said he plans to begin cleanup efforts Monday and will also have his roof inspected.

hero.headline: Stuart city commission ousts mayor, fires city manager in sweeping leadership shakeup
hero.body:
The Stuart City Commission voted Monday night to replace Mayor Sean Reed with Commissioner Eula Clarke and fire City Manager Michael Giardino after just four months on the job. The changes followed a recent election that flipped the commission majority less than a week ago. Commissioner Laura Giobbi opposed the mayoral change and walked out of the meeting before the city manager vote.

The commission voted 3 to 1 to dismiss Giardino and moved to bring back former City Manager Michael Mortell, who was fired by the previous commission 10 months ago. Commissioner Campbell Rich defended the move by referencing concerns over Florida's Amendment 3, which would significantly reduce property tax revenue for municipalities. Rich said the city needs the most experienced leadership possible to navigate that potential budget crisis.

Giobbi said over the phone she felt Giardino was very capable of running city operations and that the move was politically motivated and not necessary. She had argued that Reed should have been allowed to serve a full year as mayor. Reed posted on Facebook that he was disappointed his fellow commissioners felt it was necessary to remove him as mayor prior to the board's scheduled reorganization in December.

Resident Catherine Collier Kyroulis expressed concern about the direction of the changes, saying going backwards is not the correct direction. Resident Andy Noble, who spoke during public comment at the meeting, said the outcome restored some faith that the democratic process works. The new interim city manager acknowledged the weight of the evening, calling it a night of change and a very unusual night.

cards.headline: Martin County man crashes SUV into church after fleeing deputies, faces DUI charges
cards.teaser: A Martin County man who crashed into a church is accused of driving under the influence and fleeing from police after deputies say he swerved onto the grass while traveling northbound on SW Washington Avenue through a residential neighborhood.
cards.body:
Geremias Pascual, 28, was seen swerving onto the grass while traveling northbound on SW Washington Avenue through a residential neighborhood Monday, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. Despite deputies attempts to stop him, Pascual refused to stop. Deputies used a PIT maneuver to slow down the SUV Pascual was traveling in, but the maneuver did not work. Pascual only started going faster after the attempted PIT maneuver.

Pascual then crashed into a tree, a power pole, and the side of a local church. The damage to the church destroyed its air-conditioning unit and caused thousands of dollars in damages. Deputies ordered Pascual to step out of the vehicle and placed him under arrest.

Pascual is being charged with fleeing and eluding, DUI, and four counts of criminal mischief or damage to property.

hero.teaser: A 19-year-old Fort Pierce woman was arrested Monday after deputies say she used two fake $50 bills to pay for an $83.90 food delivery order on August 22.
hero.body:
A Fort Pierce woman was arrested Monday for allegedly using counterfeit bills to pay for a food delivery order that occurred in late August. Adrianna Marie Sheppard, 19, faces multiple charges after deputies say she used two fake $50 bills to pay for an $83.90 meal delivery on August 22.

The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office responded to a reported theft involving the food delivery in which the customer used counterfeit currency as payment. Deputies investigated the incident in which two counterfeit $50 bills were allegedly used to pay for the order. The case remained under investigation for several weeks before authorities located the suspect.

On Monday, deputies learned that Sheppard was staying at a residence on Miramar Avenue in Fort Pierce. Upon arrival at the location, they quickly identified Sheppard as the person who provided the fake money to pay for the food delivery. She was promptly arrested at the residence.

Sheppard was charged with fraud utter bank bill, note, check or draft, possession of counterfeited bank bill, note, check or draft, and larceny. The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office handled the investigation into the counterfeit currency case.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie raises annual trash fee to $482 despite ongoing pickup complaints
hero.teaser: The Port St. Lucie City Council approved a $14.83 increase to the annual solid waste assessment Monday night, raising the fee from $467.33 to $482.16 per dwelling unit starting in October.
hero.body:
The Port St. Lucie City Council approved Resolution 26-R70 Monday night, raising the annual solid waste assessment by $14.83 per dwelling unit, from $467.33 to $482.16 for the fiscal year beginning in October. The council approved the item with no public comment or discussion. The assessment pays for garbage collection, disposal services, facilities and related solid waste programs and is collected through property tax bills.

The increase amounts to about $1.24 more per month for residential properties. City officials said the increase is required under Port St. Lucie's solid waste franchise agreement with FCC Environmental Service and reflects rising costs for labor, equipment, vehicle maintenance and fuel. The new $482.16 assessment remains below the city's previously established maximum rate of $513.70.

The increase comes as Port St. Lucie's trash service remains a major issue for residents. The city previously reached a $24 million settlement with Waste Pro over poor service. Voters are expected to decide in November whether to bring back twice-weekly garbage pickup.

cards.body:

The meeting resulted in Clarke replacing Mayor Sean Reed, a new vice mayor, and efforts to reinstate former City Manager Michael Mortell, who was fired by the previous commission 10 months ago.

Reed posted a statement on Facebook saying he remained proud of his work and disappointed that fellow commissioners removed him as mayor before the board's scheduled reorganization in December.

The commission voted 3 to 1 to dismiss Giardino just four months after he started as city manager. Commissioner Campbell Rich defended the move, citing concerns over Florida's Amendment 3, which would significantly reduce property tax revenue for municipalities. Rich said the city needed the most experienced person to negotiate through that difficult period, not someone with training wheels. Giobbi said over the phone she felt Giardino was very capable of running operations and that the move was politically motivated.

Resident Catherine Collier Kyroulis expressed concern about the direction of the changes, saying going backwards is not the correct direction. Resident Andy Noble, who spoke during public comment, said the decisions restored some faith that the democratic process works and that elections have consequences. Noble said he hopes the city can move forward together despite the divisions.

hero.headline: All 36 Border Collies surrendered in Palm City cruelty case; adoptions open Sept. 1
hero.body:
All 36 Border Collies removed from a Palm City home earlier this month have been legally surrendered to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, clearing the way for medical evaluations and eventual adoptions. The dogs were rescued Aug. 10 from a home on Southwest Alligator Street, where investigators said they found them living without air conditioning and surrounded by feces, urine-soaked materials and debris. Many arrived at the shelter dirty, severely matted and covered in dried waste.

Paige ODonnell, 62, was arrested in the case. She faces 72 charges, including 36 third-degree felony counts of animal cruelty and 36 misdemeanor counts alleging animals were kept without sufficient exercise and air. Her bond was set at $270,000, and a judge ordered that she not have pets if released.

Since the rescue, shelter staff have removed the dogs matted fur and cleaned away the layers of dried feces as the animals begin their recovery. The Humane Society said it will complete medical testing and behavioral evaluations so potential adopters have clear information about each dogs needs. The dogs will also be spayed or neutered, microchipped and vaccinated on a phased schedule.

Adoption applications for the Border Collies, including applications from nonprofit rescue groups, will be available beginning Sept. 1 through the Humane Society's website and Facebook page. The shelter said applicants will be carefully screened to find appropriate placements. Adoption fees will be $140 for adult Border Collies and $175 for puppies. The shelter is asking people not to call about the dogs so its phone lines remain available for urgent needs. While it does not need pet food or supplies at this time, it is accepting donations to its Emergency Medical Fund to help cover veterinary care for the Border Collies and other shelter animals.

cards.headline: Ronald Corbin, Martin County High School choral teacher for 34 years, dies
cards.teaser: Ronald Corbin, who taught choral music at Martin County High School in Stuart for 34 years and led the OPUS choir until his retirement in 2014, died Saturday.
cards.body:
Corbin began his teaching career at Bartow High School in Polk County and came to Martin County High School in Stuart in 1980. He led OPUS, which stands for Outstanding People United to Sing, until he retired in 2014. The school district said he dedicated his career to helping students find their voices and discover the joy of music. Corbin was also known for volunteering as a scorekeeper for basketball and volleyball and traveling across the state to support Martin County High School athletics.

His choirs consistently earned superior ratings at district and state performance assessments and were recognized as Choirs of Distinction by the Florida Vocal Association. Corbin was added to the FVA Roll of Distinction in 2014. In 2017, he received the R. Wayne Hugoboom Distinguished Service Award from the Florida chapter of the American Choral Directors Association. The Corbin Musical Arts Center at Martin County High School was dedicated in his name in 2015.

In 2018 at Cleveland Clinic in Weston, Corbin received a new kidney from his daughter, Candice Corbin, who was also one of his former students. After ending his 40-plus years of teaching, he remained a familiar face and voice at the Stuart school. Last March, alumni gathered to honor Corbin in song.
cards.article_text: Corbin, a popular choral teacher at Martin County High School for 34 years, died Saturday. He began his teaching career at Bartow High School in Polk County, and in 1980 came to the school in Stuart. He led OPUS, which stands for Outstanding People United to Sing, until he retired in 2014 "after dedicating his career to helping students find their voices and discover the joy of music," the school district posted on Instagram. "Our thoughts and hearts go to the family, friends, and generations of Martin County students who had the privilege of knowing Mr. Ron Corbin." He was known for more than being a choir teacher. Corbin volunteered as a scorekeeper for basketball and volleyball, and traveled across the state to support Martin County High School athletics. Corbin gave so much of his life to our students, our schools and our community," the district said. "His impact cannot be measured in years or accolades—it lives on in the countless students he encouraged, the music he helped create and the memories shared by those who knew him. "We are deeply grateful for the life he shared with Martin County, and we will carry his memory with us, forever in our hearts. Once a Tiger, always a Tiger." The Florida Vocal Association also noted his passing. "His choirs consistently earned superior ratings at district and state performance assessments and were recognized as Choirs of Distinction by FVA. Corbin was added to the Roll of Distinction in 2014," the FVA wrote on Facebook. Corbin was added to the Roll of Distinction in 2014. In 2017, he received the R. Wayne Hugoboom Distinguished Service Award from the Florida chapter of the American Choral Directors Association. Corbin Musical Arts Center at Martin County High School was dedicated in his name in 2015. "We remember Ron with gratitude for his years of service, his passion for choral music, his mentorship, and the countless students and educators whose lives were enriched by his presence," FVA posted. "Our deepest condolences go to Ron's family, friends, former students, and the many members of FVA and the choral communities who loved and respected him." Corbin received a scholarship to attend Florida A M University, where he studied music. After ending his 40-plus years of teaching, he remained a familiar face and voice at the Stuart school. Last March, alumni gathered to honor Corbin in song. New kidney In 2018 at Cleveland Clinic in Weston, he received a new kidney from his daughter, Candice Corbin, who also was one of his former students. "I was walking down the street and suddenly, I felt like I was inebriated," Ronald said in an article by the Cleveland Clinic. "That's when I said, whoa, something is wrong." A follow-up appointment with his primary care doctor led to a visit with a nephrologist, who told him he had chronic kidney disease and would need to begin dialysis treatment immediately. Candice, an accomplished singer who lives in New York, began thinking about what she could do to support her dad. "I was shocked when he told me he needed to go on dialysis," Candice said. "I remember thinking, I need to learn more and figure out what happens next." She continued to monitor her dad’s health over the next three years, knowing that one day, she would undergo testing to determine whether she was a successful match. After completing initial testing in New York, Candice called her dad to share the news. "When I told him I was a match, I think we were both shocked," Candice said. "And I said, wow, this is really happening." "It just took my breath away that she would want to give me her kidney," Ronald said. Candice then began traveling to Florida to meet with Cleveland Clinic Florida's multidisciplinary transplant team to prepare herself and her dad for surgery. He received his new kidney from his daughter a few weeks before Father's Day. "I'm blessed to have her in my life, that she would think enough of me to do this for me," he said. "I don’t think there's anything I can think of that would be a better gift than the one I got." A GoFundMe fundraising effort raised more than $23,000, including members of his Tiger community. Safe after being missing In March 2023, he was found safe after going missing for almost 24 hours. Corbin was found along Interstate 95 and was taken to the hospital. He was last seen driving his gray Honda CRV heading west on St. Lucie Boulevard in Port St. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

hero.headline: Florida leads nation in ACA coverage losses as 440,000 drop plans after subsidy expiration
hero.body:
About 440,000 Floridians dropped their Affordable Care Act health insurance plans this year after Congress allowed enhanced federal subsidies to expire in January, more than any other state in the nation. The subsidy expiration forced millions of Americans to decide whether to keep insurance that often doubled or tripled in cost or risk going without coverage.

Florida's large population of gig workers, entrepreneurs and small business owners relies heavily on the federal health insurance marketplace, making the state one of the nation's most visible epicenters of the impact. Elijah Button, a 21-year-old chef in St. Cloud, gave up his ACA plan in January after a $100 monthly premium hike he couldn't afford. When he sliced his middle finger to the bone while chopping onions in June, he asked his uncle for help instead of seeking emergency care. With a butterfly bandage, splint and daily cleanings and dressings, the wound healed. Thousands more Floridians who kept coverage are struggling to get by as prices of necessities like groceries and gasoline remain steep, and health insurers project another year of double-digit premium hikes.

Congress has taken no action to replace the lost subsidy funds months after the expiration. In the deep-red state where congressional districts were recently redrawn to strongly favor Republicans, the cost of healthcare has become a major campaign issue. Republican midterm candidates have been promoting fraud crackdowns to protect federal health programs, while Democrats have been urging voters to help Congress change hands so they can restore subsidies.

The struggles in Florida reflect broader nationwide concerns over rising healthcare costs and a lack of meaningful policy to address them. Some residents are dealing with strained budgets and exorbitant medical bills, while others avoid the doctor in fear of the cost.

But having given up his Affordable Care Act health insurance plan in January because of a $100 monthly premium hike he couldn't afford, the 21-year-old in St. Cloud didn't have the money for emergency care. 'Going to the hospital for it wasn't even an option,' he said, gesturing toward his finger before preparing a pot roast for his aunt and uncle in their suburban home. 'My first thought was, 'how am I going to fix this?'' Some are dealing with strained budgets and exorbitant medical bills, while others avoid the doctor in fear of the cost. hero.headline: Vero Beach man crashes during high-speed chase, K9 finds him hiding under brush
hero.body:
A Vero Beach man is facing multiple charges after deputies say he fled a traffic stop, crashed his vehicle and hid under nearby brush. Christopher John Baptist was pulled over for a minor traffic violation but took off, reaching speeds more than 50 mph over the limit, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office.

The pursuit ended when Baptist crashed his vehicle and fled on foot. Deputies called in K9 Remy, who tracked Baptist to a nearby area and found him hiding under brush. Baptist was taken into custody.

Baptist faces charges including fleeing and eluding at high speed, speeding more than 50 mph over the posted limit, providing false identification, resisting without violence, leaving the scene of a crash, driving with a suspended license, possession of a controlled substance, possession of drug paraphernalia, and felony probation violation.

The sheriff's office shared the arrest as part of its latest enforcement updates. Baptist remains in custody as he faces the charges.

hero.headline: Ronald L. Corbin, Martin County High School choral teacher for 34 years, dies
hero.body:
Ronald L. Corbin, a choral teacher at Martin County High School in Stuart for 34 years, died Saturday. Corbin began his teaching career at Bartow High School in Polk County and came to Martin County High School in 1980. He led OPUS, which stands for Outstanding People United to Sing, until he retired in 2014.

Corbin volunteered as a scorekeeper for basketball and volleyball and traveled across the state to support Martin County High School athletics. The Corbin Musical Arts Center at Martin County High School was dedicated in his name in 2015. His choirs consistently earned superior ratings at district and state performance assessments and were recognized as Choirs of Distinction by the Florida Vocal Association.

The Florida Vocal Association added Corbin to the Roll of Distinction in 2014. In 2017, he received the R. Wayne Hugoboom Distinguished Service Award from the Florida chapter of the American Choral Directors Association. Corbin received a scholarship to attend Florida A&M University, where he studied music. After ending his 40-plus years of teaching, he remained a familiar face and voice at the Stuart school. Last March, alumni gathered to honor Corbin in song.

In 2018 at Cleveland Clinic in Weston, Corbin received a new kidney from his daughter, Candice Corbin, who was also one of his former students. A GoFundMe fundraising effort raised more than $23,000, including members of his Tiger community. In March 2023, Corbin was found safe after going missing for almost 24 hours. He was last seen driving his gray Honda CRV heading west on St. Lucie Boulevard in Port St. Lucie and was found along Interstate 95 before being taken to the hospital.
hero.article_text: Corbin, a popular choral teacher at Martin County High School for 34 years, died Saturday. He began his teaching career at Bartow High School in Polk County, and in 1980 came to the school in Stuart. He led OPUS, which stands for Outstanding People United to Sing, until he retired in 2014 "after dedicating his career to helping students find their voices and discover the joy of music," the school district posted on Instagram. "Our thoughts and hearts go to the family, friends, and generations of Martin County students who had the privilege of knowing Mr. Ron Corbin." He was known for more than being a choir teacher. Corbin volunteered as a scorekeeper for basketball and volleyball, and traveled across the state to support Martin County High School athletics. Corbin gave so much of his life to our students, our schools and our community," the district said. "His impact cannot be measured in years or accolades—it lives on in the countless students he encouraged, the music he helped create and the memories shared by those who knew him. "We are deeply grateful for the life he shared with Martin County, and we will carry his memory with us, forever in our hearts. Once a Tiger, always a Tiger." The Florida Vocal Association also noted his passing. "His choirs consistently earned superior ratings at district and state performance assessments and were recognized as Choirs of Distinction by FVA. Corbin was added to the Roll of Distinction in 2014," the FVA wrote on Facebook. Corbin was added to the Roll of Distinction in 2014. In 2017, he received the R. Wayne Hugoboom Distinguished Service Award from the Florida chapter of the American Choral Directors Association. Corbin Musical Arts Center at Martin County High School was dedicated in his name in 2015. "We remember Ron with gratitude for his years of service, his passion for choral music, his mentorship, and the countless students and educators whose lives were enriched by his presence," FVA posted. "Our deepest condolences go to Ron's family, friends, former students, and the many members of FVA and the choral communities who loved and respected him." Corbin received a scholarship to attend Florida A M University, where he studied music. After ending his 40-plus years of teaching, he remained a familiar face and voice at the Stuart school. Last March, alumni gathered to honor Corbin in song. New kidney In 2018 at Cleveland Clinic in Weston, he received a new kidney from his daughter, Candice Corbin, who also was one of his former students. "I was walking down the street and suddenly, I felt like I was inebriated," Ronald said in an article by the Cleveland Clinic. "That's when I said, whoa, something is wrong." A follow-up appointment with his primary care doctor led to a visit with a nephrologist, who told him he had chronic kidney disease and would need to begin dialysis treatment immediately. Candice, an accomplished singer who lives in New York, began thinking about what she could do to support her dad. "I was shocked when he told me he needed to go on dialysis," Candice said. "I remember thinking, I need to learn more and figure out what happens next." She continued to monitor her dad’s health over the next three years, knowing that one day, she would undergo testing to determine whether she was a successful match. After completing initial testing in New York, Candice called her dad to share the news. "When I told him I was a match, I think we were both shocked," Candice said. "And I said, wow, this is really happening." "It just took my breath away that she would want to give me her kidney," Ronald said. Candice then began traveling to Florida to meet with Cleveland Clinic Florida's multidisciplinary transplant team to prepare herself and her dad for surgery. He received his new kidney from his daughter a few weeks before Father's Day. "I'm blessed to have her in my life, that she would think enough of me to do this for me," he said. "I don’t think there's anything I can think of that would be a better gift than the one I got." A GoFundMe fundraising effort raised more than $23,000, including members of his Tiger community. Safe after being missing In March 2023, he was found safe after going missing for almost 24 hours. Corbin was found along Interstate 95 and was taken to the hospital. He was last seen driving his gray Honda CRV heading west on St. Lucie Boulevard in Port St. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

hero.headline: National Weather Service confirms EF-0 tornado touched down in Port St. Lucie Sunday evening
hero.body:
An EF-0 tornado with peak winds of 75 mph touched down in Port St. Lucie Sunday evening, damaging homes and prompting questions about why emergency alerts arrived after the storm had already passed. The National Weather Service confirmed the tornado touched down at 6:10 p.m. near Southeast Kitchen Cove Lane and Southeast Morningside Boulevard, near the Tarpon Bay Club. The tornado traveled a little more than two miles over 14 to 15 minutes before moving over the St. Lucie River, where it became a waterspout.

Will Ulrich, a warning coordination meteorologist with the National Weather Service, said the waterspout remained over the St. Lucie River for five to seven minutes, traveling from north to south before moving back onshore near the Bay St. Lucie community at about 6:20 p.m. The strongest wind gusts occurred in the Bay St. Lucie community before the circulation continued west into Port St. Lucie's Southbend area, where trees were downed and some homes had fences blown over and pool screen enclosures damaged or destroyed. No homes were damaged structurally, and there were no injuries.

Many residents said they received tornado warnings well after the storm had passed. Aron Christiansen said his alert came in at 6:28 p.m., six minutes after the tornado had already passed his home. Carol Cadotte said her alert came about 20 minutes after the tornado struck. The National Weather Service issued a Tornado Warning at 6:28 p.m., about 18 minutes after the tornado first touched down. About 145,000 people were in the Tornado Warning area.

Ulrich said this tornado was unique because it was not raining when it touched down and it did not spin out of a rotating supercell thunderstorm. The tornado was a small, shallow circulation that was not well-sampled by radar. Because these circulations can be very small and short-lived, they can be difficult for radar to detect, particularly at greater distances from the radar site. The National Weather Service said it had no known technical or dissemination issues with its systems related to this warning.
hero.article_text: The National Weather Service confirmed an EF0 tornado with peak winds of 75 mph touched down in Port St. Lucie before becoming a waterspout as it moved over the St. Lucie River Sunday evening. According to Will Ulrich, a warning coordination meteorologist with the National Weather Service, the tornado touched down at 6:10 p.m. near Southeast Kitchen Cove Lane and Southeast Morningside Boulevard, near the Tarpon Bay Club. It traveled a little more than two miles over 14 to 15 minutes. Ulrich said the tornado then moved over the St. Lucie River, where it became a waterspout. "That waterspout meandered very slowly over the St. Lucie River," Ulrich said. Ulrich said the waterspout remained over the St. Lucie River for five to seven minutes, traveling from north to south before moving back onshore near the Bay St. Lucie community at about 6:20 p.m. "We do believe that the strongest wind gusts occurred in the Bay St. Lucie community before the circulation continued west into Port St. Lucie's Southbend area, where we saw a discontinuous damage path of some trees down, along with some homes that had fences blown over and some pool screen enclosures that were damaged or destroyed," Ulrich said. See also: 'I love Mike’: Tracy Caruso defends husband, resigns from public boards Despite the tornado and the strong gusts of wind, no homes were damaged, and there were no injuries. Videos sent to CBS12 News showed funnel clouds in several areas, including Port St. Lucie, as strong winds and storms swept across the Treasure Coast and parts of northern Palm Beach County. The National Weather Service said it is also aware of damage reported in Jensen Beach. Based on preliminary information from Martin County Emergency Management, storm spotter calls and videos submitted to local media, forecasters said a brief landspout or tornado likely developed near the Treasure Coast Square Mall. The weather service said the possible tornado lofted a small amount of debris and caused minor damage. Allison Rogers lives off of Southbend Blvd, across from Jessica Clinton Park. Her fence was blown down during the storm. It sounded really breezy outside, just a little louder than normal. So, I peeked out the window, saw the whole fence come down. The shed was swirling around. It really looked like a tornado. You could see the things spinning. I was born and raised here. I've never seen anything like this, said Rogers. Rogers and her roommate were cleaning up the yard Monday morning when they discovered nails, wood beams, furniture and lawn equipment had been moved. Thankful that our screen enclosure, the house itself, the roof and everything we never lost power. It's just cosmetic fence and shed and things like that. So thankful every day that it did not get worse," said Rogers. Lots of cleanup to do, a run to Home Depot, temporary fence for the dogs, all the things. So, seems like a hurricane cleanup, but no hurricane," said Rogers. Another woman, who lives across the street from where the tornado started, had parts of her roof ripped off. She tells CBS12 News that in her nearly 30 years of living there, this is the first time she's had major damage. The storms also caused problems farther south. "My house is old, but it made it through all the hurricanes. It never lost anything ever. Through all the crazy ones we've had. This was five minutes, and my roof just peeled off like a Band-Aid," said Carol Cadotte. Cadotte voiced her frustration with receiving the alert for the Tornado well after it passed her house. "Our phones went off, and we looked at each other like, you're kidding me, right? 20 minutes later, that's something's wrong with that picture," said Cadotte. Ulrich said this tornado was unique in multiple ways. It wasn't raining when it touched down; the heavy rain came afterward, which he said is typical of how landspouts form. And unlike most tornadoes, it didn't spin out of a rotating supercell thunderstorm; it formed along the leading edge of one. "The problem with landspouts is that the circulations aren't particularly strong, such that we can very easily see it on radar. We know that there's a weak circulation, but we see weak circulations all the time, so that doesn't necessarily always lead to a tornado," Ulrich said. The storm caused problems down south. In Jupiter, a large tree fell across the road near Donald Ross Road and Central Boulevard Sunday night. Jupiter police responded and blocked the area to prevent drivers from hitting the tree. CBS12 News crews were across the Treasure Coast Monday morning as daylight provided a clearer look at the extent of the damage. If you have photos or videos of storm damage in your neighborhood, you can safely upload them to CBS12 News through our Chime In page .

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie residents question why tornado alerts arrived late or never came at all
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie residents are questioning why tornado alerts either arrived too late or never came at all after an EF-0 tornado touched down Sunday evening.
cards.body:
Some Port St. Lucie residents said they received tornado alerts too late or never received them at all after an EF-0 tornado touched down Sunday evening. Aron Christiansen said his alert came in at 6:28 p.m., six minutes after the tornado had already passed his home. Neighbor Theresa Garone said she never received an alert.

The National Weather Service issued a Tornado Warning for portions of St. Lucie County at 6:28 p.m., after the initial tornado reports in Port St. Lucie. About 145,000 people were in the Tornado Warning area. The warning was distributed through multiple channels, including NOAA Weather Radio, the Emergency Alert System on television and radio, Wireless Emergency Alerts on compatible mobile devices, and local notification services such as ALERT St. Lucie.

The National Weather Service said the exact time an individual receives an alert can vary depending on the dissemination system, cellular provider, device settings, and local notification service. The tornado was a small, shallow circulation that was not well-sampled by radar. Unlike stronger tornadoes associated with rotating thunderstorms, landspouts typically develop from rotation near the ground that stretches upward beneath a developing thunderstorm. Because these circulations can be very small and short-lived, they can be difficult for radar to detect.

cards.headline: Radar limitations made it difficult to detect Port St. Lucie tornado, meteorologist says
cards.teaser: Radar limitations made it difficult for forecasters to immediately identify the tornado threat in Port St. Lucie Sunday evening, leading to a delayed warning.
cards.body:
Some Port St. Lucie residents said their phones did not alert them until after a tornado had already hit Sunday evening. The confirmed EF-0 tornado touched down in Port St. Lucie just after 6 p.m., bringing winds of up to 75 mph and damaging several homes. Carol Cadotte said she quickly went inside her home after hearing a strange noise.

The tornado warning was not issued until 6:28 p.m., about 18 minutes after the tornado first touched down. CBS12 News StormTrac Chief Meteorologist Greg Rule said radar limitations made it difficult for forecasters to immediately identify a tornado threat. The radar beam was flying up and over the storm system, so it did not have a clear defined rotation.

Rule recommends keeping Wireless Emergency Alerts turned on through your phone. He also recommends having a NOAA Weather Radio programmed for your county and downloading the CBS12 Weather app for additional weather information and alerts. If a tornado warning is issued for your area, do not wait to see the tornado before taking action.

cards.body:
A 36-year-old man has been charged with manslaughter after Fort Pierce police say he fatally shot a 34-year-old man with a BB gun on Saturday near an elementary school. Police said the incident happened in the 2900 block of Avenue G, where a group of men in their 30s had been shooting a BB gun at trees. Investigators believe Jabari Cowart, the suspect, asked to use the BB gun and later pointed it at one of the men before pulling the trigger. The victim fell to the ground, and officers were called to the scene.

Ken Noble, marketing manager at The Tactical Store in Fort Pierce, spoke about the dangers of BB guns. He explained that BB guns, while often considered less harmful than traditional firearms, can still cause serious injury or death. Noble also shared safety advice for handling firearms, including BB guns. Fort Pierce police said Cowart is being held at the St. Lucie County jail.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce spends $31,000 to search for new city attorney after entire legal team resigns
cards.teaser: Fort Pierce's city commission approved spending $31,000 in taxpayer money to find a permanent city attorney after nearly the entire legal team resigned, leaving the city with no attorneys.
cards.body:
Fort Pierce's city commission held a heated special meeting Monday after nearly the city's entire legal team resigned, leaving the city with no attorneys and forcing officials to spend $31,000 in taxpayer money to find a permanent replacement. The mass departure followed the city's decision not to renew the current city attorney's contract, which expires in September. City staff confirmed that aside from one paralegal, the entire legal department has left.

City Commissioner Michael Broderick called the situation a self-inflicted wound and said he is not aware of any complaints, disciplinary action or poor performance reviews that would lead to the city attorney leaving. Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky suggested the resignations were not spontaneous and said he thinks the departures were orchestrated. Broderick said the departures included at least three city attorneys.

The commission's decision to spend $31,000 on an outside search firm drew sharp criticism from both Broderick and a taxpayer who spoke during public comment. City Human Resources Manager Jared Sorenson defended the decision, saying an outside firm was needed to keep the process impartial. The commission ultimately approved the $31,000 contract and appointed Deputy City Manager Camille Wallace as interim city attorney while the permanent search is conducted.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie residents describe frightening sounds and damage from EF-0 tornado
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie residents described the terrifying experience of an EF-0 tornado that touched down Sunday evening, leaving some homes damaged and debris scattered across yards.
cards.body:
An EF-0 tornado touched down in a Port St. Lucie neighborhood Sunday evening, leaving some homes damaged and residents recounting the frightening experience. Resident Allison Rogers described the terrifying noises she heard during the storm. Rogers said it sounded like there was a hurricane outside the window and that she heard a swoosh. Rogers admitted she was scared as she watched the twister from her home. Her home lost its fence and shed but never lost power.

Aron Christiansen said his roof was damaged during the tornado. He said he looked out his window and saw a bunch of dark clouds and a bunch of white, which he initially thought were birds. He looked closer and realized it was debris. Another resident, Debbie Mastrolillo, said her home was untouched by the storm.

The tornado also moved over the St. Lucie River, where one viewer captured video of it as a waterspout. Even though most homes were spared, some residents said the experience was unsettling. While some residents are still clearing debris, many are relieved that no one was injured.

hero.body:

Deputies responded on August 22 to a reported theft involving a food delivery in which the customer used two counterfeit $50 bills as payment for an $83.90 order.

On Monday, deputies learned that the person who used the counterfeit money was staying at a residence on Miramar Avenue in Fort Pierce. Upon arrival, deputies identified Adrianna Marie Sheppard, 19, as the person who provided the fake money.

Sheppard was arrested and charged with fraud utter bank bill, note, check or draft, as well as possession of counterfeited bank bill, note, check or draft and larceny. The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office investigated the incident.

The arrest came three days after the initial counterfeit currency incident was reported. Deputies located Sheppard at the Miramar Avenue residence and took her into custody following the investigation.
