hero.headline: EF0 tornado touches down in Port St. Lucie, damages 20 to 30 homes along 2-mile path
hero.body:
An EF0 tornado touched down in Port St. Lucie Sunday evening, damaging 20 to 30 homes along a 2.1-mile path with winds between 65 and 75 mph. The National Weather Service confirmed the tornado began at 6:10 p.m. near Southeast Kitchen Cove Lane and Southeast Morningside Boulevard, near the Tarpon Bay Yacht Club, before moving over the St. Lucie River and returning to land in the Bay St. Lucie community.

Will Ulrich, warning coordination meteorologist with the National Weather Service Melbourne office, announced the findings Monday morning during a press conference at Jessica Clinton Park. The tornado, classified as a landspout, moved over the St. Lucie River where it became a waterspout for five to seven minutes before returning onshore around 6:20 p.m. The strongest wind gusts occurred in the Bay St. Lucie community, causing numerous downed trees and large branches along with damage to tile-roofed homes.

The tornado continued west into Port St. Lucie communities near the Southbend area, causing downed trees, blown-over fences, and damaged or destroyed pool screen enclosures before dissipating. The entire event lasted 14 to 15 minutes. Damage included roof damage, soffit damage, and pool enclosures lifted from their foundations, with approximately 20 to 30 percent of roof covers removed from some homes.

No injuries were reported from the tornado. Residents spent Monday cleaning up debris from pools, yards, and damaged structures. Aaron Christiansen pulled patio furniture from his submerged pool after his patio broke apart during the storm, while Janelle Pierre-Louis reported her front door caved in with dirt coming through cracks. The National Weather Service worked with Port St. Lucie Emergency Management and St. Lucie County Emergency Management to conduct the damage survey.

It produced minimal structural damage, including roof damage, soffit damage and pool enclosures lifted from their foundations.The tornado then moved over the St. Lucie River, where it became a waterspout for approximately five to seven minutes, meandering slowly from north to south over the water before moving back onshore in the Bay St. Lucie community around 6:20 p.m."The strongest wind gusts likely occurred in the Bay St. Lucie community," Ulrich said, where the tornado caused numerous downed trees and large branches, along with damage to well-built homes with tile roofs from winds of 65 to 75 mph.The tornado continued west into Port St. Lucie communities near the Southbend area, where it caused discontinuous damage including downed trees, blown-over fences, and damaged or destroyed pool screen enclosures before dissipating.The entire event lasted approximately 14 to 15 minutes, making it unusually long for this type of tornado. Most of the damage was classified as minor, with approximately 20 to 30 percent of roof covers removed from some homes, though no homes were destroyed.No injuries were reported from the tornado, officials confirmed.Ulrich explained that landspouts form differently than traditional tornadoes, developing closer to the surface along the leading edge of thunderstorm updrafts rather than from mesocyclones. Residents reported it wasn't raining during the tornado itself, with heavy rain arriving only after the tornado passed through."This was more of boundary interactions from those daily afternoon showers and thunderstorms that we receive, and lately it has been abnormally warm," Ulrich said. "The more heat you have, the more vigorous those boundary collisions are going to be."While landspouts are more common during summer months in Florida, any one location experiencing a tornado remains historically rare.The National Weather Service worked alongside the City of Port St. Lucie Emergency Management and St. Lucie County Emergency Management to conduct interviews with residents and piece together the timeline of the event.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce enforces two-hour parking limits downtown with $50 citations
cards.teaser: Fort Pierce now issues $50 citations to drivers who exceed two-hour parking limits in parts of downtown, with the penalty increasing to $100 for repeat offenses.
cards.body:
Fort Pierce is enforcing two-hour parking limits in parts of downtown, with citations now being issued to drivers who exceed the limit. Drivers who stay longer than two hours receive a $50 citation, which increases to $100 for repeat offenses. The initiative began in July and aims to increase parking turnover, improve traffic flow, and make it easier for visitors to find available spaces.

Beryl Muise, owner of Notions Potions, said the two-hour parking limit has benefited her business. Muise said customers can now find parking spots and come into the store without getting frustrated driving around in circles. She said the spots would previously be full, making it difficult for customers with disabilities who cannot walk from the garage.

The two-hour parking limits are enforced Monday through Friday from 8:30 a.m. One restaurant, which declined to comment on camera, said two hours is not long enough for their lunch rush, especially with limited parking in front of the establishment. Muise said weekends are less congested because offices like the public defender's office and title companies have employees present Monday through Friday but not on weekends.

The two-hour parking limits are enforced Monday through Friday from 8:30 a.m. Muise said weekends are less congested, benefiting retail and restaurants. "On the weekends, it's better for the retail and the restaurants. You don't have as many offices that are here, you know? Like the public defender's office. Their employees are here, and other businesses like the title company have employees here Monday through Friday. So, on the weekend, I don't think it's as congested," she said. cards.headline: Port St. Lucie residents receive tornado emergency alert 20 minutes after storm passed
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie residents cleaning up tornado damage Monday expressed frustration with emergency alerts arriving well after the tornado had already hit their homes.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie residents cleaning up after Sunday evening's tornado said they received emergency alerts on their phones long after the storm had passed. Carol Cadotte, who lives near where the tornado started, said her phones went off 20 minutes after the tornado ripped parts of her roof off. Aaron Christiansen said he received the emergency alert after the storm had already hit his home.

Cadotte said her house is old but made it through all the hurricanes without ever losing anything. The five-minute tornado peeled her roof off. She said in her nearly 30 years of living there, this was the first time she had major damage.

Christiansen had about 10 seconds to react before the storm hit after he saw debris flying through his window. His patio furniture was submerged in his pool, his pool fence was blown toward his home, and debris was scattered across the ground. Christiansen, originally from Minnesota, said his experience with tornado-like weather helped him know what precautions to take.
cards.article_text: The National Weather Service confirmed an EF0 tornado with peak winds of 75 mph touched down in Port St. Lucie before becoming a waterspout as it moved over the St. Lucie River Sunday evening. According to Will Ulrich, a warning coordination meteorologist with the National Weather Service, the tornado touched down at 6:10 p.m. near Southeast Kitchen Cove Lane and Southeast Morningside Boulevard, near the Tarpon Bay Club. It traveled a little more than two miles over 14 to 15 minutes. Ulrich said the tornado then moved over the St. Lucie River, where it became a waterspout. "That waterspout meandered very slowly over the St. Lucie River," Ulrich said. Ulrich said the waterspout remained over the St. Lucie River for five to seven minutes, traveling from north to south before moving back onshore near the Bay St. Lucie community at about 6:20 p.m. "We do believe that the strongest wind gusts occurred in the Bay St. Lucie community before the circulation continued west into Port St. Lucie's Southbend area, where we saw a discontinuous damage path of some trees down, along with some homes that had fences blown over and some pool screen enclosures that were damaged or destroyed," Ulrich said. See also: 'I love Mike’: Tracy Caruso defends husband, resigns from public boards Despite the tornado and the strong gusts of wind, no homes were damaged, and there were no injuries. Videos sent to CBS12 News showed funnel clouds in several areas, including Port St. Lucie, as strong winds and storms swept across the Treasure Coast and parts of northern Palm Beach County. The National Weather Service said it is also aware of damage reported in Jensen Beach. Based on preliminary information from Martin County Emergency Management, storm spotter calls and videos submitted to local media, forecasters said a brief landspout or tornado likely developed near the Treasure Coast Square Mall. The weather service said the possible tornado lofted a small amount of debris and caused minor damage. Allison Rogers lives off of Southbend Blvd, across from Jessica Clinton Park. Her fence was blown down during the storm. It sounded really breezy outside, just a little louder than normal. So, I peeked out the window, saw the whole fence come down. The shed was swirling around. It really looked like a tornado. You could see the things spinning. I was born and raised here. I've never seen anything like this, said Rogers. Rogers and her roommate were cleaning up the yard Monday morning when they discovered nails, wood beams, furniture and lawn equipment had been moved. Thankful that our screen enclosure, the house itself, the roof and everything we never lost power. It's just cosmetic fence and shed and things like that. So thankful every day that it did not get worse," said Rogers. Lots of cleanup to do, a run to Home Depot, temporary fence for the dogs, all the things. So, seems like a hurricane cleanup, but no hurricane," said Rogers. Another woman, who lives across the street from where the tornado started, had parts of her roof ripped off. She tells CBS12 News that in her nearly 30 years of living there, this is the first time she's had major damage. The storms also caused problems farther south. "My house is old, but it made it through all the hurricanes. It never lost anything ever. Through all the crazy ones we've had. This was five minutes, and my roof just peeled off like a Band-Aid," said Carol Cadotte. Cadotte voiced her frustration with receiving the alert for the Tornado well after it passed her house. "Our phones went off, and we looked at each other like, you're kidding me, right? 20 minutes later, that's something's wrong with that picture," said Cadotte. Ulrich said this tornado was unique in multiple ways. It wasn't raining when it touched down; the heavy rain came afterward, which he said is typical of how landspouts form. And unlike most tornadoes, it didn't spin out of a rotating supercell thunderstorm; it formed along the leading edge of one. "The problem with landspouts is that the circulations aren't particularly strong, such that we can very easily see it on radar. We know that there's a weak circulation, but we see weak circulations all the time, so that doesn't necessarily always lead to a tornado," Ulrich said. The storm caused problems down south. In Jupiter, a large tree fell across the road near Donald Ross Road and Central Boulevard Sunday night. Jupiter police responded and blocked the area to prevent drivers from hitting the tree. CBS12 News crews were across the Treasure Coast Monday morning as daylight provided a clearer look at the extent of the damage. If you have photos or videos of storm damage in your neighborhood, you can safely upload them to CBS12 News through our Chime In page .

cards.headline: Tornado moves through Port St. Lucie neighborhood on Hurricane Andrew anniversary
cards.teaser: Marlene Torres returned home Sunday night from celebrating her birthday in Jensen Beach to find the tornado had moved through her Port St. Lucie neighborhood, on the same date as the Hurricane Andrew anniversary.
cards.body:
Marlene Torres was celebrating her birthday in Jensen Beach Sunday night before returning home to find the storm had moved through her Port St. Lucie neighborhood. Her birthday fell on Monday, August 24, which is also the anniversary of Hurricane Andrew. Her home was not damaged, but she needed an electrician to fix her meter.

Torres was living in Miami when Hurricane Andrew hit the region. She said the tornado cannot be compared to Andrew, which was life-altering for the longest time with repairs taking months and months. Torres said she is thankful not to have to go through that again.

Mitch Brewer had debris piled out front, most of it from a shed he had tied down. Brewer said it looks like the shed caught some heavy updrafts and left. He said he had been thinking about demolishing the old shed at some point, but the storm beat him to it. Brewer said living in the mid-South made him familiar with tornadoes. Florida sees about 65 to 70 tornadoes a year and has a higher frequency per 10,000 square miles than any other state, including Oklahoma.
cards.article_text: Lucie residents spent Monday cleaning up after a storm tore through the area Sunday night, leaving behind damaged structures, debris-filled pools and downed foliage.The National Weather Service determined it was an EF-0 tornado, with 65-75 mph winds.Aron Christiansen spent the morning pulling debris out of his pool after already retrieving furniture from the bottom. Video from a neighbor's camera captured the moment his patio broke apart during the storm. Half of the patio is now out on the curb, set to be salvaged for recycling."I looked out the windows last night, saw a bunch of debris flying. I thought it was birds at first; they were white, [so I] thought they might be ibises. [I looked] closer, and there's debris, and had about 10 seconds before it hit our house," Christiansen said.Janelle Pierre-Louis said she was surprised by the amount of damage to her backyard foliage after dealing with damage at the front of her house first."My front door caved in; our door is kind of old. Dirt came through the cracks. It was a hot mess," Pierre-Louis said. "We've got to clean up and start all over."Around the corner, Mitch Brewer had debris piled out front — most of it from a shed he had tied down."It looks like it caught some heavy updrafts and left," Brewer said.Brewer said he had been thinking about demolishing the old shed at some point, but Mother Nature beat him to it. He said living in the mid-South made him familiar with tornadoes.Florida sees about 65 to 70 tornadoes a year, according to the Florida Climate Center, and has a higher frequency per 10,000 square miles than any other state, including Oklahoma.Marlene Torres was in a good mood Sunday night before returning home to find the storm had moved through her neighborhood."I had just come back from Jensen Beach celebrating my birthday, which is today," Torres said. "I came home and witnessed the tornado."Her home was not damaged, but she needed an electrician to fix her meter."I'm the only one with no electricity because my power was more damaged than other folks in the area, so that is the situation, but I can't complain; it could be worse," Torres said.Monday, August 24, is also the anniversary of Hurricane Andrew. Torres said she was living in Miami when the historic hurricane hit the region."You can't compare Andrew to this. It was life-altering for the longest time. The repairs took months and months and months," Torres said.Torres said she is thankful not to have to go through that again."Here I am picking up sticks and stones," Torres said while laughing.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. cards.headline: National Weather Service explains landspout formation after Port St. Lucie tornado
cards.teaser: The Port St. Lucie tornado formed as a landspout along the leading edge of a thunderstorm updraft, making it difficult to detect on radar before it touched down Sunday evening.
cards.body:
Will Ulrich of the National Weather Service said the Port St. Lucie tornado was unique because it formed as a landspout rather than spinning out of a rotating supercell thunderstorm. Landspouts form closer to the surface along the leading edge of thunderstorm updrafts. The circulations are not particularly strong, making them difficult to see on radar before they form.

Ulrich said it was not raining when the tornado touched down, with heavy rain arriving only after it passed through. This is typical of how landspouts form. Ulrich explained the more heat present, the more vigorous boundary collisions become, and it has been abnormally warm lately.

The tornado was unusually long for this type, lasting 14 to 15 minutes. While landspouts are more common during summer months in Florida, any one location experiencing a tornado remains historically rare. The National Weather Service worked with Port St. Lucie Emergency Management and St. Lucie County Emergency Management to conduct interviews with residents and piece together the timeline of the event.
cards.article_text: The National Weather Service has confirmed that an EF0 tornado touched down Sunday evening in St. Lucie County, damaging about 20 to 30 homes along a 2.1-mile path.WATCH THE FULL PRESS CONFERENCE BELOW:Will Ulrich, warning coordination meteorologist with the National Weather Service Melbourne office, announced the findings Monday morning during a press conference at Jessica Clinton Park following a damage survey of the affected areas.The tornado, classified as a landspout, first touched down around 6:10 p.m. near Southeast Kitching Cove Lane and Southeast Morningside Boulevard, close to the Tarpon Bay Yacht Club. It produced minimal structural damage, including roof damage, soffit damage and pool enclosures lifted from their foundations.The tornado then moved over the St. Lucie River, where it became a waterspout for approximately five to seven minutes, meandering slowly from north to south over the water before moving back onshore in the Bay St. Lucie community around 6:20 p.m."The strongest wind gusts likely occurred in the Bay St. Lucie community," Ulrich said, where the tornado caused numerous downed trees and large branches, along with damage to well-built homes with tile roofs from winds of 65 to 75 mph.The tornado continued west into Port St. Lucie communities near the Southbend area, where it caused discontinuous damage including downed trees, blown-over fences, and damaged or destroyed pool screen enclosures before dissipating.The entire event lasted approximately 14 to 15 minutes, making it unusually long for this type of tornado. Most of the damage was classified as minor, with approximately 20 to 30 percent of roof covers removed from some homes, though no homes were destroyed.No injuries were reported from the tornado, officials confirmed.Ulrich explained that landspouts form differently than traditional tornadoes, developing closer to the surface along the leading edge of thunderstorm updrafts rather than from mesocyclones. Residents reported it wasn't raining during the tornado itself, with heavy rain arriving only after the tornado passed through."This was more of boundary interactions from those daily afternoon showers and thunderstorms that we receive, and lately it has been abnormally warm," Ulrich said. "The more heat you have, the more vigorous those boundary collisions are going to be."While landspouts are more common during summer months in Florida, any one location experiencing a tornado remains historically rare.The National Weather Service worked alongside the City of Port St. Lucie Emergency Management and St. Lucie County Emergency Management to conduct interviews with residents and piece together the timeline of the event.

hero.headline: Florida Lt. Gov. Jay Collins leaves future in politics uncertain after primary loss
hero.body:
Florida Lt. Gov. Jay Collins said he is focused on finishing his term and helping reunite Republicans following his loss in the gubernatorial primary, but he has not decided whether he will pursue another political campaign after leaving office in January. Collins finished second to U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds in the Republican primary, receiving about 25% of the vote compared with Donalds' nearly 48%. Collins carried 17 counties, most of them across North Florida, giving him a regional political footprint despite the decisive statewide loss.

Donalds, who was endorsed by President Donald Trump, will face Democratic nominee David Jolly in the November general election. The winner will succeed term-limited Gov. Ron DeSantis. Collins said he and Donalds have spoken since the primary and reconciled after a contentious Republican contest in which the two candidates traded attacks over their records and conservative credentials. Collins said he hopes Donalds succeeds and argued that Republicans must put their primary differences aside to defeat Jolly.

DeSantis appointed Collins as Florida's lieutenant governor in August 2025, filling the vacancy left by Jeanette Nuez. At the time, DeSantis called the Army Special Forces veteran the Chuck Norris of Florida politics. Collins had served in the Florida Senate since 2022 and emerged as a reliable ally of the governor. He sponsored the 2023 law allowing eligible Floridians to carry concealed weapons without a state permit and later championed legislation expanding required public-school instruction on the history of communism. Collins entered the governors race promising to preserve the DeSantis administration's conservative agenda. DeSantis stopped short of endorsing Collins or any other candidate in the primary.

Collins said he will spend the administration's closing months traveling the state, working with communities and making the lieutenant governor's office more visible. He is not announcing another campaign, but he is not closing the door on politics either. Another bid for office and a return to the private sector are both possibilities. Collins said he does not have to be a politician or be in politics to be a leader. For now, Collins said his immediate future is making his current post a priority.

hero.teaser: An EF0 tornado with maximum estimated wind gusts between 65 and 75 mph touched down in Port St. Lucie Sunday evening and moved over the St. Lucie River as a waterspout.
hero.body:
The National Weather Service confirmed an EF0 tornado touched down in Port St. Lucie Sunday evening with peak winds of 75 mph. The tornado began at 6:10 p.m. near Southeast Kitchen Cove Lane and Southeast Morningside Boulevard, near the Tarpon Bay Club. It traveled a little more than two miles over 14 to 15 minutes.

The tornado then moved over the St. Lucie River, where it became a waterspout. Will Ulrich, a warning coordination meteorologist with the National Weather Service, said the waterspout remained over the St. Lucie River for five to seven minutes, traveling from north to south before moving back onshore near the Bay St. Lucie community at about 6:20 p.m.

The strongest wind gusts occurred in the Bay St. Lucie community before the circulation continued west into Port St. Lucie's Southbend area. The weather service said the tornado caused damage including trees down, fences blown over, and some pool screen enclosures that were damaged or destroyed. No homes were damaged, and there were no injuries.

hero.headline: Sheriff's helicopter crew spots garage fire on Southwest Martin Highway, helps save Palm City home
hero.body:
A Martin County Sheriff's Office helicopter crew spotted a large fire late Sunday night and alerted firefighters in time to prevent flames from spreading to a nearby home on Southwest Martin Highway in Palm City. The MCSO Air One pilot and tactical flight observer were on patrol around 10:30 p.m. when they noticed flames coming from a detached garage and immediately alerted deputies and Martin County Fire Rescue.

Firefighters arrived to find the roughly 1,600-square-foot structure engulfed in flames with its roof already gone. The fire was threatening the main home on the property. Crews were able to contain the blaze before it reached the house. The homeowners were not home at the time.

Firefighters found a Class C motorhome and a Jeep inside the structure. The garage and both vehicles were completely destroyed.

The State Fire Marshal was notified. The cause of the fire remains under investigation. The sheriff's office said the helicopter crew's discovery allowed emergency crews to reach the property in time to keep the flames from spreading to the home.

hero.headline: Indian River County Sheriff credits Flock Safety cameras in Vero Beach homicide arrest, sparking privacy debate
hero.teaser: License plate reader cameras helped Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers track a homicide suspect to a West Virginia motel, but the technology is drawing mixed reactions from Treasure Coast residents.
hero.body:
Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers credited Flock Safety license plate reader cameras with leading to an arrest in a Vero Beach homicide case after tracking a suspect to a West Virginia motel. The arrest came after what Flowers described as a cold-blooded murder in Vero Beach that triggered a multi-state manhunt. The Flock Safety system is a nationwide network of cameras connected to a searchable law enforcement database.

Many residents welcomed the technology's role in catching the suspected killer. Larry, a Treasure Coast resident, said he thinks keeping criminals out of people's lives does justice to the community. Meghan Ford, a Treasure Coast visitor, said she sees value in the system for serious cases such as horrible crimes and missing children.

But Michael Maslak, a Stuart resident, questioned where the line should be drawn on privacy. Recent reports indicate some officers have misused the Flock Safety system to track romantic partners, fueling controversy. In response, Flock Safety announced changes requiring searches to include a case number and mandating that all agencies use a new audit system designed to flag suspicious activity.

hero.headline: National Weather Service confirms EF0 tornado touched down in Port St. Lucie Sunday evening
hero.body:
The National Weather Service confirmed an EF0 tornado with peak winds of 75 mph touched down in Port St. Lucie Sunday evening, damaging 20 to 30 homes along a 2.1-mile path. Will Ulrich, warning coordination meteorologist with the National Weather Service Melbourne office, announced the findings Monday morning during a press conference at Jessica Clinton Park following a damage survey of the affected areas.

The tornado, classified as a landspout, first touched down at 6:10 p.m. near Southeast Kitching Cove Lane and Southeast Morningside Boulevard, close to the Tarpon Bay Yacht Club. It produced minimal structural damage, including roof damage, soffit damage and pool enclosures lifted from their foundations. The tornado then moved over the St. Lucie River, where it became a waterspout for approximately five to seven minutes, meandering slowly from north to south over the water before moving back onshore in the Bay St. Lucie community around 6:20 p.m.

The strongest wind gusts occurred in the Bay St. Lucie community, where the tornado caused numerous downed trees and large branches, along with damage to well-built homes with tile roofs from winds of 65 to 75 mph. The tornado continued west into Port St. Lucie communities near the Southbend area, where it caused discontinuous damage including downed trees, blown-over fences, and damaged or destroyed pool screen enclosures before dissipating. Allison Rogers, who lives off Southbend Boulevard across from Jessica Clinton Park, said her fence was blown down during the storm.

The entire event lasted approximately 14 to 15 minutes, making it unusually long for this type of tornado. No injuries were reported from the tornado. The National Weather Service worked alongside the City of Port St. Lucie Emergency Management and St. Lucie County Emergency Management to conduct interviews with residents and piece together the timeline of the event.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce man charged with manslaughter after BB gun shooting kills 34-year-old on Avenue G
hero.body:
A Fort Pierce man faces a manslaughter charge after a 34-year-old man died following a BB gun shooting on August 22, 2026, in the 2900 block of Avenue G. Fort Pierce Police officers responded to reports of a gunshot victim and found the 34-year-old male suffering from an injury. He was transported to Lawnwood Hospital, where he later died.

The investigation revealed that a group of males had been shooting a BB gun at trees when the suspect, Jabari Cowart, 36, asked to use the BB gun. During the interaction, Cowart pointed the BB gun in the victim's direction and fired. Shortly thereafter, the victim collapsed.

Cowart was charged with manslaughter and taken to the St. Lucie County Jail. The circumstances surrounding the incident remain under investigation by Fort Pierce Police.

The shooting occurred Saturday, and the charges were filed as investigators determined the victim's death resulted from the BB gun incident. Police have not released the name of the victim.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce left without city attorneys after nearly entire legal team resigns
hero.body:
Fort Pierce's city commission held a heated special meeting Monday after nearly the city's entire legal team resigned, leaving the city with no attorneys and forcing officials to spend $31,000 in taxpayer money to find a permanent replacement. The mass departure followed the city's decision not to renew the current city attorney's contract, which expires in September. City staff confirmed that aside from one paralegal, the entire legal department has left.

City Commissioner Michael Broderick told WPTV the situation is a self-inflicted wound. He said he is not aware of any complaints, disciplinary action or poor performance reviews that would lead to the city attorney leaving. Broderick said the departures included at least three city attorneys. Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky suggested the resignations were orchestrated, though he did not say who he believed orchestrated the mass resignation.

Broderick expressed concern that the lack of legal representation could make it easier for developers to push projects through, particularly on South Hutchinson Island, where a 900-unit residential project is already pending at Causeway Cove. Dzadovsky disagreed, arguing the absence of legal staff would actually slow development down because it would take longer to have city attorney legal review.

The commission approved the $31,000 contract for an outside search firm despite sharp criticism from Broderick and taxpayer Kevin Keene during public comment. City Human Resources Manager Jared Sorenson defended the decision, saying an outside firm was needed to keep the process impartial. The commission appointed Deputy City Manager Camille Wallace as interim city attorney while the permanent search is conducted.

hero.headline: Sheriff's helicopter spots massive barn fire on Southwest Martin Highway in Palm City
hero.body:
A Martin County Sheriff's Office helicopter flying over Palm City on Sunday night spotted a barn engulfed in flames on Southwest Martin Highway. Martin County Fire Rescue crews responded to the scene, where they found a 1,600-square-foot barn fully involved in fire with its roof already gone by the time they arrived.

Firefighters entered the structure and discovered a Class C motorhome and a Jeep inside the burning barn. Crews worked to extinguish the flames throughout the building and continued monitoring hot spots to prevent any rekindling of the fire.

Officials reported that no one was injured in the incident. Firefighters successfully contained the blaze and prevented it from spreading beyond the barn to surrounding areas or structures.

The State Fire Marshal was notified about the fire. The cause of the blaze remains under investigation, and no further details about what may have started the fire have been released at this time.

hero.headline: National Weather Service to update Port St. Lucie on possible tornado that struck Sunday
hero.body:
A possible tornado or landspout struck a Port St. Lucie neighborhood near Southbend Boulevard and Southeast Navy Avenue on Sunday evening, and the National Weather Service Melbourne office will hold a press conference Monday morning at Jessica Clinton Park to provide an official update on the event. Resident Aaron Christiansen witnessed debris swirling in the air around 6 p.m. before having just 10 seconds to take cover with his family and pets.

The storm left substantial damage in the neighborhood. Christiansen's patio furniture was blown into his pool, his pool fence was destroyed and blown toward his home, debris was scattered across the ground, and plants were blown away. Christiansen received the official emergency alert only after the storm had already passed through the area.

Christiansen, originally from Minnesota, said his experience with tornado-like weather helped him know what precautions to take. He and his family and pets were not injured. He plans to begin cleanup efforts Monday and will also have his roof inspected.

Weather officials are expected to provide details about the storm's classification, whether it was a confirmed tornado or landspout, wind speeds, and the extent of the damage path. The National Weather Service typically conducts damage surveys following significant weather events to determine official ratings and provide analysis for future preparedness efforts.

hero.headline: Vero Beach homicide arrest using Flock Safety cameras sparks privacy debate in Indian River County
hero.body:
Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers credited Flock Safety license plate reader cameras with leading to an arrest in a Vero Beach homicide case after tracking a suspect to a West Virginia motel, sparking debate among residents about privacy and surveillance technology. The arrest followed what Flowers described as a cold-blooded murder in Vero Beach that triggered a multi-state manhunt. The Flock Safety system is a nationwide network of cameras connected to a searchable law enforcement database.

Flowers defended the technology's role in the investigation. "We got a murderer behind bars because of this. We got this guy off the streets because of the Flock system," Flowers said. Many residents welcomed the technology's effectiveness in the case. Larry, a Treasure Coast resident, said he thinks it is a good thing if the system can keep criminals out of residents' lives. Meghan Ford, a Treasure Coast visitor, said she sees value in using the system for serious cases like finding people who have committed horrible crimes or locating missing children.

Other community members expressed concerns about privacy as the system's use expands. "We don't have that much privacy anymore, so where do you draw the line?" Michael Maslak, a Stuart resident, said. Ford echoed the tension, saying the technology feels like an invasion of privacy for people doing the right thing in life. Recent reports indicate some officers have misused the Flock Safety system to track romantic partners, fueling controversy around the technology.

Flock Safety announced changes requiring searches to include a case number and mandating that all agencies use a new audit system designed to flag suspicious activity. Maslak said the technology is a great idea but needs to be kept under control. Treasure Coast residents say they hope regulations will continue to evolve alongside the technology's expanding uses.

hero.headline: Tornado touches down in Port St. Lucie, National Weather Service surveys damage Monday
hero.body:
The National Weather Service announced late Sunday night that it will conduct a storm survey Monday morning after a tornado touched down near Jessica Clinton Park in Port St. Lucie. The agency said a brief landspout tornado occurred in the vicinity of Jessica Clinton Park near Southbend Boulevard and SE Navy Avenue, lofting debris and producing minor damage to homes in the area.

The National Weather Service in Melbourne said the tornado likely started as a funnel cloud that touched down on the St. Lucie County side, just west of the St. Lucie River. Emergency Management officials reported several homes with minor structural damage near SE Wake Road, Navy Avenue, and West Snow Road in the Southbend area of Port St. Lucie. The tornado may have continued east toward the St. Lucie River, where it became a waterspout.

A tornado warning was issued for parts of St. Lucie and Martin counties on Sunday. Several residents submitted photos and videos of apparent funnel clouds in the sky from Port St. Lucie, Jensen Beach and Palm City. Radar data showed only a weak circulation signature at the time of the reported damage, suggesting the circulation was likely shallow and near the surface, consistent with a landspout-type event.

Aaron Christiansen, a Port St. Lucie resident who lives near Southbend Boulevard and SE Navy Avenue, said he was home around 6 p.m. Sunday when he noticed debris through his window. He took cover with his dogs in his bedroom and had about 10 seconds to react before the storm hit. His patio furniture was submerged in his pool, his pool fence was blown toward his home, and debris was scattered across his yard. Christiansen, originally from Minnesota, said his experience with tornado-like weather helped him know what precautions to take. He and his family and pets were not injured. Christiansen said he received the emergency alert after the storm had already hit and plans to begin cleanup efforts Monday and have his roof inspected.

hero.headline: Indian River County Sheriff credits Flock Safety cameras in Vero Beach homicide arrest, sparking privacy debate
hero.body:
Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers credited Flock Safety license plate reader cameras with leading to an arrest in a Vero Beach homicide case. Flowers said the system, a nationwide network of cameras connected to a searchable law enforcement database, played a key role in tracking a suspect to a West Virginia motel after what he described as a cold-blooded murder that triggered a multi-state manhunt.

Many residents welcomed the technology's role in catching a suspected killer. Larry, a Treasure Coast resident, said he thinks it is a good thing if the community can keep criminals out of their lives. Meghan Ford, a Treasure Coast visitor, said she sees value in the system for serious cases. "I think it's great for finding people that have committed horrible crimes, maybe missing children, I think it's a great idea to do that," Ford said.

Some community members expressed concern about privacy as the system's use expands. "We don't have that much privacy anymore, so where do you draw the line?" Michael Maslak, a Stuart resident, said. Ford echoed that tension, saying she feels it is a little invasion of privacy for those doing the right thing in life.

Recent reports indicate some officers have misused the Flock Safety system to track romantic partners, fueling controversy around the technology. In response, Flock Safety announced changes requiring searches to include a case number and mandating that all agencies use a new audit system designed to flag suspicious activity. Maslak said the key is keeping the technology in check and under control.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce police identify suspect in South 14th Street homicide from July
hero.body:
Fort Pierce police identified a suspect in a deadly shooting that occurred July 5 on South 14th Street. The Fort Pierce Police Department announced that 28-year-old Cornelius Trevon Ivory was identified as the suspect in the homicide and faces charges of first-degree murder, attempted first-degree murder, possession of a firearm and possession of a firearm by a convicted felon.

The shooting happened at about 3:43 a.m. on July 5. A 28-year-old woman sustained a non-life-threatening injury to her hand, while a 28-year-old man sustained multiple gunshot wounds and was transported to a local hospital. The police department announced on July 7 that the man died from his injuries.

An initial investigation revealed that the victims were involved in an earlier altercation at the 5800 block of Okeechobee Road before returning to their residence. As the victims arrived home, a man not believed to be involved in the altercation on Okeechobee Road approached them and fired a weapon before leaving the area. Detectives developed probable cause for Ivory's arrest through an investigation that included eyewitness accounts, information from community members, law enforcement databases and assistance from the Palm Bay Police Department.

Fort Pierce Police obtained an arrest warrant charging Ivory in connection with the killing. Authorities said he was served with an arrest warrant while in the St. Lucie County Jail involving possession of weapon by a convicted felon on July 24. Ivory remains in the jail, and his first appearance in the latest case was Friday. Investigators credited members of the public who came forward with information during the case, as well as the Palm Bay Police Department for assisting in the investigation.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie man charged with five counts of sexual activity with a minor
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie police arrested a 48-year-old man Thursday morning after SWAT officers executed a search warrant at his home on Southwest Jaslo Avenue.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie police arrested 48-year-old Virgil Jason Vinz without incident around 6 a.m. Thursday at a residence in the 900 block of Southwest Jaslo Avenue. The Port St. Lucie Police Department's SWAT team executed the warrant. Vinz is charged with five counts of sexual activity with a minor, a second-degree felony under Florida law, and six counts of contributing to the delinquency or dependency of a child, a first-degree misdemeanor.

The SWAT response drew attention from neighbors, several of whom reported hearing loud booms before seeing officers outside the home. Police spokesperson Brandon Martinez said the sounds were not gunshots but Noise Flash Diversionary Devices used during the SWAT team's entry into the home. Martinez said the devices are used for the safety of both officers and individuals when conducting high-risk operations.

Court records show Vinz pleaded no contest and was adjudicated guilty in 2023 on charges of battery on a law enforcement officer and contributing to the delinquency of a child. Records also show he later violated probation before completing Mental Health Court in October 2024. Jail records show Vinz remained in the St. Lucie County Jail as of Thursday night, with bond pending.

cards.headline: Disciplined St. Lucie County firefighters challenge investigation as residents call for reinstatement
cards.teaser: Three terminated St. Lucie County Fire District firefighters and community members questioned the integrity of a hazing investigation at a district meeting, calling for accountability and reinstatement.
cards.body:
Three terminated St. Lucie County Fire District firefighters and community members urged the district to reinstate the disciplined firefighters at a meeting Wednesday, alleging the investigation into hazing incidents was limited and mischaracterized. The fire district disciplined five firefighters following an independent investigation into alleged hazing incidents after videos surfaced that appeared to show the firefighters administering electric shocks to newer employees. Three firefighters were terminated.

Jordan Hutchinson, one of the terminated firefighters, said the firefighters were held accountable and that district leadership needs to be held accountable as well. The former firefighters are calling the disciplinary action retaliation for filing complaints against district leadership. Many residents at the meeting argued that the investigation produced a limited report, with some allegations reviewed internally and others by independent investigators.

A motion was made at the meeting to suspend the district chief and attorney, but the vote failed 4-1. The dispute has now moved to arbitration.

Authorities have not said what evidence was recovered from the home or what prompted the investigation and say they are limited in what they can discuss while the case remains active. "As a father of three myself, we take it very serious anytime there is a child involved," Martinez said. Martinez said officers are familiar with Vinz from previous encounters but emphasized the current case is separate from any prior incidents. Court records show Vinz pleaded no contest and was adjudicated guilty in 2023 on charges of battery on a law enforcement officer and contributing to the delinquency of a child. Records also show he later violated probation before completing Mental Health Court in October 2024. hero.headline: Multi-million dollar crane crashes off 90th Avenue in Vero Beach
hero.teaser: A six-axle crane went off the road and flipped on 90th Avenue near Oslo Road on August 19. Residents say the crash highlights road safety concerns they have been raising with the county for months.
hero.body:
Crews are working to pull a multi-million dollar, six-axle crane out of a ditch along 90th Avenue near Oslo Road in Vero Beach after it went off the road and flipped on August 19. The stretch of 90th Avenue between 4th Street and Oslo Road will be closed until the truck is removed.

Sally Rogers, who lives down the road from where the crane came to rest, said this is not the first crash she has seen on the narrow stretch of road. She said crews closed 82nd Avenue and rerouted traffic for the Oslo Road project, and drivers looking for a fast route to State Road 60 and I-95 found 90th Avenue instead. Rogers said dump trucks and semi trucks have learned this is a quick, straight shot to 60 to get on 95.

Rogers said dump trucks are not supposed to be using this route under the project's haul route plan. She also raised concerns about a bridge at 4th Street, saying she has not seen a posted weight limit and does not know whether it can handle heavier commercial traffic. Rogers said she has asked Indian River County to conduct a traffic study on the road and wants county officials to come see the road for themselves. County officials say they are looking into the matter. FDOT confirmed that this stretch of 90th Avenue is maintained by Indian River County.

She said August 19th was when she first noticed the crane in the ditch. She drives this stretch of 90th Avenue constantly. "Every single day," Rogers said, when asked how often she travels the road. She said she has driven it for 11 years. Rogers said this is not the first crash she has seen on this stretch of road, which she describes as narrow. She said she does not know for certain what caused each past crash, but she believes the road itself is part of the problem. See also: 'Disgusting and shameful': Lantana mayor condemns vandalism at police memorial Rogers pointed to a recent detour as the reason commercial trucks are on this road at all. She said crews closed 82nd Avenue and rerouted traffic for the Oslo Road project , and drivers looking for a fast route to State Road 60 and I-95 found this road instead. "The dump trucks and the semi trucks have learned that this is a thruway to 60 to get on 95," Rogers said. "It's quick, it's easy, it's a straight shot." Rogers said there is no signage warning drivers the road narrows, and she said dump trucks are not supposed to be using this route at all under the project's haul route plan. She said trucks were assigned to 82nd Avenue, and only started coming this way once that road closed. Rogers also raised concerns about a bridge at 4th Street, saying she has not seen a posted weight limit and doesn't know whether it can structurally handle the heavier commercial traffic now crossing it. She described another hazard when it rains. Water pools on the low side of the road and has nowhere to drain, she said, which hides what's underneath. "You don't know if there's a hole. You don't know if there's a soft spot. You don't know if there's a washout happening," Rogers said. Rogers said the traffic has made her change her own driving habits. When she sees a truck or semi approaching on the narrower sections, she said she pulls over and waits. "I stopped on the bridge, pulled off on the side there at 4th Street and waited for the semi to come and pass, because I know it's not wide enough to comfortably pass," Rogers said. "I'd rather not." She recounted a close call involving her husband, who was driving his Dodge 3500 dually when he passed another truck pulling a trailer on the road. "The trailers actually touched," Rogers said. Rogers said she has asked Indian River County to conduct a traffic study on the road. She said the response so far has been noncommittal. "Maybe we'll do that, but I think right now we should wait," Rogers said the county told her. Her request now is simple: she wants county officials to come see the road for themselves. They need to lay eyes on it," Rogers said. Bring a county dump truck to go the opposite direction, and pass the county dump truck in the narrowest part of the road." Crews remain on scene working to remove the crashed crane. CBS12 News is asking the county if they plan on adding signage or directing trucks to go a different route. County officials say they're looking into the matter. hero.headline: Publix removes 10-item limit from express checkout lanes across Florida stores
hero.body:
Publix is removing the 10-item limit at its express checkout lanes across its nearly 1,500 stores in the Southern United States, including locations throughout Florida. The grocery chain said in a statement that the change is intended to improve checkout efficiency and reduce wait times at checkout.

The change is already underway at many stores and will soon expand to all Publix locations. The company made the announcement Saturday as it continues to compete in a crowded grocery market across the Southeast.

According to the American Customer Satisfaction Index, Publix ranked as the nation's No. 2 grocery store chain in 2026, behind Trader Joe's. The retailer operates stores across the Southern United States, with a significant presence in Florida where the company is headquartered.

The elimination of the item limit represents a shift in the company's checkout strategy. Express lanes have traditionally been reserved for customers with a small number of items to allow for faster transactions. Publix stated the new policy is designed to reduce overall wait times, though the company did not provide details on how removing the limit would achieve that goal or whether the lanes would retain the express designation.

cards.headline: Indian River County creates Attainable Housing Trust to support development
cards.teaser: The Indian River County Commission voted unanimously August 4 to approve a landmark Attainable Housing Trust that will operate under the guidelines of the State Housing Initiatives Partnership program and will encourage the use of surplus county-owned lands to more effectively support attainable housing developments in the county.
cards.body:
The Indian River County Commission voted unanimously August 4 to approve a landmark Attainable Housing Trust that will operate under the guidelines of the State Housing Initiatives Partnership program and will encourage the use of surplus county-owned lands to more effectively support attainable housing developments in the county. Previously on May 27, the members of the Affordable Housing Advisory Committee voted unanimously to recommend the County Commission approve the draft ordinance. County SHIP Administrator Siphi Chinyanganya provided a comprehensive review of the proposal that morning.

The Attainable Housing Trust is a separate fund from the SHIP local housing assistance program, but aligns with SHIP-based practices. It will be administered by the SHIP administrator but will maintain independent accounting and compliance. The SHIP administrator plans to seek Attainable Housing Trust funding from voluntary developer contributions, proceeds from the sale or disposition of county-owned property, grants, donations and interlocal contributions, private philanthropy donations and interest earnings on the trust fund balance itself. The Trust has safeguards including recorded affordability covenants, income limits and compliance requirements and long-term affordability protections. This will be a 50-year lien so that it remains affordable and developers will be responsible for ongoing compliance following conveyance.

Chairman Deryl Loar said the Trust is another tool for the county's toolbox. It is a trust that allows us, like other counties and municipalities, to have a mechanism in place, he said. District 2 Commissioner Joseph Flescher made a motion for approval, which Commissioner Joseph Earman seconded. The motion then passed unanimously.
cards.article_text: Chairman Deryl Loar VERO BEACH – The Indian River County Commission voted unanimously Aug. 4 to approve a landmark Attainable Housing Trust that will operate under the guidelines of the State Housing Initiatives Partnership program and will encourage the use of surplus county-owned lands to more effectively support attainable housing developments in the county. Previously on May 27, the members of the Affordable Housing Advisory Committee voted unanimously to recommend the County Commission approve the draft ordinance. County SHIP Administrator Siphi Chinyanganya provided a comprehensive review of the proposal that morning. “We’re going to explain what the Attainable Housing Trust is and we’re hoping the ordinance will be approved today,” she said. “It supports affordable and attainable housing development. The ordinance establishes the Trust focused on land acquisition, land banking and partnerships with for-profit and non-profit organizations. We’re going to look at the legal framework, the ordinance overview and the implementation process of the Trust.” Chinyanganya first pointed out the distinction between the Attainable Housing Trust and the traditional SHIP program that provides local governments funding for affordable housing. “This is a separate fund from the SHIP local housing assistance program, but it aligns with SHIP-based practices,” she explained. “It will be administered by the SHIP administrator but will maintain independent accounting and compliance. So, while the SHIP program operates under the local housing assistance plan, the trust fund would maintain separate accounting compliance and reporting requirements. The purpose of this fund is to have affordable housing recognized as a public purpose authorized under Section 125-379 of Florida Statutes, which encourages counties to identify and use surplus county-owned lands for affordable housing.” The SHIP administrator plans to seek Attainable Housing Trust funding from voluntary developer contributions, proceeds from the sale or disposition of county-owned property, grants, donations and interlocal contributions, private philanthropy donations and even interest earnings on the trust fund balance itself. She emphasized the formal county hierarchy that will oversee all facets of attainable housing development under the AHT. “At the top of the Trust will be the Board of County Commissioners [with] final authority,” she continued. “The Community Services Department will administrate the program and coordinate any events. The Affordable Housing Advisory Committee will provide an advisory role; Planning Development will review and assess properties to be acquired; and finance, county administration and the county attorney will have oversight. The SHIP administrator will develop and publish a request for qualifications to create a register of development partners. The AHAC will review the RFQ and make recommendations for eligible development partners to the BOCC, and then the BOCC will approve the eligible development partners added to the register.” As far as the disposition of properties, the Planning Development Department will first evaluate the location, zoning and infrastructural viability of each property to assess developmental feasibility. The county attorney’s office will then verify the title status and draft acquisition and conveyance language, as well as securing BOCC authorization to purchase or accept the property. Planning Development staff will subsequently classify the property as surplus and designate it for attainable housing. The SHIP administrator and Community Services staff will in turn present available properties to the AHAC. The AHAC will offer available properties to partners on the register in order of ranking. Procurement and the SHIP administrator will coordinate the property conveyance following BOCC approval. The Trust has been in safeguards for the county as well. “There will be recorded affordability covenants, income limits and compliance requirements and long-term affordability protections,” Chinyanganya explained. “This will be a 50-year lean so that it remains affordable [and] developers will be responsible for ongoing compliance following conveyance. It limits county exposure to land transactions and ensures legal and financial safeguards. We also have financial controls through a special revenue fund.” Chairman Deryl Loar offered his perspective at the conclusion of her presentation, which brought a few chuckles from the dais. “This is actually another tool for our toolbox,” he said. “It is a trust that allows us – like other counties and municipalities – to have a mechanism in place. For example, if Commissioner [Joseph] Earman, donates $100,000 for affordable housing when he retires, we will certainly accept it, put it in trust and it will be policed as we do the current SHIP program.” When no members of the public came forward to comment afterward, District 2 Commissioner Joseph Flescher made a motion for approval. “Commissioner Earman just said that I was retiring beforehand, so I want to set up my commitment as well and we’ll take a look at that,” he said as laughter again broke out in the Chambers. “Motion to approve.” Commissioner Earman seconded that motion, which then passed unanimously. cards.headline: Clear the Shelters waives adoption fees Saturday at Vero Beach animal shelter
cards.teaser: The Humane Society of Vero Beach and Indian River County teams up with NBCUniversal Local for the annual Clear the Shelters special adoption event Saturday, August 22, from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m.
cards.body:
The Humane Society of Vero Beach and Indian River County teams up with NBCUniversal Local for the annual Clear the Shelters special adoption event Saturday, August 22, from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. For one day only, adoption fees will be waived, making it easier than ever for families to welcome a new best friend into their lives. We have so many wonderful dogs and cats that deserve homes, and Clear the Shelters is the perfect way for families to discover them, said Nichola Redmond, HSVB Chief Executive Officer. With adoption fees waived, we hope everyone who visits the shelter finds their new fur baby to bring home.

HSVB, located at 6230 77th Street in Vero Beach, is filled with loving adult cats and dogs ready for second chances. For those unable to attend the August 22 event, the shelter will also waive adoption fees for available adult cats and dogs during the week of August 23-30. Since launching in 2015, Clear the Shelters has helped more than 1 million pets find homes nationwide. This year, Hills Pet Nutrition joins as a presenting sponsor, providing adoption kits at select shelters that include starter bags of Hills Science Diet food, coupons and other helpful supplies for new pet families.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce police identify suspect in July 5 homicide on South 14th Street
hero.body:
Fort Pierce police have identified 28-year-old Cornelius Trevon Ivory as the suspect in a July 5 homicide on South 14th Street and charged him with first-degree murder. The shooting occurred at approximately 3:43 a.m. when a man approached two victims at their residence and fired a weapon before leaving the area. A 28-year-old woman sustained a non-life-threatening injury to her hand, while a 28-year-old man suffered multiple gunshot wounds and was transported to a local hospital, where he died from his injuries on July 7.

Investigators determined the victims had been involved in an earlier altercation at the 5800 block of Okeechobee Road before returning to their residence. The shooter was not believed to be involved in the altercation on Okeechobee Road. Detectives developed probable cause for Ivory's arrest through an extensive investigation that included eyewitness accounts, information from community members, law enforcement databases, and assistance from the Palm Bay Police Department.

Ivory faces charges of first-degree murder, attempted first-degree murder, possession of a firearm, and possession of a firearm by a convicted felon. He was served with the arrest warrant while in the St. Lucie County Jail on July 24, where he was being held on unrelated charges involving possession of a weapon by a convicted felon. His first appearance in the homicide case was Friday.

Ivory remains in the St. Lucie County Jail. Investigators credited members of the public who came forward with information during the case. The investigation remains active, and anyone with additional information is encouraged to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department.

cards.headline: Terminated St. Lucie County firefighters challenge hazing investigation at district meeting
cards.teaser: Three fired St. Lucie County firefighters questioned the integrity of a hazing investigation at a district meeting Wednesday, calling the disciplinary action retaliation for filing complaints against leadership.
cards.body:
Three terminated St. Lucie County firefighters challenged the investigation that led to their firing at a St. Lucie County Fire District meeting Wednesday, alleging the probe into hazing incidents was limited and mischaracterized. The fire district disciplined five firefighters following an independent investigation into alleged hazing incidents after videos surfaced that appeared to show the firefighters administering electric shocks to newer employees. Three firefighters were terminated.

Jordan Hutchinson, one of the terminated firefighters, said at the meeting that the disciplinary action was retaliation for filing complaints against district leadership. Many residents argued that the investigation produced a limited report, with some allegations reviewed internally and others by independent investigators. Community members urged the district to reinstate the disciplined firefighters.

A motion was made at the meeting to suspend the district chief and attorney, but the vote failed 4-1. The dispute has now moved to arbitration.

hero.headline: Martin County deputy stops $600,000 gold bar scam targeting senior
hero.teaser: A Martin County senior nearly lost his life savings of $600,000 to a gold bar scam before a sheriff's deputy intervened and stopped the transaction.
hero.body:
A Martin County senior nearly lost $600,000 in a gold bar scam, but was able to get his money returned through the efforts of a Martin County Sheriff's Office deputy. The victim was told by someone claiming to represent the victim's financial institution that the victim's bank account was compromised and the safest way to protect his money was to back it up with gold. The victim was instructed to send $600,000, his life savings, to a legitimate gold vendor, where the gold would then be picked up by a third party driver and supposedly be delivered to the bank, according to a sheriff's office Facebook posting.

Martin County Sheriff's Office Deputy Sgt. Jasmaine McKinney arrived and spoke directly to the gold vendor and worked with the victim and the business to stop the transaction. The gold had not yet been picked up or shipped out. The vendor cooperated with law enforcement, canceled the transaction and helped ensure the victim's money was returned.

The victim confirmed this week that he had received a full refund of his $600,000.

According to a sheriff’s office Facebook posting, the victim was told by someone claiming to represent the victim’s financial institution that that victim’s bank account was compromised and the safest way to protect his money was to “back it up” with gold. hero.headline: St. Lucie Mets fall 6-3 to Lakeland Flying Tigers at Clover Park
hero.body:
The Lakeland Flying Tigers defeated the St. Lucie Mets 6-3 on Friday night at Clover Park in Port St. Lucie. The loss extended the Mets' losing streak to seven consecutive games and marked their 11th loss in the last 12 games. Lakeland scored the first four runs of the game before the Mets mounted a late rally.

Yovanny Rodriguez hit a solo home run to lead off the bottom of the seventh inning to cut the Mets deficit to 4-2. Aiden Robbins homered in the eighth inning off Jose Guzman to make it 4-3. Eli Serrano III followed with a double and advanced to third base on a fly out, but Guzman struck out Rodriguez looking to end the inning and strand Serrano III on third. The first two batters of the top of the ninth drew walks against Jonathan Jimenez and Miguel Mejias, and both runners scored on a ground ball error and sacrifice fly to extend the Lakeland lead to 6-3.

Dylan Carey went 3 for 4 with three singles in the loss. Bohan Adderley went 2 for 4 with a double. The Mets used seven pitchers. Starter Camden Lohman pitched a scoreless first inning. Nate Isler, the Mets 10th round draft pick out of Dartmouth, pitched the second inning and gave up three runs in his professional debut, surrendering a home run to Jude Warwick. Mets 14th round pick Zach Crotchfelt out of Troy made his professional debut in the third inning and retired the side in order with a strikeout. Jimenez pitched the longest outing, going 3.0 innings and being charged with one earned run.

Lakeland reliever Xiomer Guacache pitched 3.1 innings after a 1 hour and 18 minute rain delay to get the win. He allowed two runs on four hits. Lakeland starter Malachi Witherspoon struck out five in 3.0 scoreless innings. Guzman pitched the final two innings and was credited with his fifth save. The Mets now stand at 17-34 in the second half and 50-67 overall, while the Flying Tigers improved to 26-24 and 57-58. The teams play the fifth game of their series at Clover Park on Saturday, when the Mets will wear special jerseys to celebrate the 100th anniversary of St. Anastasias School in Fort Pierce. A postgame fireworks show is scheduled.

hero.headline: Field of Greens to open first Treasure Coast location in Port St. Lucie
hero.body:
Field of Greens will open its first Treasure Coast location Aug. 29 at 10400 SW Discovery Way in Port St. Lucie, serving salads, smoothies, wraps, bowls and plant-forward meals for breakfast and lunch. The Florida-based chain specializes in fresh, nutrient-rich dishes and scratch cooking.

The new location marks a milestone for the company. Founded in West Palm Beach in 2003, this will be the tenth Field of Greens location. Port St. Lucie is the company's first venture outside of Palm Beach County, according to Dan Morris, Field of Greens vice president. Morris said the community is seeing tremendous growth and represents an opportunity to bring the restaurant's fresh, healthy offerings to new audiences.

The menu includes soups, sandwiches, wraps, bowls, vegan options and cold-pressed juices. Prices at the North Palm Beach location range from $5 for a cup of soup to $14 for the Full of Life Salad, made with arugula, spinach, roasted chicken, quinoa, craisins, almonds, cherry tomato, mint, feta and basil honey. The restaurant also offers a children's menu and desserts.

Field of Greens plans to open additional locations next year in the Martin Downs Village Center plaza in Palm City, Avenir in Palm Beach Gardens and President Donald J. Trump International Airport. The Port St. Lucie location offers both counter service and takeout from 9 a.m. to close.

hero.headline: Vero Beach man arrested on attempted murder charge after birthday party assault
hero.body:
Collin Ryan Smith, 25, of the 4900 block of Corsica Square in Vero Beach, was arrested on July 17 on charges including attempted murder after a birthday party ended and no one would take him to a local bar. Indian River County Sheriff's deputies responded to a home in the 2400 block of 86th Drive in Vero Beach at about 1:49 a.m. on July 17 for a disturbance in progress.

Four people told deputies that Smith wanted someone to take him to a local bar as the party settled down. When no one offered, he started yelling and waking up people in the house. One woman told Smith to leave but he grabbed her hair and dragged her down a hallway into a kitchen where he got on top of her and began choking her until she was unconscious. Another woman told officers that when she came out of her room, Smith grabbed her by the hair, pulled her outside and threw her to the ground. A third woman said she saw Smith throw a woman into a ditch outside the house and when she tried to stop him, he hit her in the mouth and threw her to the ground. Smith then pressed her against the side of a car and pressed her neck, causing a restriction of blood flow to her head.

A man at the house intervened by fighting Smith off the three women. A neighbor said when he heard screaming, he went outside and saw Smith pick a woman up and slam her to the ground. Deputies found a bullet in one woman's bedroom, which she said fell out of Smith's pocket. Smith then left in a Ford pickup truck and was subsequently stopped in the 1400 block of 96 Street in Vero Beach.

Smith was booked into the Indian River County Jail on July 17 at 3:49 a.m. He was in the Indian River County Jail as of July 21 on no bond for possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon. He also faces $150,000 bond for attempted murder, $50,000 bond for two counts of battery by strangulation, $25,000 bond for aggravated battery, $5,000 bond for criminal mischief, and $5,000 bond each for DUI, driving while license suspended, refusal to submit to a DUI test, and possession of drug paraphernalia. Officers said Smith smelled of alcohol and refused to take a breathalyzer test. A glass smoking device was found in his pocket.

cards.teaser: A Sebastian man accused of fatally shooting a Vero Beach hairdresser was arrested Wednesday night by U.S. Marshals at a West Virginia motel. Sheriff Eric Flowers credited the department's license plate reader technology as critical to the rapid arrest.
cards.body:
Matthew Allen Waggle, 33, faces a first-degree murder charge in the death of Dawn Kriskewic, 52, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. Detectives are working to extradite Waggle from West Virginia to face charges locally. Deputies responded to a 911 call at approximately 8:41 a.m. Sunday reporting a woman in the roadway in the 500 block of 1st Street in Vero Beach. First responders found Kriskewic suffering from an apparent gunshot wound and immediately began life-saving measures. Kriskewic was transported to a trauma center where she was later pronounced dead.

Sheriff Eric Flowers said during a Thursday news conference that Waggle and Kriskewic were in an on-and-off relationship, and that the victim had recently ended things with the suspect. According to investigators, Waggle traveled by Greyhound bus from an unknown location to the Orlando area, then took an Uber ride directly to Kriskewic's Vero Beach home Sunday morning. Security footage captured Waggle walking to the residence, having a brief interaction with Kriskewic, shooting her and then leaving the scene. The sheriff said Waggle was at the location for approximately 10 to 15 minutes before fleeing the area after the shooting.

After the shooting, Waggle took another Uber back to Orlando, boarded a Greyhound bus to North Carolina, and ultimately traveled to a motel near Dunbar, West Virginia. Detectives determined that Waggle's ex-wife was making calls to a specific West Virginia motel, which helped lead authorities to his location. Marshals arrested Waggle at the motel Wednesday night. Flowers credited the department's license plate reader technology, including the Flock system, as critical to the rapid arrest. I'm not standing here four days later telling you about this guy being in custody in West Virginia, Flowers said. So, for everybody who wants to talk about how bad this system is, we got a murderer behind bars because of this.
cards.article_text: A Sebastian man accused of fatally shooting a Vero Beach hairdresser was arrested Wednesday night by U.S. Marshals at a West Virginia motel, ending a multi-state manhunt that began after the domestic violence homicide Sunday morning in Indian River County. Matthew Allen Waggle, 33, faces a first-degree murder charge in the death of Dawn Kriskewic, 52, according to the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office. Detectives are working to extradite Waggle from West Virginia to face charges locally. Deputies responded to a 911 call at approximately 8:41 a.m. Sunday reporting a woman in the roadway in the 500 block of 1st Street in Vero Beach. First responders found Kriskewic suffering from an apparent gunshot wound and immediately began life-saving measures, according to the sheriff’s office. Kriskewic was transported to a trauma center where she was later pronounced dead. Investigators classified her death as a domestic violence homicide. Sheriff Eric Flowers said during a Thursday news conference that Waggle and Kriskewic were in an on-and-off relationship, and that the victim had recently ended things with the suspect. “She had actually told her co-workers, ‘If he calls, if he shows up, I want nothing to do with him. Tell him, I’m not here,’” Flowers said. “She had broken things off with him, he had moved away and somehow she knew that he could potentially be coming to the area.” According to investigators, Waggle traveled by Greyhound bus from an unknown location to the Orlando area, then took an Uber ride directly to Kriskewic’s Vero Beach home Sunday morning. “You see that video of him walking, he was dropped off around the corner, he made his way in, we’ve got him on video, on Ring doorbells, on a variety of different security cameras,” Flowers said. The sheriff said Waggle was at the location for approximately 10 to 15 minutes before fleeing the area after the shooting. Security footage captured Waggle walking to the residence, having a brief interaction with Kriskewic, shooting her and then leaving the scene. After the shooting, Waggle took another Uber back to Orlando, boarded a Greyhound bus to North Carolina, and ultimately traveled to a motel near Dunbar, West Virginia, according to investigators. The sheriff’s office real-time crime center played a crucial role in tracking Waggle’s movements across state lines. Detectives determined that Waggle’s ex-wife was making calls to a specific West Virginia motel, which helped lead authorities to his location. Marshals arrested Waggle at the motel Wednesday night. His ex-wife was also taken into custody at the scene and is cooperating with investigators. “At this moment, we don’t have charges on her, but we are actively speaking with her,” Flowers said. Investigators said Waggle left the firearm used in the shooting and other evidence near the scene in Vero Beach. The gun was later determined to belong to Waggle’s ex-wife, according to the sheriff’s office. Flowers credited the department’s license plate reader technology, including the Flock system, as critical to the rapid arrest. “I’m not standing here four days later telling you about this guy being in custody in West Virginia,” Flowers said. “So, for everybody who wants to talk about how bad this system is, we got a murderer behind bars because of this.” The investigation moved from discovering Kriskewic’s body Sunday morning to making an arrest in West Virginia by Wednesday night — a timeline Flowers called “unbelievable police work.” Two Indian River County detectives were in West Virginia interviewing Waggle and his ex-wife at the time of Thursday’s announcement. Waggle will be extradited back to Indian River County to face the first-degree murder charge. Detectives are questioning her to determine what she knew about Waggle's plans. She is not currently facing any charges.

Detectives responded to a 911 call about a woman lying in the roadway at the 1st Street address on August 16. Waggle was found at the West Virginia motel about six miles west of Charleston.

cards.headline: Body camera video shows U.S. Marshals arrest Vero Beach murder suspect in West Virginia
cards.body:
The Indian River County Sheriff's Office released body camera footage showing U.S. Marshals arresting Matthew Waggle, wanted for the murder of his ex-girlfriend Dawn Kriskewic in Vero Beach, at a motel in West Virginia on Wednesday night. Kriskewic was shot to death in front of her home on First Street in Vero Beach last Sunday. The video captures officers shouting commands during the arrest, including "Get the (expletive) down!" and "Give me your hands!" as they placed Waggle in handcuffs.

Sheriff Eric Flowers said Kriskewic had told co-workers at her hair salon that if Waggle called or showed up, she wanted nothing to do with him and instructed them to tell him she was not there. "He murdered her in cold blood in the street," Flowers said. Investigators believe Waggle traveled to Vero Beach from Orlando using an Uber, stayed just long enough to kill Kriskewic, and then left town in another Uber.

Flowers explained at a news conference Thursday how investigators tracked Waggle to the West Virginia motel where he was arrested. Waggle currently remains in jail in West Virginia.

Authorities in Florida are working on extraditing Waggle back to Indian River County to face charges. The sheriff credited the department's Real Time Crime Center and Flock license plate cameras with helping locate Waggle.
