hero.headline: Fired St. Lucie County firefighters challenge hazing investigation at district meeting
hero.body:
Three firefighters terminated by St. Lucie County Fire District following an investigation into alleged hazing incidents appeared at a district meeting Wednesday to challenge the integrity of the investigation and call for their reinstatement. The firefighters were among five disciplined after an independent investigation into incidents that included videos appearing to show firefighters administering electric shocks to newer employees.

Jordan Hutchinson, one of the terminated firefighters, told the district board that the investigation was limited and mischaracterized. He and other former firefighters are calling the disciplinary action retaliation for filing complaints against district leadership. Community members urged the district to reinstate the firefighters at the meeting.

Many residents at the Wednesday meeting argued that the investigation produced a limited report, with some allegations reviewed internally and others by independent investigators. One resident asked the board to bring the firefighters home. A motion was made at the meeting to suspend the district chief and attorney, but the vote failed 4-1.

The dispute has now moved to arbitration. Hutchinson said the firefighters were held accountable and that district leadership needs to be held accountable as well.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County residents call for reinstatement of three fired firefighters at board meeting
cards.teaser: Nearly every public speaker at Wednesday's St. Lucie County Fire District Board meeting urged leaders to reinstate three firefighters terminated following a hazing investigation.
cards.body:
A St. Lucie County Fire District Board meeting Wednesday turned into a show of support for three firefighters who were fired following an investigation into hazing allegations, with nearly every public speaker urging district leaders to reinstate them. The packed meeting lasted about three hours. While board members spent part of the meeting discussing the district's upcoming budget, much of the public comment period focused on criticism of Fire Chief Jeff Lee and the controversy surrounding the firefighters' terminations.

Two of the terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin, addressed the board publicly for the first time since their firings. Both questioned the integrity of the investigation that led to the disciplinary action. The former firefighters alleged district leadership retaliated against them after they raised concerns with the Board of Commissioners and filed internal grievances months before they were fired. Fire Chief Jeff Lee said he has been trying for weeks to reinstate the terminated firefighters but is currently unable to do so.

The St. Lucie County Fire District fired the three senior firefighters and suspended two others last month over hazing allegations after videos surfaced showing rookie firefighters being shocked with a modified bug zapper. During the meeting, a motion was made to suspend both Fire Chief Lee and the district's attorney, but the motion failed. The dispute is now in arbitration. Fire Board Chair and Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin was absent from Wednesday's meeting.
cards.article_text: Lucie County Fire District Board meeting turned into a show of support for three firefighters who were fired following an investigation into hazing allegations, with nearly every public speaker urging district leaders to reinstate them. The packed meeting lasted about three hours Wednesday. While board members spent part of the meeting discussing the district's upcoming budget, much of the public comment period focused on criticism of Fire Chief Jeff Lee and the controversy surrounding the firefighters' terminations. Several speakers called on the board to bring the terminated firefighters back. "I'm asking you respectfully to bring these firefighters home," one speaker told the board. Others questioned the district's handling of the investigation. "I think you've made a mockery of these three men," another speaker said. "It seems like you retaliated against these guys." See also: Deputies arrest man, 27, accused of traveling to meet 14-year-old in Hallandale Beach Another commenter said to the chief, "I don't know how you sleep at night." Last month, the St. Lucie County Fire District fired three senior firefighters and suspended two others over hazing allegations after videos surfaced showing rookie firefighters being shocked with a modified bug zapper. Two of the terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin, addressed the board publicly for the first time since their firings. Both questioned the integrity of the investigation that led to the disciplinary action. "We were held accountable. They need to be held accountable," Hutchinson said. The former firefighters alleged district leadership retaliated against them after they raised concerns with the Board of Commissioners and filed internal grievances months before they were fired. "There is absolutely a culture problem, and ultimately we were trying to address a problem, and in doing so this is what's happened to us," Baldwin said. Fire Chief Jeff Lee also addressed the crowd, saying he has been trying for weeks to reinstate the terminated firefighters but is currently unable to do so. "For anybody to assume, or make assumption that I don't care about the people of this fire district, they're wrong," Lee said. Lee also acknowledged that the district does not currently have a formal process for handling internal complaints involving the fire chief. "I can't fix that problem. The board has to fix that problem," Lee said. Hutchinson and Baldwin said they want their jobs back but are not willing to withdraw their complaints against the fire district and the chief. "All we've been trying to do is make sure nobody else in this fire department ends up where we are right now," Hutchinson said. "We've been trying to fix the process the entire time, and even after being fired, we're still here today trying to fix the process." The dispute is now in arbitration. During the meeting, a motion was also made to suspend both Fire Chief Lee and the district's attorney, but the motion failed. Fire Board Chair and Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin was absent from Wednesday's meeting . Board members did not provide a reason for her absence. CBS12 reached out to Martin for comment but had not received a response.

cards.headline: Off-duty St. Lucie County deputy spots burglary suspect, leads to arrest near Port St. Lucie
cards.body:
An off-duty St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office deputy spotted and helped capture a suspected burglar Friday in the Spanish Lakes One community near Port St. Lucie. Herman Nettles, 44, was taken into custody on U.S. 1 after the deputy recognized him from an internal alert about burglaries in the 55-plus community.

Deputy Martinez-Delgado had been assigned to investigate the burglaries and attempted car burglaries earlier this week. Information about the case, including a photo of Nettles and a map showing the location of eight reported incidents, was shared with sheriff's office personnel. Two days later, the off-duty deputy noticed Nettles while she was driving and alerted responding deputies.

Nettles is being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on a charge of burglary of an unoccupied conveyance unarmed. Following the investigation, he will face a total of eight charges, including five counts of attempted burglary of an unoccupied conveyance unarmed and three counts of burglary of an unoccupied conveyance unarmed.

Sheriff Richard Del Toro said Deputy Martinez-Delgado's quick recognition and immediate action helped bring the suspect into custody. Robert Quinn, a Spanish Lakes resident, praised the deputy's attention to duty while off the clock.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce police identify suspect in deadly shooting day after Fourth of July
hero.body:
Fort Pierce Police Department identified Cornelius Trevon Ivory as the suspect in a shooting on South 14th Street that killed a 28-year-old man the day after the Fourth of July. Investigators obtained a warrant charging Ivory in connection with the shooting. Ivory was served with the warrant while in custody at the St. Lucie County Jail, where he is being held on unrelated charges.

The shooting occurred at about 3:43 a.m. on South 14th Street. When officers arrived, they found two victims suffering from gunshot wounds. A woman had been shot in the hand, while a 28-year-old man suffered multiple gunshot wounds.

The 28-year-old man was taken to a hospital, where he later died. Police announced the identification of Ivory as the suspect on Friday.

Ivory faces charges in connection with the shooting. He remains in the St. Lucie County Jail on both the new charges and the unrelated charges for which he was already in custody.

hero.headline: Florida TaxWatch releases county-by-county analysis of Amendment 3 property tax proposal
hero.body:
Florida TaxWatch launched an online resource center Friday to help voters understand Amendment 3, a property tax measure on the November ballot that would cut local property tax revenue by an estimated $45.8 billion over five years. The Florida Property Tax Resource Center includes an interactive county map, local millage rates, frequently asked questions and estimates showing potential revenue losses for local governments across the state.

Amendment 3 would expand Florida's homestead exemption for non-school property taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. School property taxes would remain unchanged. The proposal would also reduce the annual assessment-growth cap on non-homestead properties, including rental homes, second homes and commercial properties, from 10% to 5%. The measure must receive at least 60% support from voters to become part of the Florida Constitution.

Florida TaxWatch has not yet taken an official position on the amendment. President and CEO Jeff Kottkamp said the organization will announce its recommendation in a broader constitutional amendment guide expected next month. The new resource center does not include a calculator showing how much individual homeowners could save because cities and counties could respond to the revenue loss by cutting services, increasing millage rates or imposing new fees and special assessments, according to TaxWatch.

Opponents of the amendment argue the proposal would shift costs rather than eliminate them, potentially forcing communities to reduce spending on police, firefighters, emergency medical services, libraries and other local programs. Jackson Peel with Save Our Services said Amendment 3 is a scam and a tax shift that will either raise costs or take away services Floridians rely on. The ballot summary was recently rewritten after a Leon County judge found the Legislature's original wording biased and misleading. A private calculator created by Casey Vockell of My Exemption Check found that a Hillsborough County home assessed at $500,000 could save less than $209 per month by 2028, though the estimate does not account for any later decisions by local governments.

School property taxes would remain unchanged.The proposal would also reduce the annual assessment-growth cap on non-homestead properties from 10% to 5%. That category includes rental homes, second homes and commercial properties.The measure must receive at least 60% support from voters to become part of the Florida Constitution.TaxWatch has not yet taken an official position on the amendment. Kottkamp said the organization will announce its recommendation in a broader constitutional amendment guide expected next month.No personalized estimateOne feature missing from the new resource center is a calculator showing how much an individual homeowner could save.TaxWatch said such a figure would be too speculative because cities and counties could respond to the revenue loss by cutting services, increasing millage rates or imposing new fees and special assessments.However, a private calculator we previously featured allows homeowners to enter their taxable value and local millage rates to generate an estimate.The tool was created by Casey Vockell of My Exemption Check.“The impact to the local taxing authorities is going to be bad, but the benefit to the taxpayer is not going to be nearly as big as one might think,” Vockell said.In one example, the calculator found that a Hillsborough County home assessed at $500,000 could save less than $209 per month by 2028.The estimate does not account for any later decisions by local governments that could reduce or offset those savings.Opponents warn of service cutsThe amendment’s critics argue the proposal would shift costs rather than eliminate them, potentially forcing communities to reduce spending on police, firefighters, emergency medical services, libraries and other local programs.“The language on voters’ ballots may have changed, but that doesn’t change the fact that Amendment 3 is still a scam and a tax shift,” said Jackson Peel with Save Our Services. “That’s either going to raise our costs or take away services that Floridians rely on every day.”The ballot summary was recently rewritten after a Leon County judge found the Legislature’s original wording biased and misleading.

hero.headline: Vero Beach Table Tennis Club faces closure as owner seeks community support
hero.teaser: The Vero Beach Table Tennis Club is on the verge of closing due to unpaid rent and utilities combined with financial difficulties from the pandemic.
hero.body:
Tyson McCoy, owner of the Vero Beach Table Tennis Club, said the club is facing closure due to unpaid rent and utilities, combined with financial difficulties during the pandemic. "The first four years here, it's been a rough battle," McCoy said. McCoy said he worries about what closure would mean for his members and others who rely on the club.

Member Daniel Freedman has been coming to the club for three years and said keeping it open is a priority. "We have to do whatever we can to make sure that this club stays open," Freedman said. Fellow member Cielo Galman said the club has built something rare. "Table tennis has a very strong social culture," Galman said. "They're like a second family to me."

McCoy created a GoFundMe to help support the club. The community has already donated $2,400. "I'm not much of a crier, but it definitely brings a tear to my eye that we have so many supporters that feel about this club the way that I do," McCoy said.

cards.headline: Multi-million dollar crane crashes off 90th Avenue in Vero Beach as residents raise traffic concerns
cards.teaser: Crews are working to pull a six-axle crane out of a ditch along 90th Avenue near Oslo Road in Vero Beach after it went off the road and flipped on August 19.
cards.body:
Crews are still working to pull a multi-million dollar, six-axle crane out of a ditch along 90th Avenue near Oslo Road in Vero Beach, after it went off the road and flipped on August 19. For people who live nearby, the crash is the latest example of a problem they say they've been warning the county about for months. Sally Rogers lives down the road from where the crane came to rest and said she has driven this stretch of 90th Avenue constantly for 11 years.

Rogers said this is not the first crash she has seen on this stretch of road, which she describes as narrow. She pointed to a recent detour as the reason commercial trucks are on this road at all. She said crews closed 82nd Avenue and rerouted traffic for the Oslo Road project, and drivers looking for a fast route to State Road 60 and I-95 found this road instead. "The dump trucks and the semi trucks have learned that this is a thruway to 60 to get on 95," Rogers said. "It's quick, it's easy, it's a straight shot."

Rogers said there is no signage warning drivers the road narrows, and she said dump trucks are not supposed to be using this route at all under the project's haul route plan. She said she has asked Indian River County to conduct a traffic study on the road. County officials say they're looking into the matter. FDOT confirmed that this stretch of 90th Avenue between 4th Street and Oslo Road is maintained by Indian River County and will be closed until the truck is removed.

She said she has driven it for 11 years. Rogers said this is not the first crash she has seen on this stretch of road, which she describes as narrow. She said she does not know for certain what caused each past crash, but she believes the road itself is part of the problem. See also: 'Disgusting and shameful': Lantana mayor condemns vandalism at police memorial Rogers pointed to a recent detour as the reason commercial trucks are on this road at all. She said crews closed 82nd Avenue and rerouted traffic for the Oslo Road project , and drivers looking for a fast route to State Road 60 and I-95 found this road instead. "The dump trucks and the semi trucks have learned that this is a thruway to 60 to get on 95," Rogers said. "It's quick, it's easy, it's a straight shot." Rogers said there is no signage warning drivers the road narrows, and she said dump trucks are not supposed to be using this route at all under the project's haul route plan. She said trucks were assigned to 82nd Avenue, and only started coming this way once that road closed. Rogers also raised concerns about a bridge at 4th Street, saying she has not seen a posted weight limit and doesn't know whether it can structurally handle the heavier commercial traffic now crossing it. She described another hazard when it rains. Water pools on the low side of the road and has nowhere to drain, she said, which hides what's underneath. "You don't know if there's a hole. You don't know if there's a soft spot. You don't know if there's a washout happening," Rogers said. Rogers said the traffic has made her change her own driving habits. When she sees a truck or semi approaching on the narrower sections, she said she pulls over and waits. "I stopped on the bridge, pulled off on the side there at 4th Street and waited for the semi to come and pass, because I know it's not wide enough to comfortably pass," Rogers said. "I'd rather not." She recounted a close call involving her husband, who was driving his Dodge 3500 dually when he passed another truck pulling a trailer on the road. "The trailers actually touched," Rogers said. Rogers said she has asked Indian River County to conduct a traffic study on the road. She said the response so far has been noncommittal. "Maybe we'll do that, but I think right now we should wait," Rogers said the county told her. Her request now is simple: she wants county officials to come see the road for themselves. They need to lay eyes on it," Rogers said. Bring a county dump truck to go the opposite direction, and pass the county dump truck in the narrowest part of the road." Crews remain on scene working to remove the crashed crane. CBS12 News is asking the county if they plan on adding signage or directing trucks to go a different route. County officials say they're looking into the matter. hero.headline: Florida Tax Watch launches online tool showing county-by-county impact of Amendment 3 property tax measure
hero.body:
Florida Tax Watch has launched a Property Tax Resource Center that allows voters to see how Amendment 3 would affect property taxes in each of Florida's counties and municipalities before the November election. The online tool provides a breakdown of the proposed property tax measure's projected five-year impact across the state.

Amendment 3 would expand the homestead exemption to $250,000 by 2028, which could reduce local property taxes by nearly $46 billion over five years statewide. The amendment requires 60% voter approval to pass. The Florida Tax Watch website features a state map where users can highlight any county to view projected impacts for each fiscal year. The tool also allows users to click through to see the impact on individual municipalities within each county.

Each county receives rankings in different categories through the tool. St. Lucie County ranks first in the state for millage and 16th in per capita property tax levies. The online resource includes data for counties across Florida, including Palm Beach, St. Lucie, Martin, Indian River and Okeechobee.

Palm Beach County plans to launch its own online tool in September where homeowners can calculate the direct impact the amendment would have on their individual property taxes. Palm Beach County Property Appraiser Dorothy Jacks said the tool will give taxpayers a clear, personal picture of what a yes vote would mean for them. Jacks said she wants to convey to taxpayers the exact number they would continue to pay in addition to what they would save on the homestead exemption increase. Several other Florida counties have similar online tools available.

hero.headline: Woman surrenders 36 Border Collies rescued from Palm City hoarding case
hero.teaser: Paige O'Donnell has legally surrendered the 36 Border Collies rescued from her Palm City home, clearing the way for the dogs to be adopted starting in September.
hero.body:
Paige O'Donnell has legally surrendered the 36 Border Collies rescued from her Palm City home, the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast confirmed Friday. Staff will complete thorough medical testing and evaluations so adopters receive clear information about any long-term needs before placement decisions are made. The dogs also will be prepared for spay and neuter services, microchipping and vaccinations on a phased schedule.

Adoption applications will be available on the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast's website and Facebook page beginning in September. Applicants will be highly vetted to ensure appropriate matches, and applications for 501(c)(3) rescue groups also will be available beginning Sept. 1. To keep phone lines available for urgent shelter needs and services, the shelter is asking the public not to call about the Border Collies at this time.

O'Donnell faces 72 charges in what the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast calls the worst animal hoarding case it has ever seen. The dogs were rescued from her hoarded home in Palm City earlier this month. Deputies found the dogs living in deplorable conditions, with fur matted with feces and debris. We shaved 9 pounds off of one dog filled with feces and urine, Sarah Fisher, spokesperson for the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, said. Fisher said some dogs arrived with metal and glass fragments trapped in their fur.

The dogs also will be prepared for spay/neuter services, microchipping and vaccinations on a phased schedule alongside animals already in the shelter’s care.Adoption applications will be available here and the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast's Facebook page beginning Sept. Applicants will be highly vetted to ensure appropriate matches, and applications for 501(c)(3) rescue groups also will be available beginning Sept. 1.To keep phone lines available for urgent shelter needs and services, the shelter is asking the public not to call about the Border Collies at this time.WATCH BELOW: Healing begins for animals rescued in Martin County hoarding casesO'Donnell faces 72 charges in what the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast calls the worst animal hoarding case it has ever seen. The dogs were rescued from her hoarded home in Palm City earlier this month. A WPTV investigation helped renew the sheriff's office probe into the case.Deputies found the dogs living in deplorable conditions, with fur matted with feces and debris. Court documents show O'Donnell exhibited deceptive behavior during the investigation, blaming strong odors on "missed trash collection" and "old seafood."The rescued Border Collies underwent what shelter staff call "medical grooming," a process that involves carefully shaving severely matted fur while checking for injuries and infections underneath."We shaved 9 pounds off of one dog filled with feces and urine," Sarah Fisher, spokesperson for the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, said.Fisher previously told WPTV that some dogs arrived with metal and glass fragments trapped in their fur. During the initial rescue, she said staff found "lots of pieces of metal — rusted metal, sharp metal — that have been stuck in their fur, along with shards of glass."WATCH BELOW: Deputies describe 'the filth' involved in rescuing 36 neglected dogsThe Humane Society of the Treasure Coast says many of the rescued animals are already beginning to heal.Cesar Perea, associate vice president of rescue for American Humane Society, said the emotional and physical recovery process for animals often begins quickly once they are removed from dangerous conditions."As soon as you start providing care, you immediately start to see the animal's personality come out," Perea said. "When they were in that situation, they were completely shut down."Perea said trauma in rescued animals can appear as emotional shutdown, inactivity and fear, but he has seen dramatic turnarounds in many hoarding cases across the country."Within two weeks, you wouldn't even recognize that animal," Perea said. "They start getting a little more active and joyful. They start behaving like the pets that they're meant to be."WATCH BELOW: 'Worst case we've ever seen': Humane Society caring for 36 rescued dogsPerea said animal hoarding can still qualify as criminal neglect under the law when animals are denied proper veterinary care, food or safe living conditions. He said communities should watch for several warning signs that animal hoarding may be occurring nearby."The smell will probably be your first indicator," Perea said. "If you see a lot of animals, more animals than you usually see people having as pets, that's also a big indicator."Perea said the situation can escalate when people feel compassion for animals but lack the resources to properly care for them."It becomes overwhelming very quickly when people feel that compassion to want to help animals, but then they don't have the resources or the ability to continue to manage and provide a level of care that's acceptable," Perea said.The case has prompted legislative action from State Rep. hero.headline: Florida Tax Watch launches online tool showing Amendment 3 property tax impact by county
hero.teaser: Florida Tax Watch launched a Property Tax Resource Center that breaks down the proposed property tax measure by county and municipality, including St. Lucie, Martin, and Indian River counties.
hero.body:
Florida Tax Watch launched a Property Tax Resource Center that allows voters to see the projected impact of Amendment 3 on property taxes by county and municipality across the state. Amendment 3 would expand the homestead exemption to $250,000 by 2028, which could cut local property taxes by nearly $46 billion over five years. The amendment needs 60% support to pass in November.

The website allows users to navigate to a state map, highlight any county, and see the projected five-year impact of Amendment 3 along with totals for each fiscal year. Users can also click through to see the impact on individual municipalities within each county. St. Lucie County ranks first in the state for millage and 16th in per capita property tax levies.

Palm Beach County is launching its own online tool in September where homeowners can see the direct impact the amendment would have on their individual property taxes. Palm Beach County Property Appraiser Dorothy Jacks said the tool is designed to give taxpayers a clear, personal picture of what a yes vote would mean for them. The online tool includes data for Palm Beach, St. Lucie, Martin, Indian River and Okeechobee counties.
